chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXIX
paragraphs:
“If you have heard a word, let it die with you.”
—_Ecclesiasticus_.

At about three that afternoon, on the same day he had received Lydgate, Mr. Bulstrode was still in his manager’s room at the bank. A clerk came in to tell him that his horse was ready and that Mr. Garth was outside, asking to speak to him.
“Certainly,” said Bulstrode, and Caleb came in. “Please take a seat, Mr. Garth,” the banker added in his most agreeable voice.
“I’m glad you caught me before I left. I know your time is valuable.”
“Oh,” Caleb said quietly, slowly inclining his head as he sat down and put his hat on the floor.

He leaned forward, looking at the ground, his long fingers hanging between his knees. One finger after another moved, as if each were taking part in the thought that occupied his broad, calm forehead.

Like everyone who knew Caleb, Mr. Bulstrode was accustomed to his slow beginnings whenever he had something important to say. He rather expected another proposal to buy some houses in Blindman’s Court and knock them down: the air and light admitted to the spot would amply repay the loss of property. Caleb sometimes troubled his employers with schemes of this kind, but Bulstrode had generally supported his improvements, and the two had worked well together. When Caleb spoke again, however, he said in a rather lowered voice—
“I’ve just been at Stone Court, Mr. Bulstrode.”
“I hope you found everything in order,” said the banker. “I was there yesterday myself. Abel has done well with the lambs this year.”
“Well, no,” said Caleb, looking up seriously. “Something is wrong. There’s a stranger there, and I think he’s very ill. He needs a doctor. That’s what I came to tell you. His name is Raffles.”
He saw the shock run through Bulstrode’s body. The banker had thought his fears on this subject were too constantly alert for anything to surprise him. He had been wrong.
“Poor soul!” he said compassionately, though his lips shook a little. “Do you know how he got there?”

“I brought him myself,” Caleb answered calmly. “I picked him up in my gig. He’d got off the coach and was walking just past the turning by the toll-house when I caught up with him. He remembered seeing me with you once at Stone Court and asked me to take him there. I could see he was ill. It seemed right to get him under a roof. And I think you ought to get medical advice for him without delay.” As he finished, Caleb picked up his hat and slowly rose.

“Of course,” said Bulstrode, whose thoughts were racing. “Perhaps you would be kind enough to call at Mr. Lydgate’s on your way, Mr. Garth—or wait! At this hour he may be at the hospital. I’ll send my man there on the horse with a note at once, and then ride to Stone Court myself.”

Bulstrode quickly wrote his note and went out to give the instructions himself. When he returned, Caleb was still standing with one hand on the chair back and his hat in the other. One thought dominated Bulstrode’s mind: “Perhaps Raffles only told Garth about his illness. Garth may wonder, as he must have wondered before, why this disreputable fellow claims to know me so well. But he’ll know nothing. And he’s well disposed towards me—I can help him.”
He longed for something to confirm that hopeful guess. But any question about what Raffles had said or done would reveal his fear.

“I’m extremely grateful, Mr. Garth,” he said with his usual politeness. “My servant will be back in a few minutes. Then I shall go and see what can be done for this unfortunate man. Was there anything else you wanted to discuss? If so, please sit down.”

“Thank you,” Caleb said, declining with a small movement of his right hand. “I have to ask you, Mr. Bulstrode, to put your business into someone else’s hands. You’ve treated me generously over the lease of Stone Court and everything else, and I’m grateful. But I must give it up.” Certainty pierced Bulstrode like a knife.
“This is very sudden, Mr. Garth,” was all he could say at first.
“It is,” Caleb answered. “But my mind is made up. I must give it up.”

His firmness was gentle, yet he could see Bulstrode shrinking beneath that gentleness. The banker’s face looked withered, and his eyes turned away from Caleb’s steady gaze. Caleb pitied him deeply. But he could not have invented excuses for his decision, even if excuses would have helped.
“I take it that some slanders from that unhappy creature have led you to this,” said Bulstrode, now desperate to know the full extent of the damage.
“Yes. I can’t deny that what he told me has made me act.”

“You are a man of conscience, Mr. Garth—a man who, I trust, knows he must answer to God. You wouldn’t want to hurt me by being too quick to believe a slander.” Bulstrode searched for arguments that might reach his listener. “That is a poor reason to end a relationship which, I think I can fairly say, benefits us both.”

“I wouldn’t hurt anyone if I could help it,” Caleb said, “even if I thought God would overlook it. I hope I’d still feel for another human being. But, sir, I can’t help believing that Raffles told me the truth. And I can’t be at peace working with you, or taking any benefit from you. It troubles my mind. I must ask you to find another agent.”

“Very well, Mr. Garth. But surely I’m entitled to know the worst of what he told you. I must know what vile accusations I may be exposed to.” Anger was beginning to mix with Bulstrode’s humiliation before this quiet man who refused his favors.

“There’s no need,” Caleb said, moving his hand and bowing his head a little. His voice still expressed his wish to spare this pitiable man. “Nothing he told me will pass my lips unless something I don’t yet know forces me to speak. If you harmed people for profit, and cheated them out of their rights to get more for yourself, I dare say you regret it. You’d like to go back, and you can’t. That must be bitter.” Caleb paused and shook his head. “It isn’t my place to make your life harder.”
“But you do—you do make it harder,” Bulstrode cried, driven into a sincere appeal. “You make it harder by turning your back on me.”

“That I have to do,” Caleb said still more gently, raising his hand. “I’m sorry. I’m not judging you and saying, he’s wicked and I’m righteous. God forbid. I don’t know everything. A man may do wrong and then want only what’s right, though he can’t get his life free of the wrong he’s done. That’s a hard punishment. If that’s your position, well, I’m very sorry for you. But there’s something inside me that won’t let me go on working with you. That’s all, Mr. Bulstrode. As far as I’m concerned, everything else stays buried. Good day to you.”

“One moment, Mr. Garth!” Bulstrode said quickly. “Then I have your solemn assurance that you will repeat to no one, man or woman, this malicious account—even if it contains some measure of truth?” Caleb’s anger rose, and he answered indignantly—
“Why would I say it if I didn’t mean it? I’m not afraid of you. Stories like that will never tempt me to talk.”
“Forgive me. I’m upset. I’m the victim of this depraved man.”
“Wait a moment! You need to ask yourself whether you didn’t help make him worse by profiting from his vices.”

“You’re wronging me by believing him so readily,” Bulstrode said. As in a nightmare, he found himself unable to deny outright whatever Raffles might have said. Yet it was a relief that Caleb had not stated the charges and demanded that outright denial.

“No,” Caleb said, raising a hand in protest. “I’m willing to believe better when there’s proof of better. I’m not taking any good chance away from you. And as for talking, I think it’s a crime to expose a man’s sin unless I’m sure it has to be done to protect innocent people. That’s how I see it, Mr. Bulstrode. I don’t need an oath to make my word good. Good day.”

Some hours later, at home, Caleb mentioned to his wife that he had had a few differences with Bulstrode. As a result, he had given up the idea of taking Stone Court and, in fact, had stopped doing any business for him.

“He wanted to interfere too much, did he?” Mrs. Garth asked. She supposed her husband had been touched at his most sensitive point: prevented from choosing the materials and ways of working he thought right.
“Oh,” Caleb said, gravely bowing his head and moving his hand. Mrs. Garth knew this meant he intended to say no more.
Bulstrode, meanwhile, had mounted almost at once and set off for Stone Court, eager to get there ahead of Lydgate.

His mind teemed with pictures and guesses that gave voice to his hopes and fears, just as vibrations passing through our whole bodies become the tones we hear. The deep humiliation of Caleb Garth’s knowing his past and rejecting his patronage alternated with, and almost yielded to, relief that Garth, of all people, was the one Raffles had spoken to. It seemed a promise that Providence meant to save him from worse consequences: there was still a chance of secrecy. Raffles was ill; he had been brought to Stone Court instead of somewhere else. Bulstrode’s heart fluttered at the possibilities these events opened up. If he were freed from all danger of disgrace—if he could breathe in complete freedom—he would devote his life more fully to God than ever. He offered up this vow inwardly as though it could hasten the outcome he desired. He tried to believe in the power of that prayerful resolve—its power to bring about a death. He knew he ought to say, “Your will be done,” and he said it often. But the fierce wish remained that God’s will might be the death of the man he hated.

Yet the change in Raffles shocked him when he reached Stone Court. Apart from the man’s pallor and weakness, Bulstrode would have thought the change entirely mental. Gone was his loud, tormenting manner. In its place was an intense, unfocused terror. He seemed anxious to appease Bulstrode’s anger because the money was gone—he’d been robbed—half of it had been taken. He had only come here because he was ill and someone was hunting him, someone was after him. He hadn’t told anyone anything; he’d kept his mouth shut. Bulstrode did not understand these symptoms. He saw the new nervousness as a chance to frighten Raffles into truthful admissions, and accused him of lying about his silence: he had just told everything to the man who picked him up in the gig and brought him to Stone Court. Raffles denied it with solemn oaths. In fact, the connections in his consciousness had broken down. His detailed, terror-filled account to Caleb Garth had come from a sequence of delusions that had now sunk back into darkness.

Bulstrode’s heart sank again. He could neither control this wretched man’s mind nor trust anything he said about the question that mattered most: had he really told no one else in the neighborhood besides Caleb Garth? The housekeeper, with no sign of embarrassment, said that after Mr. Garth left, Raffles had asked for beer. Since then he had said nothing and seemed very ill. Bulstrode could reasonably conclude that she had heard no disclosures. Like the servants at The Shrubs, Mrs. Abel supposed the stranger belonged to that troublesome sort of “kin” who plagued the rich. At first she had connected him with Mr. Rigg: wherever property had been left, the buzzing attendance of such large bluebottles seemed natural enough. How he could also be Bulstrode’s “kin” was less clear. But Mrs. Abel agreed with her husband that there was “no knowing.” That idea gave her mind plenty to feed on, and she shook her head over it without investigating further.
Lydgate arrived within the hour. Bulstrode met him outside the wood-paneled parlor where Raffles lay, and said—

“I’ve asked you to see an unfortunate man who worked for me many years ago. He later went to America and, I fear, returned to an idle and dissolute life. Since he is destitute, I have some obligation to him. He had a slight connection with Rigg, the former owner here, and that is how he found his way to this house. I believe he’s seriously ill. His mind seems affected. I feel bound to do everything I can for him.”

Lydgate vividly remembered his last conversation with Bulstrode and had no wish to say more than necessary. He answered with a slight bow. Just before entering the room, however, he turned automatically and asked, “What is his name?” Knowing names is as much a professional skill for a doctor as for a working politician.
“Raffles. John Raffles,” said Bulstrode, hoping that whatever happened to the man, Lydgate would never learn anything more about him.
After examining the patient thoroughly and considering his condition, Lydgate ordered him put to bed and kept as quiet as possible. He then went into another room with Bulstrode.
“A serious case, I imagine,” the banker said before Lydgate could speak.

“No—and yes,” Lydgate answered with some hesitation. “It’s hard to judge the possible effects of longstanding complications. But he began with a strong constitution. I wouldn’t expect this attack to kill him, though his system is certainly in a delicate state. He needs careful watching and attention.”
“I shall stay here myself,” Bulstrode said. “Mrs. Abel and her husband have no experience. I can easily spend the night, if you’ll take a note to Mrs. Bulstrode for me.”
“I hardly think that’s necessary,” said Lydgate. “He seems frightened and subdued enough. He might become harder to manage. But there’s a man here, isn’t there?”
“I’ve spent a few nights here more than once when I wanted quiet,” Bulstrode said casually. “I’m quite willing to do it now. Mrs. Abel and her husband can help me or take over if necessary.”
“Very well. Then I need only give the instructions to you,” said Lydgate, unsurprised by a little eccentricity in Bulstrode.
“Then you think he has a good chance?” Bulstrode asked when Lydgate had finished his directions.

“Yes, unless there are further complications that I haven’t yet detected,” Lydgate said. “He may grow worse, but I wouldn’t be surprised if he improved within a few days, provided my treatment is followed. You must be firm. Remember, if he asks for alcohol of any kind, don’t give it to him. In my view, men in this condition are killed more often by the treatment than by the disease. Still, new symptoms may develop. I’ll come again tomorrow morning.”

Lydgate waited for the note to Mrs. Bulstrode and then rode away. At first he made no guesses about Raffles’s past. Instead, he went over the whole debate about the right treatment for alcoholic poisoning of this kind, a debate recently revived by the publication of Dr. Ware’s extensive American experience. Lydgate had already taken an interest in the question while abroad. He strongly opposed the common practice of allowing alcohol and repeatedly giving large doses of opium, and had acted on that conviction several times with good results.

“The man is ill,” he thought, “but there’s plenty of life left in him. I suppose Bulstrode is helping him out of charity. Strange how hardness and tenderness sit side by side in people. Towards some people Bulstrode is the least sympathetic man I’ve ever met, yet he has taken endless trouble and spent a great deal on charitable work. I suppose he has a test for deciding whom Heaven cares about. He’s decided it doesn’t care about me.”

That bitterness sprang from a plentiful source and spread through his thoughts as he approached Lowick Gate. He had not been home since his first meeting with Bulstrode that morning; the banker’s messenger had found him at the hospital. For the first time, he was returning without any possible solution in reserve, any hope of raising enough money to save what made his married life bearable. Those things protected him and Rosamond from a stripped-bare existence in which they would have to recognize how little comfort they could give each other. Going without tenderness himself was easier to bear than knowing his own tenderness could not compensate her for the loss of other things. His pride suffered keenly from past humiliations and those still ahead. Yet even to him that pain was almost indistinguishable from the sharper one that overpowered it: the prospect of Rosamond seeing him chiefly as the cause of her disappointment and unhappiness. He had never liked the economies poverty demanded, nor imagined them as part of his future. Now he was beginning to picture two people who loved each other and shared a store of thoughts, laughing over their shabby furniture and their calculations about what they could afford for butter and eggs. But that glimpse of poetry was as remote from him as the carefree golden age. Poor Rosamond’s mind had no space wide enough to make luxuries look small. He dismounted in deep sadness and entered the house expecting nothing to cheer him but dinner. Before the evening ended, he thought, he ought to tell Rosamond that he had applied to Bulstrode and failed. He should waste no time preparing her for the worst.

But dinner stood waiting a long time before he could eat. On entering, he learned that Dover’s agent had already installed a man in the house. When he asked for Mrs. Lydgate, he was told she was in her bedroom. Upstairs he found her lying on the bed, pale and silent, with no response, even in her expression, to anything he said or any look he gave her. He sat beside the bed, leaned over her, and spoke in something close to a cry of prayer—
“Forgive me for making you so miserable, my poor Rosamond! Let us just love each other.”

She looked at him without speaking, the same blank despair on her face. Then tears filled her blue eyes and her lip began to tremble. The strong man had borne too much that day. He let his head fall beside hers and sobbed.

When she went to her father early next morning, he did not stop her. He now felt he ought to let her do as she wished. She returned half an hour later and said that her father and mother wanted her to stay with them while things were so wretched. Her father said he could do nothing about the debt: if he paid this one, half a dozen more would follow. She had better come home until Lydgate could provide a comfortable home for her. “Do you object, Tertius?”
“Do what you like,” Lydgate said. “But we haven’t reached the crisis yet. There’s no need to hurry.”
“I wouldn’t leave before tomorrow,” Rosamond replied. “I’ll need to pack my clothes.”
“Oh, I’d wait a little beyond tomorrow. You never know what may happen,” Lydgate said with bitter irony. “I might break my neck, and that could make things easier for you.”

It was a misfortune for both Lydgate and Rosamond that his tenderness towards her, prompted by feeling as well as deliberate resolve, kept giving way to these bursts of anger, sometimes sarcastic, sometimes reproachful. She thought them wholly unjustified. The revulsion caused by those moments of harshness threatened to make even his more constant tenderness unwelcome.
“I can see you don’t want me to go,” she said with cold gentleness. “Why can’t you say so without being so violent? I shall stay until you ask me to do otherwise.”

Lydgate said nothing more and went out to visit his patients. He felt battered and broken. There was a dark line beneath his eyes that Rosamond had never seen before. She could not bear to look at him. Tertius had a way of taking things that made everything much worse for her.

chapters.title: Book VII: Two Temptations — Chapter LXX
paragraphs:
“Our actions follow us across the years;
What we have been has made us what we are.”

Once Lydgate had left Stone Court, Bulstrode’s first concern was to search Raffles’s pockets. If the man had lied about coming straight from Liverpool because he was ill and penniless, hotel bills would surely reveal where he had stopped. His pocketbook was stuffed with bills, but none showed a stay anywhere else since Christmas except one dated that morning. Crumpled in a coat-tail pocket with an advertisement for a horse fair, it charged him for three days at an inn in Bilkley, the town holding the fair, at least forty miles from Middlemarch. The bill was large. Since Raffles had brought no luggage, he had probably left his traveling case in payment to keep enough money for the journey. His purse was empty, and his pockets held only two sixpences and a few pennies.

These signs that Raffles had really stayed away from Middlemarch since his memorable Christmas visit reassured Bulstrode. What pleasure could Raffles’s bullying vanity get from telling old scandals about a Middlemarch banker far away among people who had never heard of him? And if he did talk, what harm could it do? The urgent thing now was to watch him while there was any risk of that coherent delirium, that inexplicable urge to tell everything, which seemed to have seized him with Caleb Garth. Bulstrode was especially afraid that seeing Lydgate might provoke it again. He sat alone with Raffles all night, telling the housekeeper only to lie down fully dressed so that she could come when called. He explained that he did not feel sleepy and wanted to make sure the doctor’s directions were followed. He followed them faithfully, although Raffles constantly begged for brandy and cried that he was sinking, that the earth was sinking beneath him. Restless and sleepless, he nevertheless remained frightened and manageable. When offered the food Lydgate had prescribed, which he refused, and denied the things he wanted, he seemed to focus all his terror on Bulstrode. He begged him not to be angry, not to starve him in revenge, and swore vehemently that he had never said a word against him to anyone alive. Even this was something Bulstrode would not have wanted Lydgate to hear. A more alarming sign of the delirium’s sudden changes came in the dawn twilight: Raffles seemed to imagine a doctor was present and told him that Bulstrode meant to starve him to death for telling, when he had never told anything.

Bulstrode’s natural authority and determination served him well. Frail-looking and nervous himself, he found the strength he needed in the pressure of circumstances. Throughout that difficult night and morning he looked like a corpse restored to movement but not to warmth, ruling through a cold, unshakable stillness. Inside, his mind worked fiercely on the dangers he must guard against and the means of securing himself. He prayed; he told himself how wretched this man’s spiritual condition was, and how he must accept the punishment God had appointed for him instead of wishing harm to someone else. But through all these efforts to make words harden into a settled state of mind, vivid pictures of the events he desired kept breaking through and spreading. And justifications followed the pictures. He could not help imagining Raffles dead and himself delivered. What would the removal of this miserable creature amount to? He was unrepentant—but weren’t convicted criminals unrepentant too? The law still decided their fate. If Providence decreed death here, it was no sin to see that as the desirable outcome, provided he did nothing to hasten it and carefully followed the prescribed treatment. Even that treatment might be mistaken: human prescriptions were fallible. Lydgate himself had said treatment could hasten death—why not his own treatment? Of course, in questions of right and wrong, intention was everything.

So Bulstrode tried to keep his intention apart from his desire. He assured himself that he meant to follow instructions. Why, then, had he begun questioning whether those instructions were right? It was only desire’s familiar trick: seizing on any irrelevant doubt, gaining more room wherever consequences were uncertain, in every dark patch that seemed beyond the reach of law. Still, he did follow the instructions.

His anxieties kept turning towards Lydgate. Remembering their meeting the previous morning, he felt things that had never troubled him at the time. Then he had cared little about Lydgate’s distress over the proposed change at the hospital, or the feelings his refusal might arouse. He had considered himself justified in rejecting such an excessive request. Now he looked back and saw that he had probably made Lydgate an enemy. He wanted to win him over—or, rather, to make him feel a strong personal obligation. He regretted not having made the financial sacrifice at once, unreasonable though it might have been. If Raffles’s ravings led to unpleasant suspicions or even actual knowledge, an important service to Lydgate would have given Bulstrode some protection in the doctor’s mind. But perhaps regret had come too late.

A strange, pitiful struggle in this unhappy soul! For years he had wanted to be better than he was. He had disciplined his selfish passions and dressed them in austere robes, walking among them as though they were a devout choir. Now terror had broken into their ranks. They could no longer chant, only cry out in their ordinary voices for safety.

It was almost midday when Lydgate arrived. He explained that he had intended to come earlier but had been held up. Bulstrode noticed how shattered he looked. The doctor at once concentrated on his patient, asking detailed questions about everything that had happened. Raffles was worse. He took almost no food, remained stubbornly awake, and tossed about deliriously, though without violence. Contrary to Bulstrode’s frightened expectations, he scarcely noticed Lydgate and went on talking or muttering incoherently.
“What do you make of his condition?” Bulstrode asked when they were alone.
“His symptoms have grown worse.”
“Then you have less hope?”
“No. I still think he may recover. Will you be staying here yourself?” Lydgate looked at Bulstrode as he asked the abrupt question. It unsettled the banker, though no suspicion had prompted it.

“Yes, I think I shall,” Bulstrode answered, controlling himself and speaking deliberately. “Mrs. Bulstrode knows why I’m staying. Mrs. Abel and her husband lack the experience to be left entirely on their own. Responsibility of this kind is hardly part of their employment. I presume you have some new instructions.”

Lydgate’s main new instruction concerned giving very small doses of opium if the sleeplessness continued for several more hours. He had brought some in his pocket as a precaution. He explained precisely how much Bulstrode should give and when the doses must stop, emphasizing the danger of continuing beyond that point. He also repeated that Raffles must have no alcohol.
“From what I can see,” he concluded, “excessive sedation is the one thing I would seriously fear. He may pull through even with very little food. He still has considerable strength.”

“You look ill yourself, Mr. Lydgate. That’s most unusual—I might say I’ve never seen it before,” Bulstrode said. His concern was as different from yesterday’s indifference as his present disregard of exhaustion was from his usual anxious care of himself. “I fear you’re under great strain.”
“Yes, I am,” Lydgate answered curtly, hat in hand and ready to leave.
“Some new trouble, I’m afraid?” Bulstrode asked. “Please sit down.”

“No, thank you,” Lydgate said with a touch of pride. “I told you yesterday where my affairs stood. The only thing to add is that a bailiff has now actually been put into my house. A short sentence can cover a great deal of trouble. Good morning.”

“Wait, Mr. Lydgate, please wait,” said Bulstrode. “I’ve been thinking the matter over. Yesterday you took me by surprise, and I didn’t consider it deeply enough. Mrs. Bulstrode is worried about her niece, and I too should be sorry to see your circumstances change disastrously. There are many demands on me. Still, on reflection I think I ought to make a small sacrifice rather than leave you without help. You said, I believe, that a thousand pounds would clear all your obligations and put you on firm ground again?”

“Yes,” said Lydgate, a rush of joy sweeping every other feeling aside. “That would pay everything I owe and leave a little to spare. I could begin reducing our expenses. And in time my practice might improve.”
“Wait a moment, Mr. Lydgate, and I’ll write a check for that amount. I know that help in these circumstances needs to be complete if it’s to do any good.”
As Bulstrode wrote, Lydgate turned to the window. He thought of his home, of a life so promising at the start now rescued from defeat, its good purposes still intact.

“You can give me a written promise of repayment, Mr. Lydgate,” said the banker, bringing him the check. “In time, I hope, you’ll be able to repay it gradually. For now, it gives me pleasure to think you’ll be free of further difficulties.”
“I’m deeply grateful,” Lydgate replied. “You’ve given me back the prospect of working with some happiness and some chance of doing good.”

It seemed perfectly natural to him that Bulstrode should have reconsidered his refusal. This matched the more generous side of the banker’s character. But as he urged his horse into a canter, eager to get home, tell Rosamond the news, and draw cash from the bank for Dover’s agent, an unwelcome thought crossed his mind like a dark-winged omen. What a change a few months had made in him! He was delighted to put himself under a heavy personal obligation—delighted to receive money for himself from Bulstrode.

The banker felt he had done something to remove one source of anxiety, yet found little relief. He did not measure how much corrupt motive lay behind his desire for Lydgate’s goodwill. But it was no less active for being unmeasured, like an irritant in his blood. A man makes a vow, yet keeps the means of breaking it. Does he consciously mean to break it? Not at all. But the desires that would break it work obscurely within him. They enter his imagination and loosen his muscles at the very moment he is repeating his reasons for the vow. Raffles recovering quickly, free again to exercise his hateful powers—how could Bulstrode wish for that? The picture that promised release was Raffles dead. Indirectly he prayed for that release, begging that, if possible, his remaining days on earth might be freed from the threat of a disgrace that would destroy his usefulness as God’s instrument. Lydgate’s opinion gave little reason to expect that prayer to be answered. As the day wore on, Bulstrode grew irritated by the persistent life of the man he longed to see sinking into death’s silence. His imperious will stirred murderous impulses against this mere animal life, over which will alone had no power. He told himself he was becoming too exhausted. Tonight he would leave the patient to Mrs. Abel, who could call her husband if she needed help.

By six o’clock Raffles had managed only brief, troubled snatches of sleep, waking more restless than ever and crying continually that he was sinking away. Bulstrode began giving the opium as Lydgate had directed. Half an hour or more later, he called Mrs. Abel and told her he was too worn out to keep watching. He must leave the patient in her care. He repeated Lydgate’s directions about the amount of each dose. Until then Mrs. Abel had known nothing of the doctor’s prescriptions. She had simply prepared and brought whatever Bulstrode asked for, and done what he told her. Now she asked what she should do besides give the opium.

“Nothing for the moment, except offer him soup or soda water. Come to me if you need further instructions. Unless there’s an important change, I won’t come back into the room tonight. Ask your husband for help if you need it. I must get to bed early.”
“You certainly need to, sir,” Mrs. Abel said, “and to have something more nourishing than you’ve had.”

Bulstrode left without worrying about what Raffles might say. His delirium had become an incoherent mutter unlikely to convey any dangerous information. In any case, that risk had to be taken. He first went downstairs to the paneled parlor and considered having his horse saddled, riding home by moonlight, and abandoning all concern for worldly consequences. Then he wished he had asked Lydgate to come again that evening. Perhaps the doctor would change his view and consider Raffles’s condition less hopeful. Should he send for him? If Raffles really was worsening, slowly dying, Bulstrode felt he could go to bed and sleep in gratitude to Providence. But was he worse? Lydgate might only say the illness was following its expected course and predict that the patient would soon sleep soundly and recover. What good would it do to send for him? Bulstrode recoiled from that answer. No belief or argument could stop him seeing one probable future: Raffles restored to health would be exactly the same man, with renewed powers to torment him. He would have to drag his wife away to spend her remaining years apart from her friends and native town, with suspicion of him lodged in her heart and estranging her from him.

He had spent an hour and a half in this struggle, lit only by the fire, when a sudden thought made him rise and light the bedroom candle he had brought downstairs. He had not told Mrs. Abel when to stop giving the opium.

He picked up the candlestick but stood still for a long time. She might already have given more than Lydgate prescribed. Yet surely he could be excused for forgetting part of an instruction when he was so exhausted. Candle in hand, he went upstairs, still unsure whether to go straight to his own room and bed or turn into the sickroom and put right his omission. He stopped in the passage, facing Raffles’s door. He could hear moans and murmurs. Still awake, then. Who could know whether it might not be better to disregard Lydgate’s prescription, since following it had brought no sleep?
He went into his own room. Before he had finished undressing, Mrs. Abel knocked. He opened the door an inch to hear her lowered voice.

“Please, sir, shouldn’t I give the poor creature some brandy or something? He feels he’s sinking away. He won’t swallow anything else—and there’d be little strength in it if he did—just the opium. And he keeps saying he’s sinking down through the earth.”
To her surprise, Mr. Bulstrode gave no answer. A struggle was taking place inside him.

“I think he’ll die for want of nourishment if this goes on. When I nursed my poor master, Mr. Robisson, I had to keep giving him port and brandy, a big glass each time,” Mrs. Abel added, with a hint of protest.

Again Bulstrode did not answer at once. She went on: “When somebody’s at death’s door, it’s no time to be saving, and I’m sure you wouldn’t want that, sir. Otherwise I’d give him some of the rum we keep ourselves. But you’ve sat up with him and done everything in your power—”
A key was pushed through the narrow opening. In a husky voice Mr. Bulstrode said, “That’s the key to the wine cooler. There’s plenty of brandy in it.”

At about six next morning, Mr. Bulstrode got up and spent some time in prayer. Does anyone imagine that private prayer must be honest, must reach the roots of what we do? Private prayer is unspoken speech, and speech gives a representation. Who can represent himself exactly as he is, even in his own thoughts? Bulstrode had not yet sorted out the tangled impulses of the past twenty-four hours.

Listening in the passage, he heard heavy, snoring breaths. Then he went into the garden and looked at the early frost on the grass and the fresh spring leaves. Coming back inside, he was startled to see Mrs. Abel.
“How is your patient? Asleep, I think?” he asked, trying to sound cheerful.

“Very deeply, sir,” said Mrs. Abel. “He drifted off between three and four. Would you go and look at him, please? I thought it was safe to leave him. My husband’s gone to the fields, and the little girl is watching the kettles.”
Bulstrode went upstairs. One glance told him that Raffles’s sleep would bring no renewal. It was a sleep flowing ever deeper into the gulf of death.
Looking round, he saw a bottle with some brandy left in it and the almost empty vial of opium. He hid the vial and took the brandy downstairs, locking it back in the wine cooler.
Over breakfast he considered riding straight to Middlemarch, but decided instead to wait for Lydgate. He told Mrs. Abel she could get on with her work. He would watch in the bedroom.

As he sat watching the enemy of his peace move irreversibly towards silence, he felt calmer than he had for many months. Secrecy folded its wing over his conscience and soothed it, seeming at that moment like an angel sent to comfort him. He took out his pocketbook and reviewed notes about the arrangements he had planned and partly made for leaving Middlemarch. Now that his absence would be short, he considered which arrangements to keep and which to cancel. His temporary withdrawal from management might still give him a suitable opportunity to make some economies he wanted. He still hoped Mrs. Casaubon would take on a large share of the hospital’s costs. The minutes passed in these reflections until a marked change in the noisy breathing drew all his attention to the bed. He was forced to think of the departing life, once obedient to his own, and of how glad he had once been to find it corrupt enough to be used as he pleased. His gladness then was what drove his gladness now that this life was ending.
And who could say Raffles’s death had been brought forward? Who knew what might have saved him?

Lydgate arrived at half past ten, in time to witness the final breath. When he entered, Bulstrode saw a sudden look cross his face: less surprise than recognition that his judgment had been wrong. For a while he stood silently beside the bed, his eyes on the dying man, though the restrained movement of his expression showed an argument continuing within him.
“When did this change start?” he asked, looking at Bulstrode.

“I didn’t sit up with him last night,” Bulstrode replied. “I was exhausted and left him to Mrs. Abel. She says he fell asleep between three and four. When I came in before eight, he was much as you see him now.”
Lydgate asked nothing more. He watched in silence until he said, “It’s over.”

That morning Lydgate had regained his hope and sense of freedom. He had set out with all his former energy, feeling strong enough to bear every disappointment in his marriage. And he knew that Bulstrode had helped him generously. But this case troubled him. He had not expected it to end this way. Yet he scarcely knew how to question Bulstrode without seeming insulting. As for questioning the housekeeper—well, the man was dead. What good would it do to suggest that someone’s ignorance or carelessness had killed him? And after all, he himself might be mistaken.

He rode back to Middlemarch with Bulstrode. They talked about many things, chiefly cholera, the Reform Bill’s prospects in the House of Lords, and the political Unions’ determination. They said nothing about Raffles except that Bulstrode mentioned arranging a grave in Lowick churchyard. As far as he knew, the poor man had no family connections except Rigg, whom Raffles had described as unfriendly to him.

Mr. Farebrother visited Lydgate after he got home. The Vicar had been out of town the day before, but by evening the news of the bailiff in Lydgate’s house had reached Lowick. Mr. Spicer, shoemaker and parish clerk, had brought it from his brother, the respectable bell-hanger in Lowick Gate. Since the evening when Lydgate had come downstairs from the billiard room with Fred Vincy, Mr. Farebrother had been worried about him. One or more visits to play at the Green Dragon might have meant little in another man. In Lydgate they were among several signs that he was changing, beginning to do things he had once treated with almost excessive contempt. Loose scraps of gossip had hinted at unhappiness in his marriage, which might play some part. But Mr. Farebrother was sure the change was chiefly connected with the debts people were reporting more and more definitely. He began to fear that any supposed resources or friends in reserve were entirely imaginary. Lydgate’s rebuff when he first tried to gain his confidence had discouraged a second attempt. The news that a bailiff was actually in the house made him resolve to overcome that reluctance.

Lydgate had just finished seeing a poor patient whose case interested him deeply. He came forward with an outstretched hand and a frank cheerfulness that surprised Mr. Farebrother. Was this another proud refusal of sympathy and help? No matter: both would be offered.

“How are you, Lydgate? I heard something that worried me, so I came to see you,” the Vicar said with the warmth of a good brother, but without any reproach. They had both sat down by now, and Lydgate replied at once—
“I think I know what you mean. You heard there was a bailiff in the house?”
“Yes. Is that true?”

“It was,” said Lydgate, speaking freely, as though the subject no longer troubled him. “But the danger has passed. The debt is paid. My difficulties are over now. I’ll be clear of debt and, I hope, able to start again on a better footing.”

“I’m very thankful to hear that,” said the Vicar, leaning back and speaking with the soft quickness that often follows a lifted burden. “That’s better than all the news in the ‘Times.’ I admit I came with a heavy heart.”

“Thank you for coming,” Lydgate said warmly. “Being happier lets me enjoy your kindness all the more. I certainly have been badly crushed. I suspect the bruises will hurt again later,” he added with a rather sad smile. “But just now all I can feel is that the torture screw has been loosened.”
After a brief silence, Mr. Farebrother spoke earnestly. “My dear fellow, let me ask one question. Forgive me if I’m being intrusive.”
“I’m sure you won’t ask anything I ought to take offense at.”
“Then—to put my mind entirely at rest—you haven’t paid these debts by taking on another that may trouble you even more in the future, have you?”

“No,” said Lydgate, coloring a little. “There’s no reason to conceal the fact: the person I owe is Bulstrode. He’s advanced me a very generous sum, a thousand pounds, and he can afford to wait for repayment.”

“Well, that is generous,” Mr. Farebrother said, making himself approve of a man he disliked. His tact kept him from dwelling even privately on the fact that he had always urged Lydgate to avoid personal obligations to Bulstrode. He quickly added, “And naturally Bulstrode must care about your welfare, after all the work you’ve done with him—work that has probably reduced your income instead of increasing it. I’m glad he has acted on that feeling.”

These kind assumptions made Lydgate uncomfortable. They sharpened an uneasiness he had first dimly felt only hours before: Bulstrode’s abrupt generosity, coming immediately after such cold indifference, might have had purely selfish motives. He let the Vicar’s assumptions stand. He could not tell the story behind the loan. But that story was more vividly present to him than ever, along with the fact the Vicar tactfully passed over: this personal indebtedness to Bulstrode was exactly what he had once been most determined to avoid.
Instead of replying, he began discussing the economies he planned and the new way he had come to look at his life.

“I’ll open a surgery,” he said. “I think I was wrong to resist that. And if Rosamond doesn’t mind, I’ll take an apprentice. I don’t like either idea, but there’s nothing degrading in doing the work conscientiously. I’ve had a severe enough chafing to start with. That should make the little irritations easier to bear.”

Poor Lydgate! That involuntary “if Rosamond doesn’t mind,” spoken as part of his thought, revealed the yoke he wore. But Mr. Farebrother’s hopes now flowed strongly alongside Lydgate’s. Knowing nothing that could cast a shadow over the future, he left with affectionate congratulations.

_Clown_. . . . It was in the Bunch of Grapes, where,
in fact, you like to sit, don’t you?
_Froth_. I do: the room is open and good in winter.
_Clown_. Well, very good then: I hope we have some truth here.
—_Measure for Measure_.

Five days after Raffles’s death, Mr. Bambridge stood at ease beneath the broad archway into the Green Dragon’s yard. Solitary reflection was not a pleasure of his, but he had only just stepped outside. In the early afternoon, anyone standing idly under that arch was as sure to attract company as a pigeon that had found something worth pecking. There was nothing tangible to feed on here, but the rational eye recognized the likelihood of gossip to nourish the mind. The first to act on that perception was Mr. Hopkins, the mild-mannered draper opposite, especially eager for a little masculine conversation because most of his customers were women. Bambridge treated him rather briefly. Naturally Hopkins was pleased to talk to _him_; he did not intend to waste much conversation on Hopkins. Soon, however, more important listeners gathered, some drifting out of the passing traffic, others strolling over specifically to see what was happening at the Green Dragon. Bambridge now found it worthwhile to say impressive things about the fine horses he had seen and bought on his recent trip north. He assured the gentlemen that if they could show him anything to beat a bay thoroughbred mare, rising four, available for inspection at Doncaster, he would oblige them by being shot “from here to Hereford.” A pair of black horses he meant to put into the training carriage also reminded him vividly of a pair he had sold Faulkner in ’19 for a hundred guineas, which Faulkner sold two months later for a hundred and sixty. Any gentleman who could disprove that was welcome to call Bambridge a very ugly name until his throat ran dry.

At this lively point in the conversation, Mr. Frank Hawley arrived. He was not the kind of man to lower his dignity by lounging at the Green Dragon. But, passing along the High Street and seeing Bambridge across the way, he strode over to ask whether the horse dealer had found the first-rate gig horse he had promised to look for. Hawley was told to reserve judgment until he saw a gray selected at Bilkley. If it did not suit him perfectly, Bambridge did not know a horse when he saw one—apparently the most inconceivable possibility. Hawley stood with his back to the street, arranging a time to inspect and try the gray, when a rider passed slowly behind him.

“Bulstrode!” two or three voices said softly together. The draper’s voice respectfully added “Mr.” None of them meant more by naming him than they would have meant by saying “the Riverston coach” when it appeared in the distance. Hawley glanced carelessly round at Bulstrode’s back. Bambridge followed the rider with his eyes and made a mocking face.

“By jingo, that reminds me,” he began, lowering his voice a little. “Your gig horse wasn’t the only thing I picked up at Bilkley, Mr. Hawley. I picked up a fine story about Bulstrode. Do you know where his fortune came from? Any gentleman who wants an interesting piece of information can have it from me free of charge. If everybody got what they deserved, Bulstrode might be saying his prayers at Botany Bay.”
“What do you mean?” Hawley asked, thrusting his hands into his pockets and moving farther under the arch. If Bulstrode proved a scoundrel, Frank Hawley could claim a prophetic soul.

“I got it from an old friend of his. I’ll tell you where I first came across him.” Bambridge abruptly raised a forefinger. “At Larcher’s sale. I knew nothing about him then, and he slipped through my fingers. After Bulstrode, no doubt. He tells me he can draw any amount of money out of Bulstrode—knows all his secrets. Anyway, he let it out at Bilkley. Likes a strong drink. Damned if I think he meant to turn informer, but he’s one of those fellows whose boasting jumps every hedge and ditch. He’d boast about a lame horse as though it raised the price. A man ought to know when to pull up.” Bambridge spoke with disgust, confident that his own boasting showed a proper appreciation of market value.
“What’s his name? Where can we find him?” Hawley asked.
“As for finding him, I left him at the Saracen’s Head to get on with it. His name’s Raffles.”

“Raffles!” cried Mr. Hopkins. “I supplied his funeral yesterday. He was buried at Lowick. Mr. Bulstrode attended. A very respectable funeral.” The listeners were deeply stirred. Bambridge burst out with an oath in which “brimstone” was the mildest word. Hawley frowned, thrust his head forward, and exclaimed, “What? Where did he die?”
“At Stone Court,” said the draper. “The housekeeper said he was related to the master. He arrived ill on Friday.”
“Why, I had a drink with him on Wednesday,” Bambridge put in.
“Did a doctor see him?” Hawley asked.
“Yes, Mr. Lydgate. Mr. Bulstrode sat up with him one night. He died on the third morning.”
“Go on, Bambridge,” Hawley insisted. “What did the fellow say about Bulstrode?”

The crowd had already grown. The town clerk’s presence guaranteed something worth hearing, and Bambridge told his story to seven listeners. It was mostly what we already know, including the facts about Will Ladislaw, with a little local color and detail added. It was the story Bulstrode had dreaded seeing exposed and hoped to bury forever with Raffles’s body—the ghost of his earlier life from which, as he rode past the Green Dragon’s archway, he trusted Providence had delivered him. Yes, Providence. He had still not admitted to himself that he had helped arrange this outcome. He had accepted what seemed to be offered. No one could prove he had done anything to speed that man’s soul on its way.

But the gossip spread through Middlemarch like the smell of fire. Frank Hawley sent a trusted clerk to Stone Court, supposedly to inquire about hay, but really to learn everything Mrs. Abel could tell him about Raffles and his illness. He thus discovered that Mr. Garth had brought Raffles there in his gig. Hawley then called at Caleb’s office to ask whether he could undertake an arbitration if needed, and casually raised the subject of Raffles. Caleb revealed nothing damaging to Bulstrode beyond the unavoidable admission that he had stopped acting for him during the past week. Hawley drew his conclusions. Convinced that Raffles had told Garth the story and that Garth had resigned as a result, he said so to Mr. Toller a few hours later. As the statement passed from person to person, it lost every trace of being an inference and became information straight from Garth. Even a careful historian might have concluded that Caleb was the chief broadcaster of Bulstrode’s wrongdoing.

Hawley soon saw that neither Raffles’s disclosures nor the circumstances of his death gave the law anything to seize on. He rode to Lowick himself to examine the register and discuss everything with Mr. Farebrother. The Vicar was no more surprised than the lawyer that an ugly secret had emerged about Bulstrode, though his sense of justice had always kept him from turning dislike into judgment. As they talked, however, another connection silently formed in Farebrother’s mind, anticipating what Middlemarch would soon loudly call the obvious result of “putting two and two together.” Alongside Bulstrode’s reasons for fearing Raffles came the thought that this fear might explain his generosity to the doctor. Farebrother resisted the idea that Lydgate had knowingly accepted anything as a bribe. But he dreaded the damage this entanglement could do to Lydgate’s reputation. Seeing that Hawley knew nothing yet about the sudden payment of the debts, he carefully steered away whenever the conversation approached it.

“Well,” he said with a deep breath, hoping to end an endless discussion of possibilities none of which could be proved in law, “it’s a strange story. So our lively Ladislaw has an unusual family history! A spirited young woman and a musical Polish patriot seemed plausible parents for him, but I’d never have guessed the addition of a Jewish pawnbroker. Still, you can never predict what a mixture will produce. Some kinds of dirt help clarify things.”
“Exactly what I’d have expected,” Hawley said, mounting. “Any damned foreign blood—Jewish, Corsican, or Gypsy.”
“I know he’s one of your black sheep, Hawley. But he really is an unselfish, unworldly fellow,” Farebrother said with a smile.
“Yes, yes, that’s your Whig bias,” answered Hawley, who often explained apologetically that Farebrother was such a damned pleasant, kindhearted man you might mistake him for a Tory.

Hawley rode home still regarding Lydgate’s attendance on Raffles only as evidence in Bulstrode’s favor. But news was spreading quickly that Lydgate had suddenly been able to remove the bailiff and pay every debt he owed in Middlemarch. Guesses and comments gathered round the news, giving it substance and speed. Soon Hawley and others were hearing it, and readily connecting this sudden access to money with Bulstrode’s wish to silence Raffles. Everyone would have guessed the money came from Bulstrode even without proof. Earlier gossip had established that neither Lydgate’s father-in-law nor his own family would help him. But direct evidence came from a bank clerk and from innocent Mrs. Bulstrode herself. She mentioned the loan to Mrs. Plymdale, who told her daughter-in-law, born a Toller, who told everyone. The affair seemed so public and important that dinners were needed to sustain it. Many invitations were issued and accepted specifically because of the Bulstrode and Lydgate scandal. Wives, widows, and unmarried ladies took their sewing out to tea more often than usual. Every public gathering, from the Green Dragon to Dollop’s, gained an excitement no debate about the Lords rejecting the Reform Bill could supply.

Almost nobody doubted that some disgraceful motive lay behind Bulstrode’s generosity. Hawley initially invited a select group, including both physicians and Mr. Toller and Mr. Wrench, specifically to examine the likely course of Raffles’s illness. He repeated all the details learned from Mrs. Abel and Lydgate’s certificate of death from delirium tremens. The medical men, all firmly attached to the established treatment of that disease, could find nothing in those details to provide definite grounds for suspicion. The moral grounds remained, however: Bulstrode’s strong reasons for wanting Raffles gone, and his giving Lydgate help at this critical moment when he must have known of the need for some time. They were also ready to believe Bulstrode unscrupulous and had no reluctance to think Lydgate as open to bribery as other proud men short of money. Even if the payment had bought only his silence about Bulstrode’s past, it reflected shamefully on Lydgate. People had long mocked him for serving the banker to advance himself and undermine his older colleagues. So, despite finding no direct evidence of guilt in the death at Stone Court, Hawley’s guests parted feeling the business had “an ugly look.”

This vague conviction of guilt that nobody could define produced plenty of head-shaking and sharp insinuations even among established professional men. In the wider public it had all the advantage mystery enjoys over fact. People preferred guessing what had happened to simply knowing it. Guesswork soon grew more confident than knowledge and could accommodate contradictions more freely. Even the definite scandal about Bulstrode’s earlier life melted, in some minds, into the general mystery: so much lively molten metal to pour out in conversation and let take whatever fantastic shapes heaven pleased.

Mrs. Dollop, the forceful landlady of the Tankard in Slaughter Lane, particularly favored this way of thinking. She often had to resist the shallow insistence on facts of customers who supposed their reports from outside counted for as much as what had “come into” her mind. She could not say how the thought had reached her, but it stood before her as clearly as if it had been “chalked on the chimney-board”: Bulstrode had said “his inside was _that black_, if the hairs on his head knew what was in his heart, he’d tear them out by the roots.”

“That’s odd,” said Mr. Limp, a thoughtful shoemaker with weak eyes and a piping voice. “I read in the ‘Trumpet’ that the Duke of Wellington said that when he changed sides and went over to the Catholics.”

“Very likely,” Mrs. Dollop replied. “If one scoundrel said it, all the more reason another should. But for all his hypocrisy, lording it over everyone as though no parson in the country was good enough for him, he had to take the Devil into his confidence, and the Devil’s got the better of him.”

“Yes, that’s an accomplice you can’t send abroad,” said Mr. Crabbe, the glazier, who collected much news and felt his way dimly through it. “But from what I can make out, some say Bulstrode was planning to run away before this, afraid of being found out.”

“He’ll be driven away now, willing or not,” said Mr. Dill, the barber, who had just come in. “I shaved Fletcher this morning, Hawley’s clerk—he’s hurt his finger. He says they all agree Bulstrode has to go. Mr. Thesiger has turned against him and wants him out of the parish. Gentlemen in this town say they’d as soon dine with a convict from the prison hulks. ‘I’d much sooner,’ Fletcher says. ‘What turns your stomach more than someone making himself unpleasant company with his religion, pretending the Ten Commandments aren’t strict enough for him, while he’s worse than half the men doing hard labor?’ Those were Fletcher’s own words.”
“Still, it will hurt the town if Bulstrode takes his money away,” Mr. Limp said shakily.
“Ah, better people spend their money worse,” said a dyer in a firm voice. His crimson-stained hands looked at odds with his good-natured face.
“But he won’t keep his money, from what I understand,” said the glazier. “Don’t they say someone can take it from him? As I understand it, if they went to law they could strip him of every penny.”

“Nothing of the kind!” the barber said. He felt himself a little above Dollop’s regular company, without enjoying it any less. “Fletcher says there’s no such thing. They could prove a hundred times whose child young Ladislaw was, and it would do no more good than proving I came from the Fens. He couldn’t touch a penny.”

“Well, look at that!” Mrs. Dollop exclaimed indignantly. “I thank the Lord for taking my children to Himself, if that’s all the law can do for the motherless. According to that, it’s no use having a father or mother at all. But believing one lawyer without asking another—I’m surprised at a clever man like you, Mr. Dill. Everyone knows there are always two sides, if not more. Otherwise why would anybody go to law? With all the law there is everywhere, it’s a poor business if proving whose child you are does you no good. Fletcher can say what he likes, but don’t try your Fletcher on _me_!”
Mr. Dill laughed as though paying a compliment to a woman more than a match for lawyers. He was willing to accept plenty of teasing from a landlady with a long unpaid account against him.

“If it comes to law, and everything people say is true, there’s more than money to look into,” said the glazier. “There’s that poor creature who’s dead and gone. From what I understand, he once used to be a much finer gentleman than Bulstrode.”

“A finer gentleman? I’ll warrant he was,” Mrs. Dollop said. “And much better-looking, from what I hear. Mr. Baldwin, the tax collector, stood right where you’re sitting and said, ‘Bulstrode got all the money he brought here by thieving and swindling.’ I told him, ‘You’re not telling me anything new, Mr. Baldwin. Looking at him has made my blood crawl ever since he came into Slaughter Lane wanting to buy the house over my head. People don’t turn the color of a dough tub and stare as if they wanted to see into your backbone for nothing.’ That’s what I said, and Mr. Baldwin can confirm it.”

“And you were right,” said Mr. Crabbe. “From what I gather, this Raffles was as sturdy and fresh-faced as you could wish, and excellent company. But he’s lying dead in Lowick churchyard, sure enough, and from what I can understand, some people know more than they _ought_ about how he got there.”

“I should think so!” Mrs. Dollop replied, slightly scornful of his apparent slowness. “A man gets lured to an isolated house. People who can afford hospitals and nurses for half the countryside choose to sit up themselves, day and night. Nobody’s allowed near him but a doctor known to stop at nothing, so poor he can barely hold together. Then suddenly he’s swimming in money and can pay Mr. Byles the butcher for all the best cuts he’s been buying on credit since Michaelmas the year before last. I don’t need anyone to tell me there’s been something going on the Prayer Book has no service for. I don’t need to sit blinking and thinking it over.”

Mrs. Dollop looked round with the authority of a landlady used to ruling her company. The bolder customers chorused agreement. Mr. Limp, however, took a drink, pressed his flattened hands together between his knees, and gazed at them with bleary concentration. It was as though Mrs. Dollop’s scorching words had dried up his wits entirely, leaving them unable to function until more liquid restored them.
“Why not dig him up and call the coroner?” the dyer asked. “It’s been done plenty of times. If there was foul play, they might find it.”

“They won’t, Mr. Jonas!” Mrs. Dollop declared. “I know doctors. Much too cunning to get caught. And this Doctor Lydgate, wanting to cut everyone open before their breath was properly out—it’s clear enough what he wanted to learn by looking inside respectable people. You can be sure he knows drugs you can neither see nor smell, before or after they’re swallowed. I’ve seen drops myself, ordered by Doctor Gambit, our club doctor, a decent man who’s brought more living children into the world than any other doctor in Middlemarch. I’ve seen drops you couldn’t tell were in the glass at all, but they’d give you cramps the next day. Use your own judgment. Don’t try telling me! All I say is, thank goodness we didn’t take Doctor Lydgate on at our club. Many a mother’s child might have lived to regret it.”

The main points of this conversation at Dollop’s had already been discussed by every class in town. They had reached Lowick Parsonage and Tipton Grange, been fully reported to the Vincy family, and prompted sad talk of “poor Harriet” among all Mrs. Bulstrode’s friends, before Lydgate clearly understood why people looked at him strangely. Bulstrode himself still did not suspect his secrets were out. He had never been used to much warmth from his neighbors, so its absence did not strike him. Besides, he had been away on various business trips. Having decided he need not leave Middlemarch, he could settle matters previously left unresolved.
“We’ll go to Cheltenham in a month or two,” he had told his wife. “Besides the air and the waters, there are great spiritual benefits there. Six weeks will do us a great deal of good.”

He genuinely believed in those spiritual benefits. He intended to live more devoutly from now on because of his recent sins, which he represented to himself as possibilities and asked forgiveness for conditionally: “if I have sinned in this.”

He said nothing more to Lydgate about the hospital, afraid of revealing too abrupt a change of plans immediately after Raffles’s death. Deep down, he believed Lydgate suspected that his instructions had been deliberately disobeyed. If so, he must also suspect a motive. But nothing had been told him about Raffles’s history, and Bulstrode did not want to give weight to vague suspicions. As for certainty that a particular treatment would save or kill, Lydgate constantly argued against such dogmatism himself. He had no right to speak and every reason to remain silent. Bulstrode therefore felt protected by Providence. The only incidents that made him seriously flinch were occasional encounters with Caleb Garth, who nevertheless raised his hat with quiet gravity.
Meanwhile, the town’s leading men were becoming firmly resolved to act against him.

A public health meeting was to take place in the Town Hall. A case of cholera in the town had made the issue urgent. After Parliament hurriedly passed an Act authorizing local levies for sanitary measures, Middlemarch had appointed a board to supervise them. Whigs and Tories had agreed on a good deal of cleaning and preparation. The present question was whether land outside the town should be acquired as a burial ground through a levy or through voluntary contributions. The meeting was open, and almost everyone of importance was expected.

Bulstrode sat on the board. Shortly before twelve he left the bank, intending to argue for voluntary contributions. Uncertainty about his plans had kept him in the background for some time. This morning he felt ready to resume his former place as an active and influential figure in the town where he now expected to end his days. Among those walking in the same direction he saw Lydgate. They joined each other, discussed the meeting’s purpose, and went in together.

Everyone of importance seemed to have arrived before them. There were still seats near the head of the large central table, and they made their way there. Farebrother sat opposite, not far from Hawley. All the medical men were present. Mr. Thesiger chaired the meeting, with Mr. Brooke of Tipton on his right.
Lydgate noticed a curious exchange of glances as he and Bulstrode sat down.

The chairman fully introduced the business, explaining the advantages of buying, through voluntary contributions, enough land to serve eventually as a general cemetery. Bulstrode rose and asked to speak. The town knew his rather high, restrained, fluent voice well from meetings of this kind. Again Lydgate saw those peculiar glances before Hawley sprang up and spoke in a firm, ringing voice. “Mr. Chairman, before anyone addresses that question, I ask leave to speak on a matter of public feeling which I and many gentlemen here consider must come first.”
Even when public manners restrained Hawley’s “awful language,” his brevity and assurance made him formidable. Thesiger granted permission. Bulstrode sat down, and Hawley went on.

“Mr. Chairman, I do not speak only for myself. I speak with the agreement and at the express request of at least eight fellow townsmen sitting around us. We all believe Mr. Bulstrode should be called upon—and I now call upon him—to resign the public offices he holds not merely as a taxpayer, but as a gentleman among gentlemen. Circumstances sometimes put actions beyond the reach of the law, though they may be worse than offenses the law can punish. Honest men and gentlemen who do not want the company of those responsible must defend themselves as best they can. That is what I and the friends I may call my clients in this matter intend to do. I do not say Mr. Bulstrode is guilty of shameful conduct. But I call upon him either to deny publicly and disprove the scandalous accusations made by a man now dead, who died in his house—the accusations that for years he engaged in wicked practices and gained his fortune dishonestly—or to leave the offices he could only have been allowed to hold as a gentleman among gentlemen.”

Every eye turned to Bulstrode. From the first mention of his name, his emotions had surged almost beyond what his frail body could bear. Lydgate, too, felt a shock: a faint foreboding seemed to have become a terrible reality. Yet the resentful hatred rising in him was checked as he looked at Bulstrode’s shrunken misery and livid face. The healer’s instinct put the sufferer’s rescue and relief before everything else.

In a flash Bulstrode saw that his life had failed after all. He was disgraced, forced to shrink before people he had habitually reprimanded. God had disowned him publicly, leaving him defenseless before the triumphant contempt of those delighted to have their hatred justified. His evasions of conscience over his accomplice’s life had achieved nothing. Those evasions now turned against him, venomous as an exposed lie with its full-grown fangs. All this rushed through him like an agony of terror that stops short of killing and leaves the ears open to the next wave of condemnation. This sudden exposure, after he had felt safe again, struck not the hardened nature of a criminal but the sensitive nerves of a man whose deepest life consisted in the mastery and influence his circumstances had taught him to seek.

Yet that same intensity gave him strength to resist. Through all his physical weakness ran the tough fiber of ambitious, self-preserving will. It had repeatedly flared up and scattered his religious fears. Now, even as the merciful looked on him with pity, it began stirring and glowing beneath his ash-pale face. Before Hawley had finished, Bulstrode knew he would answer, and that his answer would strike back. He dared not rise and say, “I am innocent; the whole story is false.” Even had he dared, his sharp sense of betrayal would have made it seem useless, like trying to cover his nakedness with a thin rag that tore at the slightest pull.

For several moments the room was silent, every man watching Bulstrode. He remained motionless, leaning heavily against the chair back. He could not risk standing. When he began speaking, he pressed both hands against the seat beside him. His voice, though rougher than usual, carried clearly. He pronounced each word distinctly, pausing between sentences as though short of breath. Turning first to Thesiger and then looking at Hawley, he said—

“Sir, as a Christian minister, I ask you to hear my protest against your approval of an attack driven by bitter hatred. My enemies gladly believe any slander a loose tongue speaks against me. Their consciences become strict where I am concerned. Suppose this malicious talk, of which I am to be the victim, accuses me of wrongdoing—” His voice rose, acquiring a sharpness almost like a low cry. “Who has the right to accuse me? Not men whose lives are unchristian, even scandalous. Not men who employ base agents to achieve their purposes, whose profession is woven out of deceit, who spend their income on sensual pleasures while I devote mine to the best purposes of this life and the next.”
At the word “deceit,” a rising noise of murmurs and hisses began. Hawley, Toller, Chichely, and Hackbutt all sprang up. But Hawley burst out so instantly that the others fell silent.

“If you mean me, sir, I invite you and anyone else to examine my professional life. As for Christian or unchristian, I reject your pious, blustering Christianity. And as for my income, I do not make a practice of supporting thieves and cheating children of their inheritance in order to promote religion and set myself up as a saintly killjoy. I make no claim to an especially delicate conscience. Your actions have required no especially delicate standard to judge them, sir. Again I call on you to explain these scandals satisfactorily or leave offices in which we, at any rate, refuse to accept you as a colleague. We decline, sir, to work with a man whose character remains under this disgraceful suspicion—a suspicion arising from recent actions as well as reports.”
“Allow me, Mr. Hawley,” said the chairman. Still fuming, Hawley gave a half-impatient bow and sat down, pushing his hands deep into his pockets.

“Mr. Bulstrode, I think we should not prolong this discussion,” Thesiger said, turning towards the pale, shaking man. “So far as Mr. Hawley has expressed a general feeling, I must agree that your profession of Christianity requires you to clear yourself, if possible, of these unfortunate accusations. For my part, I would gladly give you every opportunity and a full hearing. But your present attitude is painfully at odds with the principles you have sought to embody, principles whose honor I am bound to defend. As your clergyman, and as one who hopes you may regain respect, I advise you to leave the room for now and let the business proceed.”

After hesitating, Bulstrode picked up his hat and slowly stood. But he clutched the corner of the chair so unsteadily that Lydgate knew he could not walk out unaided. What else could he do? He could not watch a man collapse beside him for lack of help. He rose, offered his arm, and led Bulstrode out. Yet this action, which might have been simply a gentle duty prompted by compassion, was unbearably bitter to him. It felt as though he were signing his name to an association with Bulstrode whose full meaning, as others must see it, he now understood. He was convinced that the man trembling on his arm had given him a thousand pounds as a bribe, and that Raffles’s treatment had somehow been interfered with for an evil purpose. The links were plain enough: the town knew about the loan, believed it was a bribe, and believed he had knowingly accepted it as one.
While poor Lydgate’s mind struggled in the terrible grip of this revelation, duty still compelled him to take Bulstrode to the bank, send for his carriage, and wait to escort him home.
Meanwhile the meeting finished its business and broke into eager groups discussing Bulstrode’s affair—and Lydgate’s.

Mr. Brooke had previously heard only incomplete hints. Very uneasy that he had “gone a little too far” in supporting Bulstrode, he now learned the whole story. He spoke with kindly sadness to Farebrother about the ugly suspicion surrounding Lydgate. Farebrother was about to walk back to Lowick.
“Come in my carriage,” Brooke said. “I’m going to see Mrs. Casaubon. She was due back from Yorkshire last night. She’ll be glad to see me, you know.”

As they drove, Brooke chatted, kindly hoping there was nothing really wicked in Lydgate’s conduct. He had recognized him as a young man well above the ordinary when he arrived with a letter from his uncle, Sir Godwin. Farebrother said little. He was deeply saddened. Knowing human weakness so well, he could not feel certain that humiliating need had not driven Lydgate below his own standards.
Dorothea was outside on the gravel when the carriage reached the Manor gate, and came to meet them.
“Well, my dear,” Brooke said, “we’ve just come from a meeting—a public health meeting, you know.”

“Was Mr. Lydgate there?” asked Dorothea. She looked healthy and full of life, standing bareheaded in the bright April light. “I want a long consultation with him about the hospital. I’ve promised Mr. Bulstrode I’ll speak to him.”
“Oh, my dear,” Brooke replied, “we’ve been hearing bad news. Bad news, you know.”
They walked through the garden towards the churchyard gate, since Farebrother wanted to continue to the parsonage. On the way Dorothea heard the whole unhappy story.
She listened intently and asked to hear the facts and suspicions about Lydgate twice. After a short silence, she stopped at the churchyard gate and spoke to Farebrother with energy—
“You don’t believe Mr. Lydgate has done anything dishonorable? I refuse to believe it. Let’s find out the truth and clear his name!”

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXII
paragraphs:
Full souls are facing mirrors, stretching out
An endless view of lovely things ahead,
Reflecting what lies behind.

Dorothea’s impulsive generosity would have rushed to defend Lydgate against the suspicion that he had accepted a bribe. But as she considered the whole case in the light of Mr. Farebrother’s experience, her confidence met a discouraging check.

“It’s a delicate subject to raise,” he said. “How could we investigate? Either publicly, by involving the magistrate and coroner, or privately, by questioning Lydgate. There’s no firm basis for the first course, or Hawley would have taken it. As for speaking to Lydgate, I admit I’d hesitate. He would probably consider it a grave insult. I’ve found it difficult more than once to talk to him about personal matters. And to feel confident of a good outcome, we would need to know the truth about his conduct already.”

“I’m convinced he has done nothing wrong. I believe people are almost always better than their neighbors think,” Dorothea said. Some of her most intense experiences over the previous two years had turned her firmly against putting the worst interpretation on others’ actions. For the first time, she felt a little dissatisfied with Farebrother. She disliked this cautious calculation of consequences. She wanted passionate faith in justice and mercy, whose very emotional force could make them prevail. Two days later he dined at the Manor with her uncle and the Chettams. With dessert still untouched, the servants out of the room, and Mr. Brooke nodding in sleep, she returned to the subject with fresh energy.

“Mr. Lydgate would understand that when his friends hear a slander, their first wish is to clear his name. What are we alive for, if not to make life easier for one another? I can’t stand aside when a man is in trouble who advised me in _my_ trouble and cared for me when I was ill.”

Dorothea spoke and acted no more forcefully than she had at the head of her uncle’s table nearly three years earlier. The experience she had gained since gave her a stronger right to a definite opinion. But Sir James Chettam was no longer a shy, agreeable suitor. He was an anxious brother-in-law, devoted in his admiration of her, yet constantly afraid she would fall into another delusion almost as bad as marrying Casaubon. He smiled much less. His “Exactly” now more often introduced a disagreement than it had in his submissive bachelor days. Dorothea was surprised to find she had to make up her mind not to fear him, especially because he really was her best friend. Now he disagreed.
“But, Dorothea,” he protested, “you can’t take charge of a man’s life like that. Lydgate must know—or soon will know—where he stands. If he can clear himself, he will. He must act on his own behalf.”

“I think his friends must wait for an opportunity,” Farebrother added. “It is possible—I’ve felt so much weakness in myself that I can imagine even an honorable man, as I’ve always considered Lydgate, yielding to a temptation like this: accepting money offered, more or less indirectly, to buy his silence about old scandals. I can imagine it if he were under severe pressure, troubled as I’m sure Lydgate has been. I wouldn’t believe anything worse without strong proof. But some errors carry a terrible punishment: anyone who chooses can interpret them as crimes. The man has nothing to prove otherwise except his own knowledge of himself and his word.”

“How cruel!” Dorothea cried, clasping her hands. “Wouldn’t you want to be the one person who believed him innocent when everyone else spoke falsely against him? Besides, his earlier character speaks for him.”

“But, my dear Mrs. Casaubon,” Farebrother said, smiling gently at her fervor, “character isn’t carved in marble. It isn’t fixed and unchangeable. It lives and changes, and it can grow sick just as our bodies do.”

“Then it can be saved and healed,” Dorothea answered. “I wouldn’t be afraid to ask Mr. Lydgate for the truth so I could help him. Why should I be afraid? Since I’m not to have the land, James, I could do what Mr. Bulstrode suggested and take over his support of the hospital. I must consult Mr. Lydgate to understand what good we can hope to do by keeping the present plans. That gives me the best possible opportunity to ask for his confidence. He could tell me things that explain everything. Then we could all stand by him and bring him through his trouble. People praise every kind of courage except the courage they could show for their own neighbors.” Her eyes shone with moisture. The change in her voice woke her uncle, who began listening.
“It’s true that a woman may attempt some expressions of sympathy that would scarcely succeed if a man tried them,” said Farebrother, almost persuaded by her intensity.
