“Surely a woman ought to be cautious and listen to people who know more of the world,” Sir James said with his small frown. “Whatever you eventually do, Dorothea, you really should hold back for now and not volunteer to interfere in this Bulstrode affair. We don’t yet know what might emerge. You must agree?” he concluded, turning to Farebrother.
“I do think waiting would be wiser,” Farebrother replied.

“Yes, yes, my dear,” Brooke put in. He did not quite know where the discussion had got to, but offered something generally applicable. “It’s easy to go too far, you know. Don’t let your ideas carry you away. And rushing to put money into schemes—that won’t do. Garth has got me spending remarkably heavily on repairs, drainage, that sort of thing. One thing after another, and I’m very much out of pocket. I must rein it in. And you, Chettam, you’re spending a fortune on those oak fences round your estate.”
Submitting unhappily to this discouragement, Dorothea went with Celia into the library, which she generally used as a drawing room.

“Now, Dodo, do listen to James,” Celia said. “Otherwise you’ll get yourself into trouble. You always did, and you always will, when you insist on pleasing yourself. After everything, I think it’s a blessing you have James to think for you. He lets you keep your plans, only he stops people taking advantage of you. That’s the good of having a brother instead of a husband. A husband wouldn’t let you keep your plans.”
“As though I wanted a husband!” Dorothea said. “I only want my feelings to stop being checked at every turn.” Mrs. Casaubon had still not mastered herself enough to prevent angry tears.

“Really, Dodo,” said Celia, her voice a little more throaty than usual, “you _are_ contradictory. First one thing, then another. You used to give in to Mr. Casaubon quite shamefully. I believe you’d have stopped visiting me altogether if he’d asked.”
“Of course I gave in to him. It was my duty. It came from my feeling for him,” Dorothea said, looking through the prism of her tears.

“Then why can’t you think it your duty to give in a little to James?” Celia asked, feeling the force of her argument. “He only wants what’s best for you. And of course men know best about everything except the things women know better.” Dorothea laughed and forgot to cry.
“Well, I mean babies and things like that,” Celia explained. “I wouldn’t give in to James when I knew he was wrong, the way you did with Mr. Casaubon.”

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXIII
paragraphs:
Pity the burdened: this wandering sorrow
May visit you and me.

Lydgate reassured Mrs. Bulstrode by explaining that her husband had felt faint at the meeting, but he hoped to see him better soon. He would return the next day unless she sent for him earlier. Then he went straight home, mounted his horse, and rode three miles out of town simply to put himself beyond anyone’s reach.

He felt himself growing furious and unreasonable, as though tormented by stings. He was ready to curse the day he had come to Middlemarch. Everything that had happened there seemed merely preparation for this hateful catastrophe. It had blighted his honorable ambition and would make even people with the most commonplace standards think his reputation ruined beyond repair. At such moments a man can hardly remain loving. Lydgate saw himself as the victim and everyone else as the agents of his suffering. He had meant things to turn out so differently; others had forced their way into his life and defeated his purposes. His marriage seemed an absolute disaster. He was afraid to see Rosamond before exhausting this lonely rage, in case the sight of her drove him to unjustifiable behavior. Most people pass through times when their best qualities do no more than cast a warning shadow across the objects occupying their minds. Just then Lydgate’s tenderness existed only as a fear of violating it, not as a feeling that moved him to be tender. He was profoundly miserable. Only those who know the primacy of an intellectual life, one carrying the seed of ennobling thought and purpose, can understand the grief of falling from its serene activity into an all-consuming struggle with worldly troubles that wears the soul away.

How could he go on living among people who suspected him of dishonor without clearing his name? How could he silently leave Middlemarch as though retreating before a deserved condemnation? Yet how could he begin to defend himself?

The scene at the meeting had supplied no details, but it had made his position entirely clear. Bulstrode had feared disgraceful revelations from Raffles. Lydgate could now reconstruct the likely course of events. “He was afraid something would come out within my hearing. He wanted to bind me to him by a heavy obligation. That explains the sudden change from hardness to generosity. And he may have interfered with the patient’s treatment—disobeyed my instructions. I’m afraid he did. But whether he did or not, everyone believes he somehow poisoned the man and that I overlooked the crime, if I didn’t help him. And yet—and yet he may be innocent of that last offense. It’s just possible his change towards me was a sincere softening, the result of reflection, as he said. What we call ‘just possible’ is sometimes true, while the more believable story is utterly false. Despite my suspicions, Bulstrode may have kept his hands clean in his final dealings with this man.”

His position was cruel enough to numb him. Suppose he put aside everything except his own defense, treated the shrugs, cold looks, and avoidance as a formal accusation, and publicly stated every fact he knew. Who would believe him? It would be foolish to offer himself as his own witness and say, “I didn’t accept the money as a bribe.” The circumstances would always outweigh his assertion. Besides, telling everything about himself would require statements about Bulstrode that would deepen other people’s suspicions. He would have to explain that he had known nothing of Raffles when he first told Bulstrode how urgently he needed money. He had innocently accepted the loan as a response to that appeal, unaware that being called to attend this patient might have given Bulstrode a new motive. And, after all, those suspicions about Bulstrode’s motives might be unjust.

Then came the question: would he have acted exactly the same way without the money? Certainly, if Raffles had still been alive and capable of further treatment when he arrived, and if he had suspected Bulstrode of disobeying instructions, he would have investigated rigorously. Had his suspicions proved correct, he would have withdrawn from the case despite his recent heavy obligation. But without the money—if Bulstrode had never withdrawn his cold advice to declare bankruptcy—would Lydgate have asked no questions even after finding the man dead? Would reluctance to insult Bulstrode, the uncertainty of every medical treatment, and the knowledge that most of his colleagues would call his own treatment wrong have carried exactly the same weight?

That was the troubled corner of his conscience as he reviewed the facts and resisted blame. Had he been independent, he would have held most firmly to the patient's treatment and the clear rule that he must do, or ensure was done, whatever he believed best for a life entrusted to him. Instead, he had accepted that disobeying his instructions, however it happened, could not count as a crime; that prevailing medical opinion thought following them just as likely to be fatal; and that the matter was simply one of etiquette. Yet in his freer days he had repeatedly condemned turning uncertainty about disease into uncertainty about duty. He had said, “Even a wholly experimental treatment can be conscientious. My job is to care for life and do the best I can devise for it. Science ought to be more scrupulous than dogma. Dogma licenses error, but science lives by fighting error and must keep conscience awake.” Alas, scientific conscience had fallen into the degrading company of financial obligation and selfish concern.

“Is there a single doctor in Middlemarch who would question himself as I do?” poor Lydgate demanded, rebelling again against the weight of his circumstances. “Yet they’ll all think themselves justified in keeping their distance, as though I were a leper. My practice and my reputation are finished. I can see that. Even solid evidence clearing me would hardly matter to the blessed people here. They’ve marked me as tainted, and I’d remain cheap in their eyes.”

There had already been plenty of signs that puzzled him. Just as he was paying his debts and cheerfully regaining his footing, townspeople began avoiding him or looking at him strangely. In two cases he learned that his patients had called another practitioner. The reason was obvious now. His general exclusion had begun.

With Lydgate’s forceful nature, it was natural that feeling hopelessly misjudged should turn into stubborn resistance. The scowl that sometimes crossed his broad forehead meant something. Riding back into town after those first hours of raw pain, he was already deciding to stay in Middlemarch despite the worst anyone could do. He would not retreat before slander as though accepting it. He would face it fully and do nothing to suggest fear. Generosity as well as defiance made him resolve to show, without flinching, the full extent of his obligation to Bulstrode. Association with the man had indeed ruined him. If he still had the thousand pounds in his hands and all his debts unpaid, he would return the money and accept beggary rather than a rescue stained by suspicion of bribery—for remember, he was among the proudest of men. Nevertheless, he would not abandon this crushed fellow human being whose help he had used, or try to win a miserable acquittal for himself by joining the cries against someone else. “I’ll do what I believe is right and explain myself to nobody. They’ll try to starve me out, but—” His determination was still hardening when he drew near home. The thought of Rosamond pressed back into the foremost place from which wounded honor and pride had driven it.

How would Rosamond receive it? Here was another length of chain to drag, and poor Lydgate was in no mood to endure her silent rule. He felt no urge to tell her of the trouble that must soon be theirs together. He preferred to wait until events inevitably disclosed it.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXIV
paragraphs:
“In your mercy, let us grow old together.”
—BOOK OF TOBIT: _Marriage Prayer_.

A wife in Middlemarch could not remain unaware for long that the town thought badly of her husband. No close woman friend might go so far as to tell her plainly the unpleasant thing people knew or believed about him. But when a woman with plenty of leisure for thought suddenly found those thoughts occupied by something seriously damaging to her neighbors, various moral impulses encouraged her to speak. One was frankness. In Middlemarch, being frank meant taking an early opportunity to tell friends that you had a poor opinion of their abilities, behavior, or circumstances. Vigorous frankness never waited to be asked. Then there was love of truth—a broad expression which, in this setting, meant strongly objecting to a wife’s looking happier than her husband’s character justified, or seeming too pleased with her situation. The poor creature needed a hint that if she knew the truth she would take less satisfaction in her bonnet and in the light dishes for a supper party. Strongest of all was concern for a friend’s moral improvement, sometimes called her soul. This could supposedly benefit from gloomy remarks accompanied by thoughtful stares at the furniture and a manner suggesting that the speaker was keeping something back out of consideration for the listener’s feelings. Altogether, an ardent charity was busy persuading virtuous minds to make a neighbor unhappy for her own good.

Few wives in Middlemarch could have inspired more of this moral activity through their marital misfortunes than Rosamond and her aunt Bulstrode, though in different ways. Nobody disliked Mrs. Bulstrode, and she had never knowingly harmed anyone. Men had always found her a handsome, comfortable woman. They counted it among Bulstrode’s hypocrisies that he had chosen a warm-blooded Vincy instead of some pale, miserable woman suited to his low opinion of earthly pleasure. When the scandal emerged, they said, “Poor woman! Honest as daylight. You can be sure _she_ never suspected anything wrong.” Women friends talked a great deal about “poor Harriet,” imagined how she would feel on learning everything, and guessed how much she already knew. They had no malice towards her. Rather, a busy benevolence wanted to determine what she ought to feel and do. Naturally this occupied their imaginations with her whole character and history, from the days when she was Harriet Vincy to the present. Reviewing her position inevitably brought in Rosamond, whose prospects were blighted by the same trouble. Rosamond received harsher criticism and less pity. Still, as a member of the long-established Vincy family, she too was considered a victim of marrying an outsider. The Vincys had weaknesses, but they were all on the surface. No one ever had to “find out” anything bad about them. Mrs. Bulstrode was cleared of any likeness to her husband. Harriet’s faults belonged to Harriet.

“She has always liked display,” said Mrs. Hackbutt, pouring tea for a small party. “Though she’s taken to making much of religion to suit her husband. She’s tried to put herself above Middlemarch by letting everyone know she invites clergymen and heaven knows who from Riverston and places like that.”
“We can hardly blame her,” Mrs. Sprague said. “Few of the best people here wanted to associate with Bulstrode, and she had to find somebody to sit at her table.”
“Mr. Thesiger has always supported him,” said Mrs. Hackbutt. “He must regret it now.”

“But he never liked him at heart. Everyone knows that,” said Mrs. Tom Toller. “Mr. Thesiger never goes to extremes. He keeps to what’s true in evangelical religion. Only clergymen like Mr. Tyke, who want Dissenters’ hymnbooks and that low sort of religion, ever found Bulstrode to their taste.”
“I hear Mr. Tyke is terribly distressed,” Mrs. Hackbutt said. “And no wonder. They say the Bulstrodes have practically supported half his family’s needs.”
“Naturally it discredits his doctrines,” said Mrs. Sprague, an elderly woman with old-fashioned views.
“People won’t boast of being Methodistical in Middlemarch for a good while now.”
“I don’t think we should blame people’s religion for their bad actions,” said the hawk-faced Mrs. Plymdale, who had so far been listening.
“Oh, my dear, we’re forgetting,” said Mrs. Sprague. “We shouldn’t discuss this in front of you.”

“I’m sure I have no reason to be biased,” Mrs. Plymdale said, coloring. “Mr. Plymdale has always been on good terms with Mr. Bulstrode, certainly, and Harriet Vincy was my friend long before her marriage. But I’ve always kept my own opinions and told her when she was wrong, poor thing. As for religion, I must say Bulstrode could have done all this, and worse, with no religion at all. I’m not saying there hasn’t been rather too much of it—I prefer moderation myself. But truth is truth. The men tried at the criminal courts aren’t all excessively religious, I suppose.”
“Well,” said Mrs. Hackbutt, neatly changing direction, “all I can say is that she ought to leave him.”
“I can’t agree,” Mrs. Sprague replied. “She took him for better or worse, you know.”
“Surely ‘worse’ doesn’t include discovering your husband belongs in Newgate prison,” said Mrs. Hackbutt. “Imagine living with such a man! I’d expect to be poisoned.”
“Yes, I think it encourages crime if men like that can still have good wives looking after them,” Mrs. Tom Toller said.
“And poor Harriet has been a good wife,” Mrs. Plymdale added. “She thinks no man equals her husband. Though it’s true he’s never refused her anything.”

“Well, we’ll see what she does,” Mrs. Hackbutt said. “I suppose she knows nothing yet, poor creature. I do hope I won’t meet her. I’d be terrified of saying something about her husband. Do you think she’s heard any hint?”

“I hardly think so,” said Mrs. Tom Toller. “We hear _he’s_ ill and hasn’t left the house since Thursday’s meeting. But she and the girls were at church yesterday in new Tuscan straw bonnets. Hers had a feather. I’ve never noticed her religion affecting her dress.”

“She always wears very modest patterns,” Mrs. Plymdale said, a little nettled. “And I know she had that feather dyed pale lavender specifically to keep it suitable. I must say Harriet does want to do right.”
“She can’t be kept ignorant for long,” Mrs. Hackbutt observed. “The Vincys know. Mr. Vincy was at the meeting. It will be a terrible blow to him: his daughter as well as his sister.”
“Indeed,” said Mrs. Sprague. “No one thinks Mr. Lydgate can keep holding his head up here. That thousand pounds he accepted just when the man died looks dreadful. It really makes you shudder.”
“Pride comes before a fall,” said Mrs. Hackbutt.
“I’m less sorry for the former Rosamond Vincy than for her aunt,” said Mrs. Plymdale. “She needed a lesson.”
“I suppose the Bulstrodes will live abroad,” Mrs. Sprague said. “That’s what families generally do after a disgrace.”

“And it will be a crushing blow to Harriet,” Mrs. Plymdale replied. “If ever a woman was broken by something, she will be. I pity her with all my heart. With all her faults, few women are better. Even as a girl she was so orderly, always kindhearted and open. You could look in her drawers at any time and find everything the same. She’s brought Kate and Ellen up that way too. Imagine how hard it will be for her to live among foreigners.”
“The doctor says that’s what he would advise the Lydgates to do,” Mrs. Sprague said. “He says Lydgate should have stayed among the French.”

“I dare say that would suit _her_,” said Mrs. Plymdale. “There’s that sort of frivolity about her. She gets it from her mother, not her aunt Bulstrode. Her aunt always gave her good advice and, I know, would have preferred her to marry someone else.”

Mrs. Plymdale’s circumstances complicated her feelings. Besides her friendship with Mrs. Bulstrode, the great Plymdale dyeing business had profitable dealings with the banker. This made her want the mildest account of his character to be true, but also made her more afraid of appearing to excuse him. Her family’s recent marriage connection with the Tollers had brought her into the best social circle. That pleased her in every respect except her inclination towards serious religious views, which she considered best in another sense. The sharp little woman’s conscience struggled to reconcile these competing kinds of “best,” and her grief and satisfaction over recent events. Those events would humble people who needed humbling, but would also strike her old friend hard. She would have preferred to contemplate Harriet’s faults against a background of prosperity.

Meanwhile, approaching disaster had so far affected poor Mrs. Bulstrode only by intensifying the private uneasiness she had felt ever since Raffles last visited The Shrubs. She had accepted the explanation that the hateful man had arrived ill at Stone Court and her husband had stayed to nurse him because he had once employed and helped him, creating a charitable obligation in his degraded helplessness. Since then, she had been innocently encouraged by her husband’s more hopeful talk about his health and his ability to continue in business. Her peace was disturbed when Lydgate brought him home ill from the meeting. Despite reassuring words over the following days, she wept alone, convinced he was suffering from more than physical illness: something was tormenting his mind. He would not let her read to him and scarcely allowed her to sit with him, saying his nerves could not bear sounds or movement. Yet she suspected he shut himself in his private room to work on his papers. Something had happened; she was sure. Perhaps a large financial loss, concealed from her. Afraid to question him, she spoke to Lydgate on the fifth day after the meeting, having left the house only for church.
“Mr. Lydgate, please be frank with me. I want to know the truth. Has something happened to Mr. Bulstrode?”
“A slight nervous shock,” Lydgate said evasively. He felt it was not his place to reveal the painful truth.
“But what caused it?” she asked, fixing her large dark eyes on him.

“There’s often something poisonous in the air of public rooms,” he replied. “Strong men bear it, but the more delicate the constitution, the more it suffers. It’s often impossible to explain the exact timing of an attack—or rather, why someone’s strength fails at one particular moment.”

His answer did not satisfy her. She still believed a misfortune had overtaken her husband and was being hidden from her. Concealment of that sort deeply offended her nature. She asked permission for the girls to sit with their father and drove into town to make some calls. If anything was known to have gone wrong with his affairs, she reasoned, she would see or hear some sign of it.

Mrs. Thesiger was out, so she drove on to Mrs. Hackbutt’s, across the churchyard. From an upstairs window Mrs. Hackbutt saw her coming. Remembering her earlier dread of this encounter, she almost felt consistency required her to send word that she was out. Against that stood a sudden, powerful wish for the excitement of a visit during which she was absolutely determined not to hint at what filled her mind.

Mrs. Bulstrode was therefore shown into the drawing room. Mrs. Hackbutt joined her with lips more tightly closed and hands rubbing together more than usual: precautions against speaking too freely. She was determined not to ask after Mr. Bulstrode.
“I’ve been nowhere but church for almost a week,” Mrs. Bulstrode said after the opening courtesies. “Mr. Bulstrode was so ill at Thursday’s meeting that I haven’t liked to leave home.”
Mrs. Hackbutt held one hand against her chest and rubbed its palm over the back of the other, letting her eyes wander across the rug’s pattern.
“Was Mr. Hackbutt at the meeting?” Mrs. Bulstrode persisted.
“Yes,” Mrs. Hackbutt answered without changing her posture. “I believe the land is to be bought by voluntary contributions.”

“Let’s hope there are no more cholera victims to bury there,” Mrs. Bulstrode said. “It’s a terrible affliction. Still, I’ve always thought Middlemarch healthy. Perhaps it’s being used to it since childhood, but I’ve never seen a town I’d rather live in, especially our end.”

“I’m sure I should be glad for you to remain in Middlemarch always, Mrs. Bulstrode,” said Mrs. Hackbutt with a small sigh. “Still, we must learn to accept our lot wherever it takes us. There will certainly always be people here who wish you well.”

Mrs. Hackbutt longed to say, “If you take my advice, you’ll leave your husband.” But she could see the poor woman knew nothing of the thunderbolt about to strike, and felt she could do no more than prepare her a little. Mrs. Bulstrode suddenly felt cold and shaky. There was plainly something unusual behind these words. Though she had set out determined to learn everything, she now found herself unable to maintain that courage. She changed the subject to the Hackbutt children and soon left, saying she would visit Mrs. Plymdale. On the way she tried to imagine that her husband had merely had an unusually heated exchange with one of his regular opponents at the meeting—perhaps Mr. Hackbutt. That would explain everything.

But conversation with Mrs. Plymdale made that comforting explanation impossible to sustain. “Selina” greeted her with sorrowful affection and moral instruction on the most ordinary subjects, behavior hardly explained by a normal quarrel whose main effect was to upset Mr. Bulstrode’s health. Mrs. Bulstrode had thought she could question Mrs. Plymdale more easily than anyone. Now she discovered, to her surprise, that an old friend is not always the easiest confidante. Memories of their relationship in different circumstances stood between them. She disliked being informed and pitied by someone long accustomed to treating her as the superior. Mrs. Plymdale’s mysteriously relevant remarks about never abandoning her friends convinced her that some misfortune had occurred. Instead of asking with her usual directness, “What is it you’re thinking of?” she wanted to escape before hearing anything plainer. She began to feel a disturbing certainty that the trouble went beyond money. Selina, like Mrs. Hackbutt, avoided responding to anything she said about her husband, as though avoiding mention of a physical blemish.

She said goodbye in nervous haste and told the coachman to take her to Mr. Vincy’s warehouse. During that short drive, not knowing increased her dread so much that she entered her brother’s private office with trembling knees and a deathly pale face in place of her usual healthy color. Seeing her had much the same effect on him. He rose from his desk, took her hand, and spoke with his usual reckless impulsiveness—
“God help you, Harriet! You know everything.”

Perhaps that moment was worse than any that followed. It held the concentrated experience by which a great emotional crisis reveals a person’s deepest inclination and foretells the final action beyond the intervening struggle. Without the memory of Raffles, she might still have imagined only financial ruin. Now, with her brother’s look and words, the thought of her husband’s guilt flashed into her mind. Terror brought the image of him publicly disgraced. An instant of burning shame followed, when she felt only the world’s eyes upon her. Then her heart leaped to his side, sharing his shame and isolation with sorrow but without reproach. All this happened in a flash as she sank into a chair and looked up at her brother standing over her. “I know nothing, Walter. What is it?” she asked faintly.
He told her everything, simply and in slow fragments, making clear how far the scandal exceeded the evidence, particularly concerning Raffles’s death.

“People will talk,” he said. “Even when a jury acquits a man, they talk, nod, and wink. As far as the world’s concerned, he might often just as well be guilty. It’s a crushing blow, and it hurts Lydgate as much as Bulstrode. I don’t claim to know the truth. I only wish we’d never heard either man’s name. You’d have done better to stay a Vincy all your life, and Rosamond too.” Mrs. Bulstrode said nothing.
“But you must keep up as well as you can, Harriet. Nobody blames _you_. Whatever you decide, I’ll stand by you,” her brother said with rough, sincere affection.
“Help me to the carriage, Walter,” she said. “I feel very weak.”
At home she had to tell her daughter, “I’m unwell, my dear. I must lie down. Look after your father and leave me quietly alone. I won’t have dinner.”

She locked her door. Before she could walk steadily towards her allotted place, she needed time to grow used to this damaged knowledge of herself, this life cut back so cruelly. A searching new light shone on her husband’s character, and she could not judge him gently. Details from the twenty years in which she had trusted and revered him, protected by his concealments, returned to make those years seem a hateful deception. He had married her with that wicked past hidden behind him. She had no faith left with which to deny even the worst accusations. Her honest, display-loving nature made sharing a deserved disgrace as bitter as any human being could find it.

Yet this imperfectly educated woman, with her odd patchwork of phrases and habits, possessed a loyal spirit. She had shared this man’s prosperity for nearly half a lifetime, and he had consistently cherished her. Now that punishment had overtaken him, she could not abandon him in any sense. There is an abandonment that still eats at the same table and sleeps in the same bed, making the deserted soul wither all the more through loveless closeness. When she locked her door, she knew she would unlock it ready to go downstairs, join her unhappy husband in his sorrow, and say of his guilt: I will grieve, not reproach. But she needed time to gather strength, to sob farewell to the gladness and pride of her life. Once she resolved to go down, she prepared with small actions a harsh observer might call foolish. They were her way of declaring to every visible and invisible witness that she had begun a new life embracing humiliation. She removed all her jewelry and put on a plain black dress. Instead of her elaborate cap and large loops of hair, she brushed her hair flat and wore a simple bonnet-cap. Suddenly she looked like an early Methodist.

Bulstrode knew she had gone out and returned saying she was ill. He had spent those hours in agitation equal to hers. He had anticipated her hearing the truth from others and accepted that prospect as easier than confessing. Now, imagining the moment had arrived, he waited in anguish for its consequences. He had made his daughters leave. Though he allowed food to be brought, he had touched none of it. He felt himself slowly dying in misery that no one pitied. Perhaps he would never again see affection in his wife’s face. When he turned towards God, the only answer seemed to be the weight of punishment.

At eight that evening the door finally opened and his wife came in. He dared not look up. His eyes remained lowered. As she approached, she thought he looked smaller, so withered and diminished. New compassion and old tenderness swept through her like a great wave. She laid one hand on his where it rested on the chair arm, and the other on his shoulder. Gravely but kindly, she said—
“Look at me, Nicholas.”

He started slightly, raised his eyes, and looked at her for a moment in half amazement. Her pale face, her changed, mourning clothes, her trembling mouth all said, “I know.” Her hands and eyes rested gently on him. He burst into tears, and they wept together as she sat beside him. They could not yet speak of the shame she was sharing or the actions that had brought it upon them. His confession and her promise of loyalty were both silent. Open by nature, she nevertheless shrank from words expressing their shared knowledge as she would have shrunk from falling sparks. She could not ask, “How much is only slander and unfounded suspicion?” And he did not say, “I am innocent.”

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXV
paragraphs:
“Le sentiment de la fausseté des plaisirs présents, et l’ignorance de
la vanité des plaisirs absents causent l’inconstance.”—PASCAL.

Rosamond’s spirits began to recover a little once the threatening figure had left the house and all the troublesome creditors had been paid. But she was not happy. Marriage had met none of her expectations, and its promise was completely spoiled in her imagination. During this short calm, Lydgate remembered how often his distress had made him stormy, and, conscious of what Rosamond had suffered, treated her with deliberate gentleness. Yet he too had lost some of his former spirit. He still thought it necessary to speak of a less expensive way of living as something they must naturally adopt, gradually trying to reconcile her to it and restraining his anger when she replied that she wished he would move to London. When she did not say this, she listened listlessly, wondering what she had left to live for. The harsh, contemptuous things her husband had said in anger had deeply wounded the vanity he had originally brought to such delighted life. His way of seeing things, which she considered perverse, kept alive a secret aversion: all his tenderness seemed a poor substitute for the happiness he had failed to give her. Their position among their neighbors had suffered, and she could no longer look forward to Quallingham. There was nothing to look forward to anywhere, except an occasional letter from Will Ladislaw. His decision to leave Middlemarch had hurt and disappointed her. Despite what she knew and guessed of his admiration for Dorothea, she secretly believed that he admired herself much more, or must inevitably come to do so. Rosamond was one of those women who spend much of their lives imagining that every man they meet would have preferred them if there had been any hope of winning them. Mrs. Casaubon was all very well; but Will had become interested in her before he knew Mrs. Lydgate. Rosamond took his manner of talking to her—a blend of teasing criticism and extravagant compliments—as a cover for deeper feeling. With him she enjoyed that pleasant stirring of vanity, that sense of romantic drama, which Lydgate’s presence could no longer conjure up. She even imagined—and what will men and women not imagine in these matters?—that Will overstated his admiration for Mrs. Casaubon to make her jealous. Such thoughts had occupied poor Rosamond before Will left. She believed he would have suited her much better as a husband than Lydgate. Nothing could have been further from the truth. Her unhappiness in marriage came from the conditions of marriage itself, its demands for self-restraint and tolerance, rather than from her husband’s character. But the easily imagined, unreal Better had a sentimental attraction that relieved her boredom. She invented a small romance to enliven her dull existence: Will Ladislaw would always remain a bachelor and live nearby, always available to her, harboring a passion they both understood but never fully expressed, which would flicker into flame now and then in interesting scenes. His departure had disappointed her in proportion to these hopes, and had made Middlemarch far more wearisome. At first, however, she could still dream instead of the pleasures to come from knowing the family at Quallingham. Since then her marriage troubles had deepened. With no other comfort available, she kept returning regretfully to that meager romance on which she had once nourished herself. Men and women sadly misread their own symptoms, mistaking vague, restless desires sometimes for genius, sometimes for religion, and still more often for a great love. Will Ladislaw had sent conversational letters, addressed partly to her and partly to Lydgate, and she had answered them. She felt their separation was unlikely to last forever. What she now wanted most was for Lydgate to move to London: everything would be pleasant there. She had begun quietly and resolutely working towards this when a sudden, delightful prospect revived her spirits.

It arrived shortly before the memorable town-hall meeting: a letter from Will Ladislaw to Lydgate. Most of it concerned his new interest in colonization schemes, but he mentioned in passing that he might have to visit Middlemarch in the next few weeks. A very pleasant necessity, he called it, almost as good as a schoolboy’s holidays. He hoped his old place on the rug was still available and plenty of music awaited him. The date, though, was quite uncertain. As Lydgate read the letter aloud, Rosamond’s face was like a flower coming back to life: it grew lovelier and more radiant. Nothing was unbearable now. The debts were paid, Mr. Ladislaw was coming, and Lydgate would be persuaded to leave Middlemarch for London, which was “so different from a provincial town.”

That was one bright patch of morning. Soon, however, the sky darkened over poor Rosamond. A fresh gloom had settled on her husband, and he kept its cause entirely from her, afraid to expose his wounded feelings to her indifference and misunderstanding. Before long she learned a painfully strange explanation, beyond anything she had previously imagined might threaten her happiness. In her renewed good spirits, she supposed Lydgate was simply suffering an unusually bad fit of moodiness: he left her remarks unanswered and plainly avoided her as much as he could. A few days after the meeting, without consulting him, she therefore sent invitations to a small evening party. She felt sure this was a sensible move. People seemed to have been keeping their distance, and needed drawing back into their former habits of visiting. Once the invitations were accepted, she would tell Lydgate and give him some wise advice on how a medical man ought to behave towards his neighbors. Rosamond could assume the gravest little air imaginable when discussing other people’s duties. But every invitation was declined, and the last reply fell into Lydgate’s hands.
“This scrawl is Chichely’s. What’s he writing to you about?” Lydgate asked in surprise, handing her the note. She had to show it to him. He looked at her sternly and said—

“What on earth made you send invitations without telling me, Rosamond? Please—no, I insist—don’t invite anyone to this house. I suppose you’ve asked other people and they’ve refused as well.” She did not answer.
“Are you listening to me?” Lydgate thundered.
“Yes, of course I can hear you,” Rosamond said, turning her head away like an elegant, long-necked bird.

Lydgate jerked his head with no elegance at all and left the room, feeling dangerously angry. Rosamond thought only that he was becoming more unbearable, not that some particular new cause lay behind his commanding manner. His reluctance to tell her anything he knew would not interest her was becoming an unconscious habit. Of everything connected with the thousand pounds, she knew only that her uncle Bulstrode had lent it. To her, Lydgate’s hateful moods and their neighbors’ apparent avoidance had begun, inexplicably, just when their financial troubles were relieved. If the invitations had been accepted, she would have gone to ask her mamma and the others, whom she had not seen for several days. Now she put on her bonnet to find out what had become of them all. Suddenly it felt as though everyone had conspired to leave her alone with a husband determined to offend everybody. Dinner was over when she arrived, and she found her father and mother sitting by themselves in the drawing-room. They greeted her sadly with “Well, my dear!” and nothing more. She had never seen her father look so dejected. Sitting down beside him, she asked—
“Has something happened, papa?”
He gave no answer, but Mrs. Vincy said, “Oh, my dear, haven’t you heard anything? You’ll hear soon enough.”
“Is it something about Tertius?” Rosamond asked, going pale. The thought of trouble immediately attached itself to everything in his behavior that she could not explain.
“Oh, my dear, yes. To think you should have married into such trouble. Debt was bad enough, but this will be worse.”
“Wait, Lucy, wait,” said Mr. Vincy. “Rosamond, have you heard nothing about your uncle Bulstrode?”
“No, papa,” said the poor girl. Trouble now felt unlike anything she had known before: an invisible force whose iron grip made her soul faint.

Her father told her the whole story, ending, “It’s best that you should know, my dear. I think Lydgate will have to leave town. Everything has gone against him. I dare say he couldn’t help it. I’m not accusing him of doing any harm.” Until now Mr. Vincy had always been inclined to blame Lydgate as much as possible.

For Rosamond the shock was dreadful. No fate, she thought, could be more cruel than hers: she had married a man who was now the center of disgraceful suspicions. In many circumstances people inevitably feel that the shame is the worst part of a crime. To understand, in these moments, that her trouble was less than if her husband had certainly committed a crime would have required a painstaking sorting of ideas quite foreign to Rosamond’s life. All the shame seemed present already. And she had married him so innocently, believing that he and his family would bring her distinction! With her parents she remained as reserved as usual, saying only that Lydgate would have left Middlemarch long ago if he had followed her wishes.
“She’s bearing it wonderfully,” her mother said after she left.
“Yes, thank God!” said Mr. Vincy, who was deeply shaken.

But Rosamond returned home feeling justified in her aversion to her husband. What had he actually done? How had he really behaved? She did not know. Why had he kept everything from her? He said nothing about it, and naturally she could not raise the subject herself. Once she thought of asking her father to let her come home again. But as she considered it, the prospect became utterly dreary. A married woman returning to her parents’ house—life in that position would have no meaning for her. She could not picture herself accepting it.

Over the next two days Lydgate noticed a change in her and concluded that she had heard the news. Would she speak about it, or remain forever silent in a way that seemed to say she thought him guilty? We must remember that his state of mind was unhealthy: almost every encounter hurt him. Certainly Rosamond had just as much reason here to complain that he held back and failed to confide in her. But his bitterness supplied his own excuse. Was he not right to shrink from telling her, when, now she knew the truth, she felt no impulse to speak to him? Beneath this, however, an awareness of his own fault made him restless. Their silence grew unbearable. It was as though they were drifting on the same piece of wreckage, each looking away from the other.
“I’m a fool,” he thought. “Haven’t I stopped expecting anything? I married a burden, not a support.” That evening he said—
“Rosamond, have you heard something that has upset you?”
“Yes,” she replied, putting down the sewing she had been doing in a listless, half-conscious way, very unlike her usual manner.
“What did you hear?”
“All of it, I suppose. Papa told me.”
“That people believe I’ve disgraced myself?”
“Yes,” Rosamond said faintly, automatically taking up her sewing again.
Neither spoke. Lydgate thought, “If she trusts me at all—if she has any idea what sort of man I am—she ought to say now that she doesn’t believe I’ve deserved this disgrace.”

Rosamond, meanwhile, went on moving her fingers listlessly. She expected Tertius to supply whatever needed saying. What did she know about it? And if he had done nothing wrong, why did he not take steps to clear his name?

Her silence poured fresh bitterness into the mood in which Lydgate had been telling himself that no one believed in him. Even Farebrother had not come forward. He had begun questioning her in the hope that talking would dispel the cold fog between them; now despairing resentment checked his resolve. This trouble, like every other, seemed to be hers alone in her eyes. To her he was always a separate creature, doing things she disliked. Anger drove him out of his chair. With his hands thrust into his pockets, he paced the room. All the while he knew underneath that he would have to master his temper, explain everything, and make her understand the facts. He had almost learned that he must adapt himself to her nature, and that the less sympathy she could give, the more he must offer. Soon he returned to his intention of speaking openly: he must not lose this opportunity. If he could make her seriously understand that this was a slander they must face rather than escape, and that the whole trouble had sprung from his desperate need of money, he could use the moment to urge them to unite in spending as little as possible. That would let them weather the difficult time and preserve their independence. He would specify the changes he wanted and bring her to consent willingly. He was obliged to try. What else could he do?

He did not know how long he had been pacing uneasily, but Rosamond felt it had been a long time and wished he would sit down. She too had begun to see this as an opportunity to impress upon Tertius what he ought to do. Whatever the truth behind all this misery, one particular fear insisted on being heard.

At last Lydgate sat down, choosing a chair nearer Rosamond instead of his usual one. He leaned towards her and looked at her gravely before returning to the painful subject. He had brought himself under control so far, and was about to speak solemnly, as though this were an opportunity that would never come again. His lips had actually parted when Rosamond dropped her hands, looked at him, and said—
“Surely, Tertius—”
“What is it?”

“Surely you’ve finally abandoned the idea of staying in Middlemarch. I can’t keep living here. Let’s move to London. Papa says you ought to leave, and so does everyone else. Whatever unhappiness I have to bear, it will be easier somewhere else.”

The words struck Lydgate painfully. In place of the crucial outpouring he had struggled to prepare, the old argument lay before him once again. It was more than he could stand. His expression changed abruptly; he got up and left.

Perhaps the evening might have ended better if he had been strong enough to persist in giving more because she gave less. Had his energy carried him past that rebuff, he might still have changed Rosamond’s understanding and her will. We cannot be certain that any nature, however rigid or peculiar, can resist the influence of a more powerful nature. People may be overwhelmed and, for a time, transformed, becoming part of the soul that enfolds them in the fervor of its movement. But poor Lydgate carried a throbbing pain inside him, and his strength had failed before its task was done.

Mutual understanding and a shared resolution seemed as distant as ever—more distant, indeed, because the sense of having tried and failed now blocked the way. Day followed day with their thoughts still separate. Lydgate did what work remained to him in despair; Rosamond felt, with some reason, that he was treating her cruelly. There was no point in saying anything to Tertius. But when Will Ladislaw arrived, she was determined to tell him everything. Reserved though she generally was, she needed someone to acknowledge her wrongs.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXVI
paragraphs:
To mercy, pity, peace, and love
All pray in their distress,
And to these virtues of delight,
Return their thankfulness.
. . . . . .
For Mercy has a human heart,
Pity a human face;
And Love, the human form divine;
And Peace, the human dress.
—WILLIAM BLAKE: _Songs of Innocence_.

A few days later, Lydgate rode to Lowick Manor at Dorothea’s request. The invitation had not surprised him. It followed a letter from Mr. Bulstrode saying that he had resumed his preparations to leave Middlemarch and reminding Lydgate of their earlier correspondence about the Hospital, whose substance remained unchanged. Before proceeding, he had felt obliged to raise the matter again with Mrs. Casaubon; she now wished, as she had before, to discuss it with Lydgate. “Your views may possibly have undergone some change,” Mr. Bulstrode wrote, “but in that case, too, it is desirable that you should explain them to her.”

Dorothea waited for him with eager interest. Out of deference to her male advisers she had avoided what Sir James called “interfering in this Bulstrode business,” but Lydgate’s difficult position was continually on her mind. When Bulstrode approached her again about the hospital, she felt that the opportunity she had been prevented from hastening had at last arrived of itself. In her comfortable home, as she walked beneath the branches of her own great trees, her thoughts reached out towards other people’s lives while her feelings remained imprisoned. The prospect of doing some actual good within her power “haunted her like a passion.” Once another person’s need had taken definite shape in her mind, the longing to relieve it absorbed her desires and robbed her own comfort of its pleasure. She approached this meeting with confident hope, ignoring what people said of Lydgate’s reserve, ignoring the fact that she was a very young woman. When she felt moved to express her kinship with another human being, nothing could seem less relevant to Dorothea than dwelling on her age and sex.

Waiting in the library, she could do nothing except relive the scenes that had made Lydgate part of her memories. Their importance all came from her marriage and its sorrows—but no: on two occasions the thought of Lydgate had been painfully connected with his wife and someone else. That pain had subsided, yet it had awakened speculation about what his marriage might mean to him, and made her sensitive to the smallest mention of Mrs. Lydgate. These thoughts played out like a drama, brightening her eyes and holding her whole body in suspense, though she was merely looking from the brown library towards the lawn and the bright green buds standing out against dark evergreens.

When Lydgate entered, the alteration in his face almost shocked her. She had not seen him for two months, and the change was unmistakable. He had not grown thin: it was the look that even young faces soon acquire when resentment and discouragement persist. As she offered her hand, her warm expression softened his, but only into sadness.

“I’ve wanted very much to see you for some time, Mr. Lydgate,” Dorothea said when they were seated facing each other. “But I waited to ask you until Mr. Bulstrode spoke to me again about the Hospital. I know that the benefit of managing it separately from the Infirmary depends on you—or at least on the good you think you could achieve by directing it yourself. And I’m sure you won’t refuse to tell me exactly what you think.”

“You’re deciding whether to support the Hospital generously,” Lydgate replied. “In good conscience, I can’t advise you to do that on the strength of any work I might undertake. I may have to leave the town.”
His manner was abrupt. He felt the painful hopelessness of trying to carry out any purpose against which Rosamond had set her will.

“Surely not because no one believes in you?” Dorothea’s words came clearly, straight from her full heart. “I know about the dreadful misunderstandings. From the very first I knew they were misunderstandings. You have never done anything vile. You would never act dishonorably.”

This was the first declaration of faith in him that Lydgate had heard. He took a deep breath. “Thank you,” he said. Nothing more would come. It was a new and strange experience that a woman’s few words of confidence should mean so much to him.
“Please tell me exactly what happened,” Dorothea said without hesitation. “I’m certain the truth would clear your name.”

Lydgate sprang from his chair and walked towards the window, forgetting where he was. Again and again he had considered whether he could explain everything without making the appearances against Bulstrode worse, perhaps unfairly, and repeatedly he had decided he could not. So often had he told himself that his own statements would not alter people’s impressions that Dorothea’s suggestion sounded like a temptation to do something he had calmly judged unreasonable.
“Please tell me,” she said with simple earnestness. “Then we can think it through together. It’s wrong to let people falsely believe evil of someone when you can prevent it.”

Remembering where he was, Lydgate turned and saw Dorothea looking up at him with gentle, trusting seriousness. A noble nature, generous in its wishes and fervent in its kindness, changes the light in which we see things. We begin again to perceive their larger, calmer outlines, and to believe that others can understand and judge the whole of our character. This influence was beginning to reach Lydgate, who for days had seen life as someone sees it while being dragged, struggling, through a crowd. He sat down again, feeling his former self return because he was with someone who believed in that self.

“I don’t want to make things harder for Bulstrode,” he said. “He lent me money I needed, though now I wish I’d done without it. He’s being hunted down; he’s wretched, with only the frailest hold on life. But I would like to tell you everything. It will be a comfort to speak to someone who already believes me, where I won’t seem to be protesting my own honesty. You’ll understand what’s fair to someone else as well as what’s fair to me.”

“Please trust me,” Dorothea said. “I won’t repeat anything without your permission. At the very least, though, I could say you’ve explained all the circumstances and I know you’re entirely innocent. Mr. Farebrother would believe me, and my uncle, and Sir James Chettam. There are even people in Middlemarch I could approach: they don’t know me well, but they would believe me. They would know I had no motive except truth and justice. I’d take any trouble to clear your name. I have so little to do. There’s nothing better I could do in the world.”

The voice in which Dorothea offered this almost childlike picture of her actions might itself have seemed evidence that she could succeed. The penetrating tenderness of her woman’s voice appeared made to defend someone against hasty accusers. Lydgate did not pause to think her Quixotic. For the first time in his life he surrendered to the exquisite relief of relying wholly on generous sympathy, without proud reserve holding him back. He told her everything, beginning with the pressure of his difficulties and his reluctant first appeal to Bulstrode. As speaking brought relief, he expressed more fully what had passed through his mind. He explained how his treatment differed from prevailing practice, the doubts he had felt at the end, his ideal of a doctor’s duty, and his uneasy awareness that accepting the money had influenced his personal inclinations and professional conduct, though not his fulfillment of any publicly acknowledged obligation.

“I’ve since learned,” he added, “that Hawley sent someone to question the housekeeper at Stone Court. She said she gave the patient all the opium in the bottle I left, and a considerable quantity of brandy. But even leading doctors might ordinarily have prescribed that. The suspicions against me have no footing there. They rest on the fact that I accepted money, that Bulstrode had powerful reasons for wanting the man dead, and that he paid me to cooperate in some sort of malpractice against the patient—or at any rate bribed me to keep quiet. Those suspicions are the hardest to shake, because people want to believe them and they can never be disproved. Why my instructions weren’t followed is something I can’t answer. Bulstrode may still have had no criminal intention. He may even have had nothing to do with the disobedience, and simply failed to mention it. But none of that affects public opinion. This is one of those cases where a man is convicted because of his character: people believe he committed a crime in some unspecified way because he had a motive. And because I took his money, Bulstrode’s character has swallowed mine. I’m simply blighted, like a damaged ear of corn. It’s done, and nothing can undo it.”

“Oh, how hard it is!” said Dorothea. “I understand how difficult it is for you to defend yourself. But that all this should happen to you, when you intended to lead a life beyond the ordinary and discover better ways—I can’t accept that nothing can change. I know that was your purpose. I remember what you said when you first spoke to me about the hospital. No sorrow has occupied my thoughts more than that: to love what is great, to strive for it, and still to fail.”

“Yes,” said Lydgate, feeling that at last there was room for the whole meaning of his grief. “I did have ambitions. I meant my life to be different. I thought I had more strength, more control. But the worst obstacles are the ones no one except yourself can see.”

“Suppose,” Dorothea said thoughtfully, “suppose we continued the Hospital on its present basis, and you stayed, even with only a few friends to support you. The hostility would gradually fade. Opportunities would come when people would have to admit they had treated you unjustly, because they would see that your intentions were good. You might still become famous, like Louis and Laennec, whom I’ve heard you speak of. And we would all be proud of you,” she finished, smiling.

“That might work if I still had my old confidence in myself,” Lydgate said sadly. “Nothing hurts me more than the thought of turning and fleeing this slander, leaving it behind me unchallenged. Still, I can’t ask anyone to invest a large sum in a scheme that relies on me.”

“It would be well worth it to me,” Dorothea replied simply. “Just think. My money makes me very uncomfortable. People tell me I haven’t enough for the kind of great project I like best, yet I have too much. I don’t know what to do. My own fortune gives me seven hundred a year, Mr. Casaubon left me nineteen hundred a year, and I have between three and four thousand in the bank. I wanted to borrow money, repay it gradually from the income I don’t need, and buy land to establish a village that would be a school of industry. But Sir James and my uncle persuaded me the risk was too great. So you see, nothing would please me more than finding a good use for my money. I want it to improve other people’s lives. It makes me so uneasy that it all comes to me, when I don’t need it.”

A smile broke through Lydgate’s gloom. Dorothea’s childlike earnestness, her grave eyes as she said all this, were irresistible, joined in one lovable whole with her ready understanding of lofty experience. Of the lower experiences that occupy so much of the world, poor Mrs. Casaubon had only a dim, shortsighted knowledge, and her imagination did little to help it. She interpreted his smile, however, as encouragement for her scheme.
“I think you see now that you were being too scrupulous,” she said persuasively. “The hospital would be one good result; restoring your life and happiness would be another.”
Lydgate’s smile faded. “You have both the kindness and the money to do it,” he said, “if it could be done. But—”
He hesitated, looking vaguely towards the window, while she waited without speaking. At last he turned back to her and burst out—
“Why shouldn’t I tell you? You know what the bond of marriage means. You’ll understand everything.”
Dorothea’s heart began beating faster. Did he suffer in that way too? She was afraid to say anything, and he immediately continued.

“Now I can’t do anything, can’t take a single step, without thinking of my wife’s happiness. What I might choose if I were alone has become impossible. I can’t bear to see her miserable. She married me without understanding what she was entering into. Perhaps it would have been better for her if she hadn’t.”
“I know, I know. You couldn’t hurt her unless you had no choice,” said Dorothea, remembering her own life acutely.
“And she is determined not to stay. She wants to leave. All the trouble she’s had here has exhausted her,” Lydgate said, stopping again for fear of saying too much.
“But if she understood the good that might come of staying—” Dorothea protested, looking at him as though he had forgotten the reasons they had just discussed. He did not answer at once.

“She wouldn’t understand it,” he said finally and abruptly, feeling at first that the statement must stand without explanation. “And in fact I’ve lost all heart for continuing my life here.” After a pause, yielding to the impulse to show Dorothea more of his difficulty, he added, “The truth is, this trouble has reached her in a confused form. We haven’t managed to talk to each other about it. I don’t know quite what she thinks. She may be afraid I really have done something dishonorable. That’s my fault; I should speak more openly. But I’ve been suffering terribly.”

“May I visit her?” Dorothea asked eagerly. “Would she welcome my sympathy? I’d tell her that no one but you yourself has any grounds for blaming you. I’d tell her that every fair-minded person will be convinced of your innocence. I would comfort her. Will you ask whether I may come? I did meet her once.”

“I’m certain you may,” Lydgate said, taking up the suggestion with a little hope. “She would be honored—and comforted, I think—to see that at least you still respect me. I won’t tell her you’re coming; then she won’t associate it with any wish of mine. I know perfectly well I shouldn’t have left her to learn anything from other people, but—”

He stopped. For a moment neither spoke. Dorothea held back what was in her mind: how well she knew the invisible barriers that could prevent a husband and wife from speaking. Even sympathy could wound at such a point. Instead she returned to the outward circumstances of his position and said brightly—

“And if Mrs. Lydgate knew you had friends who believed in you and would support you, perhaps she would be glad for you to remain here, regain your hopes, and do what you intended. Then perhaps you would agree it was right to accept my proposal that you continue at the Hospital. Surely you would, if you still believe it offers a way to put your knowledge to use?”
Lydgate remained silent, and she could see him debating inwardly.
“There’s no need to decide at once,” she said gently. “It will be soon enough to answer Mr. Bulstrode in a few days.”
Still he hesitated; then he turned and spoke with his firmest resolve.

“No. I’d rather leave no time for wavering. I’m no longer sufficiently certain of myself—of what I could do, I mean, with my life so altered. It would be dishonest to let others undertake a serious commitment in reliance on me. In the end I might have to leave anyway; I can see little chance of anything else. It’s all too uncertain. I can’t agree to let your kindness be wasted because of me. No: let the new Hospital join the old Infirmary, and let things go on as they might have if I’d never come. I’ve kept a valuable register during my time there. I’ll send it to someone who can use it,” he finished bitterly. “For a long time I can think of nothing except earning a living.”

“It hurts me terribly to hear you sound so hopeless,” Dorothea said. “Your friends believe in your future and your ability to do great things. It would make them happy if you let them save you from this. Think how much money I have. It would lift a burden from me if you accepted some of it each year until the need to earn an income stopped tying you down. Why shouldn’t people do such things? It’s so hard to make everyone’s share at all equal. This is one way.”

“God bless you, Mrs. Casaubon!” Lydgate rose with the same energy that sounded in his words and rested his arm on the back of the large leather chair. “It’s good that you feel like that. But I’m not the man who should let himself benefit from it. I haven’t proved enough. At least I must not degrade myself by accepting a pension for work I never accomplished. It’s clear to me that I must plan only to leave Middlemarch as soon as I can. Even at best I couldn’t earn an income here for a long time, and—and necessary changes are easier in a new place. I must do what other men do: consider what will please the world and bring in money. Find a small opening in the London crowd and promote myself; set up in a spa town, or go south somewhere full of idle English people and arrange to be praised. That is the sort of shell I must crawl into and try to keep my soul alive inside.”
“But giving up the struggle like that isn’t brave,” Dorothea said.

“No, it isn’t brave,” Lydgate replied. “But what if a man fears a paralysis that keeps creeping over him?” Then his tone changed. “Yet your belief in me has given me much more courage. Everything feels more bearable since I’ve talked to you. If you can clear my name with a few others, especially Farebrother, I’ll be deeply grateful. Please don’t mention that my instructions weren’t followed. That would soon be distorted. After all, the only evidence in my favor is what people thought of me already. All you can repeat is my own account.”
“Mr. Farebrother will believe it, and others will too,” said Dorothea. “I can tell them enough about you to make it foolish to imagine you could be bribed into wickedness.”

“I don’t know,” Lydgate said, almost groaning. “I haven’t taken a bribe yet. But sometimes what people call prosperity is a faint shade of bribery. Then you will do me that other great kindness, and visit my wife?”
“Yes, I will. I remember how pretty she is,” said Dorothea, on whose mind every impression of Rosamond had been deeply engraved. “I hope she’ll like me.”

Riding away, Lydgate thought, “This young woman has a heart big enough for the Virgin Mary. She plainly gives no thought to her own future. She would pledge half her income immediately, as though she needed nothing for herself except a chair from which those clear eyes could look down on the poor mortals praying to her. She seems to possess something I’ve never seen in another woman: an inexhaustible friendship towards men. A man can be her friend. Casaubon must have inspired some heroic illusion in her. I wonder whether she could feel any other kind of passion for a man. Ladislaw? There was certainly something unusual between them. Casaubon must have suspected it. Well, her love might help a man more than her money.”

Dorothea, meanwhile, had immediately decided how to release Lydgate from his debt to Bulstrode. She was sure it formed one part, however small, of the painful pressure he endured. Still inspired by their conversation, she sat down and wrote a short letter. She argued that she had a better claim than Mr. Bulstrode to the pleasure of supplying the money Lydgate had needed. It would be unkind of him to refuse her the role of helping him in this small matter: the favor would be entirely to her, with so few clear uses for her surplus money. He could call her a creditor or anything else, so long as he granted her request. She enclosed a check for a thousand pounds and decided to take the letter next day when she visited Rosamond.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXVII
paragraphs:
“And thus thy fall hath left a kind of blot,
To mark the full-fraught man and best indued
With some suspicion.”
—_Henry V_.

The next day Lydgate had business in Brassing and told Rosamond he would not return until evening. Recently she had scarcely left the house and garden, except for church and one visit to her papa. On that visit she said, “If Tertius goes away, you’ll help us move, won’t you, papa? I suppose we’ll have very little money. I do hope someone will help us.” Mr. Vincy replied, “Yes, child, I don’t mind a hundred or two. At least I can see where that ends.” Apart from these outings, she had remained at home in listless sadness and uncertainty. Will Ladislaw’s arrival was her one source of hope and interest. She connected it with renewed pressure on Lydgate to arrange their immediate departure from Middlemarch for London, until she felt certain the arrival would powerfully bring about the departure, without having any idea how. This way of constructing a chain of events is too common to be considered a folly peculiar to Rosamond. Indeed, it is precisely such a chain whose breaking shocks us most. Understanding how an effect can be produced often means seeing possible failures and obstacles. But seeing only the cause we want, followed closely by the result we want, frees us from doubt and makes us intensely sure of our intuition. This was what happened in poor Rosamond’s mind while she arranged everything around her with her usual precision, only more slowly; or sat down intending to play the piano, then gave it up, lingering on the stool with her white fingers resting idly against the wooden front, gazing ahead in dreamy boredom. Her unhappiness had become so pronounced that Lydgate felt strangely timid before its constant, silent reproach. Strong as he was, his acute feelings for this beautiful, fragile creature, whose life he seemed somehow to have bruised, overpowered him. He avoided her gaze and sometimes started when she approached. Fear of her and fear for her returned all the more forcefully whenever exasperation had briefly driven them out.

That morning, however, Rosamond came down from her upstairs room, where she sometimes spent the entire day while Lydgate was out, dressed to walk into town. She had a letter to post to Mr. Ladislaw. Its charming discretion concealed an attempt to hurry his arrival by hinting at trouble. The maid, now their only indoor servant, noticed her coming downstairs in her outdoor clothes and thought, “Nobody ever did look so pretty in a bonnet, poor thing.”

Meanwhile Dorothea’s mind was full of her intended visit to Rosamond and the many thoughts of past and possible future that gathered around it. Until yesterday, when Lydgate had allowed her a glimpse of trouble in his marriage, Mrs. Lydgate’s image had always been linked with Will Ladislaw’s. Even in her most anxious moments—even when Mrs. Cadwallader’s painfully vivid account of gossip had disturbed her—Dorothea had tried, indeed had instinctively longed, to defend Will against any degrading suspicion. When she later met him, she initially took his words as a possible reference to feelings for Mrs. Lydgate which he had resolved not to indulge. Then she had a swift, sorrowful, forgiving sense of the attraction there might be in his constant opportunities for companionship with that beautiful woman, who probably shared his other tastes as clearly as she shared his love of music. But his farewell had followed: a few passionate words implying that Dorothea herself was the woman his love made him fear, that his love for her alone was what he intended to carry into exile without declaring it. Since that parting, believing in his love, taking proud delight in his sensitive honor and determination to give no one just grounds for accusation, Dorothea had felt entirely at peace about whatever regard he had for Mrs. Lydgate. She was certain it was innocent.

Some people’s love gives us a sense of being baptized and consecrated. Their pure belief in us commits us to goodness and integrity, and our sins become the worst kind of sacrilege, destroying the invisible altar of trust. “If you are not good, none is good”: those few words can make responsibility terrifying and give remorse a corrosive intensity.

Dorothea had such a nature. Her own passionate faults followed the few easily traced, open channels of her ardent character. Though she pitied other people’s visible mistakes deeply, her experience had not yet supplied the materials for intricate theories and suspicions of concealed wrongdoing. Yet this simplicity, which set an ideal before others through her trusting conception of them, was one of her greatest powers as a woman. From the beginning it had strongly affected Will Ladislaw. When he left her, he felt that the few words in which he had tried to express his feelings and the barrier her fortune placed between them would gain by their very brevity when Dorothea interpreted them. He felt he had found his highest valuation in her mind.

In that he was right. During the months since their farewell, Dorothea had found a sweet, though sorrowful, rest in their relationship, feeling it inwardly complete and unstained. A powerful spirit of resistance lived in her whenever she had to defend people or projects she believed in. The injustices she felt her husband had done Will, and the outward circumstances that made others look down on him, only strengthened her affection and admiration. Now the revelations about Bulstrode had brought out another fact affecting Will’s social standing, renewing Dorothea’s resistance to what was said of him in the part of her world enclosed by park fences.

“Young Ladislaw, the grandson of a thieving Jew pawnbroker” figured prominently in discussions of the Bulstrode affair at Lowick, Tipton, and Freshitt. It was a uglier label to hang on poor Will than “Italian with white mice.” Upright Sir James Chettam felt certain his satisfaction was righteous when he reflected, somewhat complacently, that another league had been added to the mountainous distance separating Ladislaw from Dorothea. Any anxiety on that score could now be dismissed as absurd. Perhaps he also enjoyed drawing Mr. Brooke’s attention to this unpleasant piece of Ladislaw’s ancestry, providing another light by which Brooke might see his own foolishness. Dorothea noticed the hostility with which Will’s connection to the painful story was repeatedly recalled. She said nothing, however. Unlike in earlier discussions of him, she was restrained by awareness of a deeper bond between them, one that must always remain sacredly secret. Her silence only enclosed her resistance in a more intense glow. This misfortune, which others seemed eager to throw at Will as a disgrace, added fervor to the thoughts that held her close to him.

She did not imagine they would ever be more closely united, yet neither had she assumed an attitude of renunciation. She simply accepted her relationship with Will as part of the sorrows of her marriage. To go on inwardly lamenting that she was not entirely happy would have seemed sinful; she was more inclined to dwell on the excess of advantages she possessed. She could bear to find the chief pleasures of tenderness in memory. Marriage suggested only an unwelcome proposal from some as yet unknown suitor, whose merits in her friends’ eyes would become a torment to her. “Somebody who will manage your property for you, my dear,” was Mr. Brooke’s alluring description of a suitable man. “I’d like to manage it myself, if I knew what to do with it,” Dorothea replied. No: she held to her declaration that she would never marry again. In the long valley of life ahead, apparently so level and empty of landmarks, guidance would come as she traveled the road and encountered her fellow travelers.

Since proposing to visit Mrs. Lydgate, Dorothea had felt this habitual attitude towards Will Ladislaw strongly throughout her waking hours. It formed a background against which she could see Rosamond without anything obstructing her interest and compassion. Evidently some separation of mind, some barrier to complete confidence, had grown up between this wife and the husband who nevertheless made her happiness his law. No outsider must touch that trouble directly. But Dorothea pitied deeply the loneliness that suspicion of her husband must have brought Rosamond. Surely showing respect for Lydgate and sympathy for her would help.

“I’ll talk to her about her husband,” Dorothea thought as the carriage took her towards town. The clear spring morning, the smell of damp earth, the new leaves showing their crumpled richness of green from half-opened coverings, seemed part of the happiness she felt after a long conversation with Mr. Farebrother. He had joyfully accepted the explanation that justified Lydgate’s conduct. “I’ll bring Mrs. Lydgate good news. Perhaps she’ll enjoy talking to me and want me as a friend.”

Dorothea had another errand in Lowick Gate, concerning a new bell with a fine tone for the schoolhouse. Since she had to leave her carriage close to Lydgate’s house, she told the coachman to wait for some packages and walked across the street. The front door stood open. The servant was taking the opportunity to look at the carriage waiting nearby when she realized that the lady it “belonged to” was approaching her.
“Is Mrs. Lydgate at home?” Dorothea asked.

“I’m not certain, my lady. I’ll find out, if you’ll come in,” said Martha. Her kitchen apron embarrassed her a little, but she had enough presence of mind to know that “mum” was not the proper address for this queenly young widow with a carriage and pair. “Please come inside, and I’ll go and see.”
“Tell her it’s Mrs. Casaubon,” Dorothea said as Martha led the way, intending to show her into the drawing-room before going upstairs to discover whether Rosamond had returned from her walk.

They crossed the wider part of the entrance hall and turned into the passage towards the garden. The drawing-room door was not latched. Without looking inside, Martha pushed it open, waited for Mrs. Casaubon to enter, and turned away. The door swung open and back again without a sound.

This morning Dorothea noticed her surroundings even less than usual, absorbed in images of things as they had been and would become. She passed through the doorway without observing anything unusual. Then a quietly speaking voice startled her with the sensation of dreaming in daylight. Unconsciously taking a step or two beyond the projecting edge of a bookcase, she saw something that made her stop, motionless and too shaken to speak. A dreadful certainty illuminated the scene, filling in every outline.

Will Ladislaw sat with his back to her on a sofa against the same wall as the doorway. Close beside him, turned towards him, was Rosamond, flushed and tearful in a way that gave her face a new brilliance, her bonnet hanging behind her. Will leaned towards her, holding both her raised hands in his and speaking with quiet intensity.

Absorbed in her distress, Rosamond had not noticed the figure silently approaching. But after the first immeasurable instant, Dorothea stepped back in confusion and found a piece of furniture blocking her. Rosamond suddenly saw her, jerked her hands free, and rose, staring at Dorothea, who had been forced to stop. Will Ladislaw sprang up and turned. Meeting the new flash in Dorothea’s eyes, he seemed to turn to marble. She immediately looked away from him to Rosamond and said steadily—
“Forgive me, Mrs. Lydgate. The servant didn’t know you were here. I came to bring an important letter for Mr. Lydgate, which I wanted to give you myself.”

She placed the letter on the little table that had blocked her retreat. Then, with one distant glance and bow that included both Rosamond and Will, she quickly left the room. In the passage she met the surprised Martha, who said she was sorry her mistress was out. Martha showed the unfamiliar lady to the door, reflecting that grand people were probably more impatient than others.
Dorothea crossed the street with her lightest, most vigorous step and quickly returned to the carriage.

“Drive to Freshitt Hall,” she told the coachman. Anyone seeing her might have thought that, though unusually pale, she had never shown more energetic self-command. That was indeed how she felt. It was as though she had swallowed a great draught of scorn that stimulated her beyond the reach of other feelings. What she had seen fell so far below her belief that her emotions recoiled from it and crowded together in agitation without an object. She needed action on which to expend that excitement. She felt capable of walking and working all day without food or drink. She would carry out the plan with which she had left that morning: visit Freshitt and Tipton and tell Sir James and her uncle everything she wanted them to know about Lydgate. His loneliness in marriage during this ordeal now had a new meaning for her and made her still more eager to champion him. In the struggles of her own married life, a quickly overwhelming pang had always prevented any such triumphant indignation. She took this feeling as a sign of new strength.

“Dodo, your eyes are so bright!” Celia said once Sir James had left the room. “And you don’t really see anything you look at—not Arthur, not anything. I know you’re going to do something uncomfortable. Is it all about Mr. Lydgate, or has something else happened?” Celia was used to watching her sister expectantly.
“Yes, dear, a great many things have happened,” Dodo answered in her rich voice.
“I wonder what,” said Celia, comfortably folding her arms and leaning forward on them.
“Oh, all the troubles of everyone on earth,” Dorothea said, raising her arms behind her head.
“Goodness, Dodo, are you going to make a scheme for them?” Celia asked, a little disturbed by this Hamlet-like outburst.
