But Sir James returned, ready to accompany Dorothea to the Grange. She completed her expedition successfully, holding firmly to her resolve until she stepped down at her own door.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXVIII
paragraphs:
“Would it were yesterday and I i’ the grave,
With her sweet faith above for monument.”

Rosamond and Will stood motionless for neither knew how long. He stared at the place where Dorothea had stood; she watched him uncertainly. To Rosamond it felt endless, though deep down what had happened pleased her almost more than it troubled her. Shallow people imagine that others’ emotions are easily governed. They trust their own small enchantments to divert the deepest currents, and believe that pretty gestures and remarks can make the unreal seem real. She knew Will had suffered a terrible blow, but she was little accustomed to imagining other minds except as material her wishes could shape. She believed in her power to soothe him or bring him round. Even Tertius, the most contrary of men, always yielded in the end. Circumstances had been stubborn, but Rosamond would still have said, as she had before marriage, that she never abandoned anything on which she had set her heart.
She reached out and rested her fingertips on Will’s sleeve.

“Don’t touch me!” he cried, his voice cutting like a whip. He sprang away from her, flushing, turning pale, then flushing again, as though the painful sting sent tingling through his whole body. Wheeling to the other side of the room, he stood facing her, fingertips in his pockets and head thrown back. His fierce gaze fixed not on Rosamond herself but on a point a few inches to one side of her.

She was deeply offended, but expressed it in signs only Lydgate had learned to read. Suddenly still, she sat down, untied her fallen bonnet, and put it aside with her shawl. The small hands she folded in front of her were icy.

It would have been safer for Will to pick up his hat and leave immediately. But he felt no impulse to go. Instead he had a dreadful desire to remain and crush Rosamond with his anger. Enduring the disaster she had brought on him without releasing his fury seemed as impossible as asking a panther wounded by a spear not to leap and bite. Yet how could he tell a woman he was ready to curse her? He raged against a restraint he was compelled to acknowledge. He hung in a dangerous balance, and Rosamond’s voice supplied the vibration that tipped it. With flute-like sarcasm she said—
“It would be easy enough to follow Mrs. Casaubon and explain that you prefer her.”

“Follow her!” he exploded, his voice sharp. “Do you imagine she would turn to look at me, or think anything I ever said to her again worth more than a filthy feather? Explain! How can a man explain himself at a woman’s expense?”
“You can tell her whatever you like,” Rosamond said, her voice trembling more.

“Do you think she would like me better for sacrificing you? She isn’t the kind of woman to feel flattered when I make myself contemptible—to think I must be faithful to her because I behaved like a coward to you.”
He began pacing with the restlessness of a wild animal watching prey beyond its reach. Soon he broke out again—

“Before this I had no hope, hardly any, of something better in the future. But I had one certainty: she believed in me. Whatever anyone said or did against me, she believed in me. Now that’s gone! She’ll always see me as a cheap fraud, too fastidious to accept heaven unless it came on flattering terms, yet secretly selling myself for any devil’s small change. She’ll think my very existence an insult to her, from the first moment we—”

Will stopped as though he had discovered something in his hands that must not be thrown down and broken. He found another outlet by seizing on Rosamond’s words again, as if they were reptiles to strangle and fling away.

“Explain! You might as well tell a man to explain how he fell into hell! Explain my preference! I never had a _preference_ for her, any more than I prefer breathing. Beside her, no other woman exists. I’d rather touch her hand in death than any other woman’s living hand.”

As these poisoned weapons struck her, Rosamond almost lost her sense of who she was. She seemed to be waking into a new and dreadful existence. There was none of the cold, determined resistance or silent self-justification she had felt during Lydgate’s fiercest anger. Every feeling had become a bewilderingly unfamiliar pain; she recoiled in fresh terror from a lash unlike any she had known. Another person’s feelings, opposed to her own, were burning and biting their way into her awareness. By the time Will stopped, she was a picture of sickened misery, her lips pale, her eyes full of dry dismay. Had Tertius stood opposite her, that suffering face would have pierced him. He would have dropped beside her to comfort her with the strong arms whose comfort she had so often undervalued.

We must forgive Will for feeling no such impulse of pity. He had felt no previous obligation to this woman, who had ruined the ideal treasure of his life, and he considered himself innocent. He knew he was being cruel, but he was not yet able to relent.

After speaking, he continued moving about half-absently while Rosamond sat entirely still. Finally he seemed to collect himself and picked up his hat, though he stood undecided for a few moments. After what he had said, ordinary polite words were difficult. Yet now that he was about to leave without another word, he shrank from the brutality of it; his anger was checked and left impotent. He went to the mantelpiece, rested his arm on it, and waited silently for he scarcely knew what. The vengeful fire still burned, and he could not retract anything. Nevertheless he remembered that he had returned to a hearth where he had enjoyed affectionate friendship, only to find calamity sitting there. Trouble had suddenly been revealed both within this home and beyond it. A foreboding tightened on him like slow pincers: this helpless woman, who had thrown herself upon him in the dreary misery of her heart, might come to enslave his life. He rebelled darkly against the possibility his quick perception showed him. When he looked at Rosamond’s ruined face, he thought himself the more pitiable of the two. Pain must first pass into the transfiguring life of memory before it can become compassion.

For many minutes they remained facing one another, far apart and silent: his face possessed by wordless rage, hers by wordless misery. The poor woman had no strength to fling any passion back at him. The terrible collapse of the illusion towards which all her hope had stretched had shaken her too completely. Her little world lay in ruins, and she felt herself swaying among them, a lonely, bewildered consciousness.

Will wished she would speak, casting some softening shadow over his own cruel words, which seemed to stare at them both and mock any attempt to renew their friendship. But she said nothing. At last, mastering himself with a desperate effort, he asked, “Shall I come and see Lydgate this evening?”
“If you wish,” Rosamond replied, barely audibly.
Then Will left the house, without Martha ever knowing he had entered it.

Once he had gone, Rosamond tried to rise but fainted back into her seat. When consciousness returned, she felt too ill to get up and ring the bell. She remained helpless until the girl, puzzled by her long absence, first thought of searching the downstairs rooms. Rosamond said she had suddenly felt sick and faint, and asked to be helped upstairs. There she flung herself on the bed fully dressed and lay apparently numb, as she had once before on a memorable day of sorrow.

Lydgate returned earlier than expected, around half past five, and found her there. Seeing that she was ill drove every other thought from his mind. As he felt her pulse, her eyes lingered on him more steadily than they had for a long time, as though his presence gave her some comfort. He noticed at once. Sitting beside her, he gently slipped his arm beneath her and bent over her. “My poor Rosamond! Has something upset you?” She clung to him, breaking into hysterical sobs and cries, and for the next hour he did nothing but comfort and care for her. He assumed Dorothea had visited, and that this disturbance of her nerves, plainly accompanied by a new turning towards him, came from the excitement of the new impressions that visit had created.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXIX
paragraphs:
“Now, I saw in my dream, that just as they had ended their talk, they
drew nigh to a very miry slough, that was in the midst of the plain;
and they, being heedless, did both fall suddenly into the bog. The name
of the slough was Despond.”—BUNYAN.

Once Rosamond was calm, Lydgate left her, hoping the sedative would soon let her sleep. He intended to spend the evening in his workroom and went into the drawing-room to collect a book. There on the table he found Dorothea’s letter addressed to him. He had not dared ask Rosamond whether Mrs. Casaubon had visited, but the letter confirmed it: Dorothea wrote that she would deliver it herself.

When Will Ladislaw arrived a little later, Lydgate’s surprise made it plain that he knew nothing of the earlier visit. Will could not bring himself to ask, “Didn’t Mrs. Lydgate tell you I came this morning?”
“Poor Rosamond is unwell,” Lydgate added as soon as they had greeted each other.
“Nothing serious, I hope?” Will said.

“No, just a slight shock to her nerves from being upset. She’s been under too much strain lately. The truth is, Ladislaw, I’m an unlucky devil. We’ve passed through several circles of purgatory since you left, and lately I’ve landed on a worse ledge than ever. I suppose you’ve only just arrived—you look rather worn out. You haven’t been in town long enough to hear anything?”
“I traveled through the night and reached the White Hart at eight this morning. I’ve been keeping to my room and resting,” Will said. He felt deceitful, but could see no alternative to the evasion.

He then listened to Lydgate’s account of the troubles Rosamond had already described in her own way. She had omitted the connection of Will’s name with the public scandal, since it did not directly concern her. He now heard of it for the first time.

“I thought I ought to tell you that your name has been mixed up in these revelations,” said Lydgate, who understood better than most how sharply Ladislaw might feel them. “You’re bound to hear as soon as you go out into town. I suppose Raffles really did speak to you?”

“Yes,” Will answered sardonically. “I’ll be lucky if gossip doesn’t make me the most disreputable figure in the whole affair. I imagine the latest account is that I conspired with Raffles to murder Bulstrode and left Middlemarch to carry out the plan.”
He was thinking, “Here is another pleasing association with my name to recommend me when she hears it. Still—what does it matter now?”

He said nothing, however, about Bulstrode’s offer. Usually open and careless about his private affairs, Will had among the finer qualities nature had given him a sensitive generosity that warned him to be silent here. He recoiled from saying he had refused Bulstrode’s money at the very moment he learned of Lydgate’s misfortune in accepting it.

Lydgate, too, withheld something even while confiding. He said nothing of Rosamond’s feelings about their troubles. Of Dorothea he said only, “Mrs. Casaubon is the one person who has come forward and said she doesn’t believe any of the suspicions against me.” Seeing Will’s expression change, he avoided mentioning her again. He knew too little of their relationship not to fear some hidden, painful effect of his words. It occurred to him that Dorothea was the real reason for this visit to Middlemarch.

Each man pitied the other, but only Will guessed the full extent of his companion’s unhappiness. When Lydgate spoke with despairing resignation of settling in London, and added with a faint smile, “We’ll have you back, old fellow,” Will felt an inexpressible sadness and said nothing. That morning Rosamond had begged him to urge the move on Lydgate. Now he seemed to be watching a magic panorama of his future, in which he slid into a joyless surrender to the small pressures of circumstance—a more common road to ruin than any single decisive bargain.

We stand at a dangerous edge when we begin passively watching our future selves, seeing our own figures led with dull acquiescence into petty wrongdoing and shabby accomplishments. Poor Lydgate stood inwardly groaning at that edge, and Will was approaching it. This evening he felt as though his cruel outburst to Rosamond had bound him to her, and he dreaded the obligation. He dreaded Lydgate’s unsuspecting affection. He dreaded his own disgust with a spoiled life, which might leave him aimlessly frivolous.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXX
paragraphs: When Dorothea had seen Mr. Farebrother that morning, she had promised to dine at the parsonage after returning from Freshitt. She and his family visited each other frequently, allowing her to say that she was not lonely at the Manor and, for now, resist the stern prescription of a lady companion. Arriving home, she was glad to remember the engagement. With an hour still left before dressing for dinner, she went straight to the schoolhouse to discuss the new bell with the schoolmaster and mistress. She attended eagerly to their small details and repetitions, creating a dramatic sense of a very busy life. On her way back she stopped to talk to old Master Bunney, who was sowing seeds in his garden. She conversed wisely with that rural sage about which crops gave the best return from a perch of land and what sixty years had taught him about soil: if it was reasonably loose and workable it would do, but if wet, wet, wet weather turned it all to mush, why then—

Discovering that sociability had made her rather late, she dressed in a hurry and arrived at the parsonage earlier than necessary. The house was never dull. Like another White of Selborne, Mr. Farebrother always had something new to report about his speechless guests and _protégés_, whom he was teaching the boys not to torment. He had recently acquired a pair of beautiful goats to serve as pets for the whole village, roaming freely like sacred animals. The evening passed pleasantly until after tea. Dorothea talked more than usual, speculating with Mr. Farebrother about the possible histories of creatures that converse so concisely with their antennae and, for all we know, may hold reformed parliaments. Then a few small, inarticulate sounds suddenly drew everyone’s attention.
“Henrietta Noble,” said Mrs. Farebrother, seeing her little sister moving anxiously among the furniture legs, “what’s wrong?”
“My tortoiseshell lozenge box is lost. I’m afraid the kitten has rolled it away,” said the tiny old lady, still involuntarily making her beaver-like noises.
“Is it a precious treasure, aunt?” Mr. Farebrother asked, raising his glasses and examining the carpet.
“It was a gift from Mr. Ladislaw,” Miss Noble answered. “A German box, very pretty. But whenever it falls, it spins away as far as it possibly can.”

“Oh, if Ladislaw gave it to you,” Mr. Farebrother said with deep understanding, rising to join the search. They finally found it beneath a chiffonier. Miss Noble seized it delightedly and said, “Last time it was under a fender.”
“My aunt’s heart is involved in this,” Mr. Farebrother told Dorothea with a smile as he sat down again.
“When Henrietta Noble becomes attached to someone, Mrs. Casaubon,” his mother said emphatically, “she’s like a dog. She would use their shoes as a pillow and sleep better for it.”
“Mr. Ladislaw’s shoes, I would,” Henrietta Noble said.

Dorothea tried to smile back. To her surprise and distress, her heart was beating violently, and every attempt to recover her earlier liveliness failed. Alarmed, afraid of revealing more of a change so clearly tied to its cause, she stood up and said softly, with undisguised anxiety, “I must leave. I’ve tired myself too much.”
Mr. Farebrother, quick to understand, rose too. “Of course. All that talking about Lydgate must have half exhausted you. Work of that kind catches up with us once the excitement is over.”
He offered his arm and accompanied her to the Manor. Dorothea made no attempt to speak, even when he said good night.

She had reached the end of her resistance and fallen helpless into the grip of an anguish she could not escape. After dismissing Tantripp in a few faint words, she locked the door. Turning from it towards the empty room, she pressed both hands hard on her head and moaned—
“Oh, I did love him!”

Then came an hour when waves of suffering shook her too violently to leave room for thought. Between sobs she could only cry in loud whispers for her lost belief, which she had planted from a tiny seed in Rome and kept alive ever since; for the lost joy of loving and trusting silently in someone others undervalued but she thought worthy; for the lost pride of a woman who believed she reigned in his memory; for the sweet, dim hope that somewhere along their paths they would meet, recognize one another unchanged, and take up the intervening years as if they were yesterday.

In that hour she repeated what solitude’s merciful eyes have witnessed for centuries in human spiritual struggle. She begged hardness, cold, and aching exhaustion to relieve the mysterious, bodiless power of her pain. She lay on the bare floor and let the night grow cold around her, her magnificent woman’s body shaken with sobs like a child in despair.

Two images, two living figures, tore her heart apart. It was as though she were a mother watching her child divided by a sword, pressing one bleeding half against her breast while her agonized eyes followed the other half, carried away by the lying woman who had never known a mother’s pain.

Here, as near as an answering smile, within the trembling bond of shared speech, was the radiant being she had trusted. He had come to her like the spirit of morning entering the dim vault where she sat married to an exhausted life. Now, with an awareness never fully awakened before, she stretched her arms towards him and cried bitterly that their closeness was only a parting vision. In the unrestrained expression of despair she discovered her own passion.

And there, distant yet constantly beside her, following every movement, was the Will Ladislaw who represented a changed belief drained of hope, an exposed illusion—no, a living man. From within her scorn, anger, jealousy, and wounded pride, no cry of sorrowful pity could yet struggle towards him. Dorothea’s anger did not easily burn itself out. It flared repeatedly into rejecting accusation. Why had he intruded his life into hers, which might have been complete enough without him? Why offer cheap affection and words born only on his lips to someone who had nothing petty to give in return? He knew he was deceiving her. At the very moment of farewell he had wanted her to believe he gave the full price of her heart, knowing he had already spent half of it. Why had he not remained among the crowd from whom she asked nothing, except to pray that they might become less contemptible?
At last even her whispered cries and groans took more strength than she had. She sank into helpless sobbing and, on the cold floor, sobbed herself to sleep.

She woke in the cold hours of early twilight, with everything dim around her. There was no startled wondering where she was or what had happened; she knew with perfect clarity that she was looking into sorrow’s eyes. Getting up, she wrapped herself warmly and sat in a large chair where she had often kept watch. Her strong constitution had endured the harsh night without illness, beyond aches and fatigue. But she had awakened into a different state. Her soul seemed released from its terrible struggle. She was no longer wrestling with grief; she could sit beside it as a permanent companion and let it share her thoughts. Thoughts now came thick and fast. Except during an overwhelming attack of pain, Dorothea could not remain inside the narrow cell of her own disaster, sunk in the stupefied misery that sees another person’s fate only as an incident in its own.

She began deliberately to relive the previous morning, forcing herself to consider each detail and what it might mean. Had she been alone in that scene? Did the event belong only to her? She made herself see its connection with another woman’s life—the woman she had set out to bring clarity and comfort to in her clouded youth. Leaving that hateful room in her first surge of jealous indignation and disgust, she had cast aside all the mercy that had prompted her visit. Her burning scorn had enveloped both Will and Rosamond; Rosamond seemed burned out of her sight forever. But the base impulse that makes a woman crueler to a rival than to an unfaithful lover could not return powerfully in Dorothea once her ruling sense of justice had subdued the turmoil and shown her a truer scale of things. All her earlier, active imagining of Lydgate’s trials and of this young marriage, with its hidden as well as visible troubles so like her own, returned with force. This vivid sympathetic experience asserted itself as acquired knowledge does, forbidding us to see as we saw in ignorance. She told her incurable grief that it must make her more helpful, instead of driving her away from effort.

And what crisis might this be in three lives whose contact with her own obliged her as though they were petitioners carrying the sacred branch? She need not invent people to rescue: they had been chosen for her. She longed for perfect Right to take its throne within her and govern her wandering will. “What ought I to do—how should I act now, this very day—if I could seize my own pain, force it to be silent, and think of those three?”

It had taken a long time to reach that question, and light was entering the room. She drew back the curtains and looked at the stretch of road visible beyond the entrance gates, with fields behind it. A man walked along the road with a bundle on his back, and a woman carried her baby. Figures moved in the field, perhaps a shepherd and his dog. Pearly light lay far away in the curving sky. She felt the vastness of the world and the countless awakenings of people to work and endurance. She belonged to that involuntary, pulsating life. She could neither observe it from her luxurious refuge as a mere spectator nor close her eyes in selfish complaint.

She did not yet see clearly what she would decide to do that day. But the sense of something she could accomplish stirred within her like an approaching murmur soon to become distinct. She removed the clothes that seemed to hold some of the weariness of her hard vigil and began washing and dressing. Soon she rang for Tantripp, who arrived in her dressing gown.

“Why, madam, you haven’t been in bed all this blessed night!” Tantripp exclaimed, looking from the bed to Dorothea’s face. Despite washing, she had the pale cheeks and pink eyelids of a mater dolorosa. “You’ll kill yourself, you _will_. Anyone would think you’d earned a little comfort by now.”

“Don’t worry, Tantripp,” Dorothea said with a smile. “I’ve slept. I’m not ill. I would like some coffee as soon as possible. And please bring my new dress. I’ll probably want my new bonnet today too.”

“They’ve been waiting there ready for over a month, madam. I’ll be grateful to see you wearing a couple of pounds’ worth less crape,” Tantripp said, bending to light the fire. “There’s reason in mourning, as I’ve always said. Three folds at the bottom of your skirt and a plain quilling in the bonnet—and if anyone ever looked like an angel, it’s you in a net quilling—that’s quite proper for the second year. At least that’s what _I_ think,” she finished, watching the fire anxiously. “And if a man married me imagining I’d wear those hideous weepers for him for two years, his own vanity would have deceived him, that’s all.”
“The fire’s all right, dear Tan,” Dorothea said in the manner of their old Lausanne days, though very softly. “Bring me the coffee.”

She curled into the large chair and rested her head against it in exhausted stillness. Tantripp went away puzzling over her mistress’s strange inconsistency: on the very morning when she looked more like a widow than ever, she asked for the lighter mourning she had previously declined. Tantripp could never have solved that mystery. Dorothea wanted to acknowledge that an active life still lay before her, even though she had buried a private joy. The old association of fresh garments with every new beginning lingered in her mind and made her reach even for that small outward assistance towards a calm resolve. The resolve was not easy.
Nevertheless, by eleven o’clock she was walking towards Middlemarch. She had decided to make a second attempt to see and save Rosamond, as quietly and unobtrusively as she could.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXI
paragraphs:
Du Erde warst auch diese Nacht beständig,
Und athmest neu erquickt zu meinen Füssen,
Beginnest schon mit Lust mich zu umgeben,
Du regst und rührst ein kräftiges Beschliessen
_Zum höchsten Dasein immerfort zu streben_.
—_Faust:_ 2r Theil.
When Dorothea returned to Lydgate’s door and spoke to Martha, he was preparing to go out in the adjoining room, its door partly open. Hearing her voice, he came to her at once.
“Do you think Mrs. Lydgate could see me this morning?” she asked, having decided it was better not to mention her earlier visit.

“I’m sure she can,” Lydgate said, keeping to himself his thoughts about Dorothea’s appearance, which had altered as much as Rosamond’s. “Please come in and let me tell her you’re here. She hasn’t been very well since you called yesterday, but she’s better this morning. I think seeing you again would probably cheer her.”

As Dorothea had expected, he plainly knew nothing of what had happened yesterday. Indeed, he seemed to suppose her visit had gone exactly as intended. She had brought a short note asking Rosamond to receive her, which she would have handed to the servant if he had not appeared. Now she was very anxious about the effect of his announcement.

After taking her into the drawing-room, he stopped, drew a letter from his pocket, and gave it to her. “I wrote this last night and meant to take it to Lowick on my ride. When you’re grateful for something beyond ordinary thanks, writing is less unsatisfactory than speaking. At least you don’t _hear_ how inadequate your words are.”
Dorothea’s expression brightened. “I have more to be grateful for, since you’ve allowed me to help you in that way. You _have_ agreed?” she asked, suddenly uncertain.
“Yes. The check will be sent to Bulstrode today.”

Without another word he went upstairs. Rosamond had only recently finished dressing and sat listlessly wondering what to do next. Even on her unhappy days, her usual diligence in small matters prompted her to begin some occupation, which she would drag through slowly or abandon for lack of interest. She looked ill but had regained her customary quiet manner, and Lydgate had been afraid to disturb her with questions. He had told her about Dorothea’s letter and check, and later said, “Ladislaw has arrived, Rosy. He sat with me last night; I expect he’ll call again today. I thought he looked rather worn and dejected.” Rosamond had not answered.

Now he approached her very gently. “Rosy, dear, Mrs. Casaubon has come again. You’d like to see her, wouldn’t you?” She flushed and gave a startled movement. This did not surprise him after the agitation yesterday’s meeting had caused—beneficial agitation, he thought, since it seemed to have turned her towards him again.

Rosamond dared not refuse. She dared not let even the tone of her voice touch yesterday’s events. Why had Mrs. Casaubon returned? She could fill that blank only with dread, for Will Ladislaw’s wounding words made every thought of Dorothea hurt afresh. Yet in this unfamiliar, humiliating uncertainty she could do nothing but comply. Without saying yes, she stood and let Lydgate place a light shawl around her shoulders. “I’m going out at once,” he said. Something then occurred to her, prompting her to ask, “Please tell Martha not to show anyone else into the drawing-room.” Lydgate agreed, thinking he understood perfectly. He took her to the drawing-room door and turned away, reflecting that he was a rather clumsy husband if his wife’s trust depended on another woman’s influence.

As Rosamond drew her soft shawl around her and approached Dorothea, inwardly she wrapped herself in cold reserve. Had Mrs. Casaubon come to discuss Will? If so, Rosamond resented the intrusion and prepared to meet every word with polite indifference. Will had wounded her pride too deeply for her to feel remorse towards him or Dorothea. Her own injury seemed much greater. Dorothea was not merely the “preferred” woman: as Lydgate’s benefactor she held another formidable advantage. In Rosamond’s confused and painful vision, this Mrs. Casaubon, this woman who dominated everything concerning her, must have come aware of her superior position and hostile enough to exploit it. Indeed, anyone who knew the outward circumstances, but not the simple impulse guiding Dorothea, might have wondered why she came.

Looking like a lovely ghost of herself, her slender grace folded in a soft white shawl, her rounded, childlike mouth and cheek inevitably suggesting innocence and gentleness, Rosamond stopped three yards from her visitor and bowed. But Dorothea had removed her gloves, following an irresistible impulse whenever she wanted to feel free. She stepped forward and offered her hand, her face sadly yet sweetly open. Rosamond could not avoid her gaze or prevent her own small hand from entering Dorothea’s gentle, motherly clasp. At once she began to doubt her assumptions. Quick to read faces, she saw that Mrs. Casaubon was pale and changed since yesterday, yet gentle, with the same firm softness as her hand. Dorothea, however, had overestimated her strength. The clarity and intensity of that morning’s thoughts continued a nervous exaltation that made her body as dangerously sensitive as the finest Venetian glass. Looking at Rosamond, she suddenly felt her heart swell and could not speak. All her effort went into holding back tears. She succeeded: only the ghost of a sob crossed her face. But it strengthened Rosamond’s impression that Mrs. Casaubon must feel very differently from what she had imagined.

Without any introductory words they sat on the two nearest chairs, which also happened to be close together. When she first bowed, Rosamond had intended to keep a great distance between them. Now she stopped imagining how things would unfold and merely wondered what would happen. Dorothea began speaking simply, growing steadier as she continued.

“I didn’t finish what I came to do yesterday. That’s why I’ve returned so soon. You won’t think me a nuisance when I explain that I wanted to talk about the unfairness shown to Mr. Lydgate. It will comfort you, won’t it, to hear things about him that he may be unwilling to say himself, precisely because they defend him and do him credit? You’ll be glad to know your husband has devoted friends who still believe in his good character. May I speak about this without your feeling I’m overstepping?”

Her warm, pleading voice seemed to flow with generous disregard above everything Rosamond had considered a barrier and a cause for hatred between them. It soothed her shrinking fears like a warm stream. Of course Mrs. Casaubon remembered those facts, but she did not intend to discuss anything connected with them. The relief was so great that Rosamond could feel little else just then. With her mind newly at ease, she answered graciously—
“I know how kind you’ve been. I’ll be glad to hear anything you wish to tell me about Tertius.”

“The day before yesterday,” Dorothea said, “I asked him to Lowick for his opinion about the Hospital. He told me everything he had done and felt in this unhappy affair that has led ignorant people to suspect him. He told me because I was very bold and asked. I believed he had never acted dishonorably, and begged him to explain what happened. He admitted he had told no one before, not even you, because he hated saying ‘I did nothing wrong’ as though that proved anything, when guilty people can say it too. The truth is that he knew nothing about this man Raffles, or any bad secrets involving him. He thought Mr. Bulstrode offered the money because kindness had made him regret refusing it earlier. His only concern for the patient was to treat him properly. He was a little troubled that the case didn’t end as he expected, but he thought then, and still thinks, that perhaps no one did anything wrong. I’ve told Mr. Farebrother, Mr. Brooke, and Sir James Chettam. They all believe in your husband. Won’t that comfort you? Won’t it give you courage?”

Dorothea’s face had grown animated. As it shone on Rosamond from so near, this self-forgetting fervor made her feel something like shy timidity before a superior. Blushing awkwardly, she said, “Thank you. You’re very kind.”

“And he felt how wrong he had been not to tell you everything. But you’ll forgive him. It was because your happiness matters to him more than anything else. He feels his life is one with yours, and nothing hurts him more than knowing his misfortunes must hurt you. He could speak to me because I’m an outsider. Then I asked whether I might visit you, because I felt so much for both your troubles. That’s why I came yesterday, and why I’m here today. Trouble is so hard to bear, isn’t it? How can we go on living, knowing someone is in trouble—in terrible pain—when we could help, and never even try?”

Carried entirely by the feeling she expressed, Dorothea forgot everything except that she was speaking from the heart of her own suffering to Rosamond’s. Emotion entered her voice more and more deeply, until its tones might have pierced to the marrow like the soft cry of a suffering creature in darkness. Without realizing it, she had again laid her hand on the small hand she had held before.

An overwhelming pang seized Rosamond, as though a hidden wound had been probed. She burst into hysterical tears, as she had when clinging to her husband the previous day. Poor Dorothea felt a great wave of her own sorrow returning: her thoughts had turned to Will Ladislaw’s possible part in Rosamond’s turmoil. She feared she might not master herself until the meeting ended. Though Rosamond had withdrawn her hand, Dorothea’s still rested on her lap as she struggled against rising sobs. She tried to control herself by thinking that this might be a turning point in three lives—not her own; there the irrevocable thing had happened—but those three lives touching hers with the solemn closeness of danger and distress. Perhaps there was still time to save the fragile creature crying beside her from the misery of false, incompatible attachments. This moment was unlike any other: she and Rosamond could never again meet with yesterday’s events so vividly alive in both. She felt their unusual relationship might give her an unusual influence, though she had no idea that Mrs. Lydgate fully understood how her own feelings were involved.

For Rosamond this crisis was even more unfamiliar than Dorothea could imagine. The first great shock had shattered the dreamworld in which she had been effortlessly confident in herself and critical of others. Now a woman she had approached with fear and aversion, convinced that jealousy must make her hateful, showed this strange, unexpected feeling. It made Rosamond’s soul reel still further with the sense that she had been walking through an unknown world which had suddenly broken in on her.

As her convulsed throat grew calmer, Rosamond lowered the handkerchief hiding her face. Her eyes met Dorothea’s as helplessly as blue flowers. After such crying, what use was it to think about her manner? Dorothea looked almost equally childlike, an unnoticed tear-mark still on her face. Pride had fallen away between them.

“We were speaking about your husband,” Dorothea said a little hesitantly. “The other day I thought suffering had changed his face sadly. I hadn’t seen him for weeks. He said he had felt very alone in this ordeal. But I think he could have borne everything better if he had been able to speak quite openly to you.”

“Tertius gets so angry and impatient whenever I say anything,” Rosamond replied, imagining he had complained about her to Dorothea. “He shouldn’t be surprised that I don’t want to discuss painful matters with him.”

“He blamed himself for not speaking,” Dorothea said. “What he said about you was that he couldn’t be happy doing anything that made you unhappy. Naturally, his marriage must influence every choice he makes. That was why he refused my suggestion that he keep his post at the Hospital: it would commit him to staying in Middlemarch, and he wouldn’t undertake anything that would hurt you. He could tell me that because he knows how much I suffered in my marriage through my husband’s illness, which frustrated his plans and made him unhappy. He knows I’ve felt how hard it is always to move in fear of hurting someone bound to us.”

Dorothea paused. She had seen a faint pleasure steal across Rosamond’s face. No answer came, so she continued with a growing tremor. “Marriage is unlike anything else. There’s something almost frightening in the closeness it brings. Even if we loved someone else more than—than the person we married, it would be useless.” Poor Dorothea, in her trembling anxiety, could only grasp at broken phrases. “I mean, marriage absorbs all our power to give or receive happiness through that kind of love. I know it may be very precious, but it kills our marriage. And then the marriage stays with us like a murder, and everything else is gone. And our husband—if he loved and trusted us, and instead of helping him we’ve made a curse of his life—”

Her voice had dropped very low. She feared she was presuming too much, speaking as if she were perfection instructing error. Absorbed in that anxiety, she did not notice that Rosamond was trembling too. Longing to express compassionate fellowship rather than blame, she placed her hands on Rosamond’s and spoke faster, more agitatedly. “I know, I know how precious the feeling may be. It takes hold before we realize it. It’s so hard—giving it up can seem like death. And we’re weak—I am weak—”

The waves of her own grief, from which she was struggling to rescue someone else, swept over Dorothea with overwhelming force. She fell silent in an agitation beyond speech. She was not crying, but felt as though something wrestled with her inwardly. Her face grew deathly pale, her lips shook, and she pressed her hands helplessly against those beneath them.

Rosamond was seized by an emotion stronger than her own and swept into a new current in which everything took on some unfamiliar, fearful, undefined aspect. Words failed her. Instinctively she kissed Dorothea’s forehead, which was very close. For a minute the two women held each other as though they had survived a shipwreck.

“What you’re thinking isn’t true,” Rosamond said in an urgent half-whisper, still feeling Dorothea’s arms around her. An unexplained necessity drove her to free herself from something that oppressed her almost like blood guilt.
They drew apart and looked at one another.
“Yesterday, when you came in—it wasn’t what you thought,” Rosamond continued in the same voice.
Dorothea stirred with surprised attention. She expected Rosamond to defend herself.

“He was telling me he loved another woman so that I would understand he could never love me,” Rosamond said, speaking faster as she continued. “And now I think he hates me because—because you misunderstood him yesterday. He says it’s my fault that you’ll think badly of him, that you’ll believe he’s false. But it won’t be my fault. He has never loved me; I know he hasn’t. He’s always had a low opinion of me. Yesterday he said no woman existed for him except you. Everything that happened was my fault. He said he could never explain it to you, because of me. He said you could never respect him again. But I’ve told you now, and he can’t reproach me anymore.”

Rosamond had unburdened herself under impulses entirely new to her. Dorothea’s emotion had overcome her and prompted the confession. As she continued, she increasingly felt that she was warding off Will’s reproaches, which still lay within her like a knife wound.

The reversal in Dorothea’s feelings was too powerful to call joy. In the tumult, the terrible strain of the night and morning resisted as pain. She could only recognize that this would become joy when her capacity to feel it returned. What she felt immediately was vast, unhindered sympathy. Caring for Rosamond no longer required a struggle. She answered her last words earnestly—
“No. He can’t reproach you anymore.”

With her usual tendency to think too highly of others’ goodness, her heart went out to Rosamond for the generous effort that had freed her from suffering. She did not reckon how much that effort reflected her own energy. After a short silence, she asked—
“You don’t regret my coming this morning?”
“No. You’ve been very good to me,” said Rosamond. “I didn’t expect you to be so good. I was very unhappy. I’m not happy now. Everything is so sad.”

“But better days will come. People will recognize your husband’s worth. And he relies on you for comfort. He loves you more than anyone. Losing that would be the worst loss of all, and you haven’t lost it,” Dorothea said.
She tried to put aside the overpowering thought of her own relief, afraid it might prevent her from drawing out some sign that Rosamond’s love was turning back towards her husband.

“Then Tertius didn’t complain about me?” Rosamond asked. She now understood that Lydgate might have told Mrs. Casaubon anything, and that this woman was certainly unlike other women. Perhaps a faint trace of jealousy entered the question. A smile began to move across Dorothea’s face as she replied—
“No, certainly not! How could you think so?” Just then the door opened and Lydgate came in.

“I’ve returned as your doctor,” he said. “After leaving, I couldn’t stop thinking about two pale faces. Mrs. Casaubon looked as much in need of care as you, Rosy. I began to feel I’d neglected my duty by leaving you together, so after going to Coleman’s I came back. I noticed you came on foot, Mrs. Casaubon, and the weather has changed. I think it may rain. May I send someone to have your carriage brought?”

“Oh, no! I’m strong; I need the walk,” Dorothea said, rising with a lively expression. “Mrs. Lydgate and I have talked a great deal. It’s time I left. People have always accused me of going too far and talking too much.”
She offered Rosamond her hand. Their quiet, earnest farewell had no kiss or other display of warmth: too much serious feeling had passed between them for its outward signs to be used lightly.
As Lydgate accompanied her to the door, she said nothing about Rosamond. Instead she told him of Mr. Farebrother and the other friends who had heard his account and believed it.
By the time he returned, Rosamond had flung herself on the sofa in resigned exhaustion.
“Well, Rosy,” he said, standing above her and touching her hair, “now you’ve spent so much time with Mrs. Casaubon, what do you think of her?”
“I think she must be better than anyone,” Rosamond replied, “and she’s very beautiful. If you go and talk to her so often, you’ll be more dissatisfied with me than ever!”
Lydgate laughed at “so often.” “But has she made you any less dissatisfied with me?”

“I think she has,” Rosamond said, looking up at him. “Your eyes look so heavy, Tertius. And do push your hair back.” He raised his large white hand to obey, grateful for this little sign of interest. Poor Rosamond’s wandering fancy had returned terribly chastened, humble enough to settle beneath the shelter she once despised. And the shelter was still there. Lydgate had sadly accepted his narrowed life. He had chosen this fragile being and taken the burden of her life into his arms. He must walk as best he could, carrying that burden tenderly.

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXII
paragraphs:
“My grief lies onward and my joy behind.”
—SHAKESPEARE: _Sonnets_.

Exiles famously live on hope and seldom remain banished unless they must. When Will Ladislaw exiled himself from Middlemarch, the only obstacle he set against returning was his own resolve. It was no iron barrier, merely a state of mind apt to dissolve into a minuet with other states of mind, bowing, smiling, and politely giving way. As the months passed, he found it increasingly difficult to explain why he should not make a short visit to Middlemarch, simply to hear something of Dorothea. If, during that brief stay, some strange coincidence brought them together, he need not feel ashamed of an innocent journey merely because he had previously expected not to make it. Since they were hopelessly separated, surely he could venture into her neighborhood. As for the suspicious friends who guarded her like dragons, time and a change of air made their opinions seem less and less important.

Then a reason quite independent of Dorothea arose, making a visit to Middlemarch seem almost a charitable duty. Will had taken an unselfish interest in a proposed settlement organized on a new plan in the Far West. The need to finance this worthy project led him to debate whether he might make honorable use of his claim on Bulstrode: could he urge the banker to devote the money once offered to him personally to carrying out a scheme likely to benefit many people? Will found the question very doubtful. His reluctance to enter any relationship with the banker again might have made him dismiss it quickly, had he not imagined that visiting Middlemarch would help him reach a sounder and more dependable judgment.

This was the purpose he offered himself as a reason for coming. He intended to confide in Lydgate and discuss the financial question with him. During the few evenings of his stay he would enjoy plenty of music and teasing conversation with beautiful Rosamond, while also visiting his friends at Lowick Parsonage. If the Parsonage happened to stand near the Manor, that was hardly his fault. Before leaving Middlemarch, pride had made him neglect the Farebrothers rather than risk the charge of indirectly seeking meetings with Dorothea. But hunger tames us, and Will had grown very hungry for the sight of a certain figure and the sound of a certain voice. Nothing had satisfied that hunger—not opera, not conversations with passionate politicians, not the flattering reception, in obscure quarters, of his first attempts at leading articles.

So he arrived confidently expecting almost everything in his familiar little world to remain predictable, even fearing the visit would offer no surprises. Instead he found that humdrum world in a dangerously unstable state, where even teasing and lyric feeling had become explosive. His first day there marked the most disastrous turning point of his life. The next morning, tormented by the nightmare of consequences and dreading the immediate choices before him, he saw the Riverston coach arrive while he ate breakfast. He hurried out and took a seat, escaping for at least a day the need to say or do anything in Middlemarch. Will Ladislaw was caught in one of those tangled crises more common in actual life than the shallow certainty of people’s judgments suggests. He had found Lydgate, whom he sincerely respected, in circumstances demanding complete, openly expressed sympathy. Yet the very reason it would have been better to avoid further closeness, or even contact, with Lydgate made that course seem impossible. Will’s sensitive temperament contained no neutral territory of indifference: everything that happened to him readily became a clash in some passionate drama. Discovering that Rosamond had made her happiness dependent on him in any degree was therefore a difficulty his angry outburst had enormously increased. He hated his cruelty, yet feared showing how fully he regretted it. He must see her again; their friendship could not simply end. Her unhappiness possessed a power he dreaded. Meanwhile the life ahead promised no more pleasure than if his limbs had been cut off and he were beginning again on crutches. During the night he had considered taking the coach to London instead of Riverston, leaving Lydgate a note with some improvised explanation. But strong ties resisted that sudden escape. The blight on his happiness in thinking of Dorothea, the destruction of the chief hope that had survived even the acknowledged need to renounce her, was too recent a misery to accept. He could not go straight into a distance that meant despair as well.

He therefore did nothing more decisive than take the Riverston coach. It brought him back before dark, resolved that he must visit Lydgate that evening. The Rubicon, as we know, looked like an insignificant stream; its importance depended entirely on invisible circumstances. Will felt compelled to cross his own little boundary ditch. Beyond it he saw no empire, only unhappy servitude.

Yet even in ordinary life we sometimes witness a noble nature’s power to save, the divine force of rescue in an act of fellowship that masters the self. Had Dorothea not walked to Rosamond after her night of anguish, she might perhaps have earned a greater reputation for discretion. But the three people gathered at Lydgate’s hearth at half past seven that evening would certainly have been worse off.

Rosamond was prepared for Will’s visit and greeted him with listless coolness. Lydgate attributed it to nervous exhaustion, never imagining any connection with Will. When she sat silently over a piece of work, he innocently made an indirect apology for her by asking her to lean back and rest. Will miserably played the friend greeting Rosamond for the first time, while his thoughts dwelt on what she had felt since yesterday’s scene. That scene still seemed to enclose them inexorably, like the painful vision of a madness shared by two people. Nothing happened to call Lydgate from the room. But when Rosamond poured tea and Will approached to collect it, she slipped a tiny folded paper into his saucer. He noticed and quickly secured it. Walking back to his inn, however, he felt no eagerness to open it. Whatever she had written would probably deepen the evening’s painful impressions. Still, by his bedside candle he unfolded it and read these few words in her neat, flowing hand:

“I have told Mrs. Casaubon. She no longer misunderstands you. I told her because she came to see me and was very kind. You have nothing to reproach me with now. I shall not have changed anything for you.”

The words did not bring unmixed happiness. As Will’s excited imagination dwelt on them, his cheeks and ears burned at the thought of what had passed between Dorothea and Rosamond. He could not know how far Dorothea might still feel her dignity injured by receiving an explanation of his conduct. Perhaps an altered association with him would remain in her mind, making an irreparable difference, a permanent flaw. His active imagination worked him into an uncertainty scarcely easier than that of a man who has escaped a wreck at night and stands on unfamiliar ground in darkness. Until that miserable yesterday—apart from one vexing moment long before in the same room and company—all their thoughts and visions of each other had belonged to a separate world. There sunshine fell on tall white lilies, no evil hid, and no other soul entered. But now—would Dorothea meet him in that world again?

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXIII
paragraphs:
“And now good-morrow to our waking souls
Which watch not one another out of fear;
For love all love of other sights controls,
And makes one little room, an everywhere.”
—DR. DONNE.

By the second morning after her visit to Rosamond, Dorothea had slept soundly for two nights. Every trace of exhaustion was gone; instead she felt an excess of strength, more than she could gather into any useful occupation. The previous day she had taken long walks beyond the grounds and visited the Parsonage twice. She never told anyone in her life why she spent that day so unprofitably. This morning she was rather cross with herself for such childish restlessness. Today would be different. What needed doing in the village? Oh dear, nothing. Everyone was well supplied with flannel and in good health; nobody’s pig had died. It was Saturday morning, when doors and doorsteps were being scrubbed everywhere, and there was no point in visiting the school. But she was trying to understand several subjects more clearly and decided to apply herself vigorously to the most serious. In the library she sat before her own small stack of books on political economy and related matters. From these she hoped to discover how best to spend money without harming her neighbors—or, which amounted to the same thing, how to do them the most good. Surely such a weighty subject, if she could grasp it, would steady her mind. Unfortunately, her mind slid off it for an entire hour. At the end she was reading sentences twice, intensely conscious of many things, but of nothing in the text. Hopeless. Should she order the carriage and visit Tipton? No: for some reason she preferred to remain at Lowick. Yet her wandering mind must be disciplined; there was an art to self-control. She paced round the brown library, considering how to catch her straying thoughts. Perhaps a simple task would work best, something requiring dogged application. What about the geography of Asia Minor, where Mr. Casaubon had often rebuked her carelessness? She went to the map cabinet and unrolled a map. This morning she could establish once and for all that Paphlagonia was not on the Levantine coast, and locate her complete ignorance of the Chalybes firmly on the shores of the Euxine. A map was an excellent object of study when your thoughts wanted to go elsewhere: its names could turn into a chant through repetition. Dorothea worked earnestly, bending over the map and speaking the names aloud in a quiet voice that often fell into rhythm. After all her profound experience, she looked amusingly girlish, nodding, counting names on her fingers, pursing her lips a little, and occasionally stopping to hold her face between her hands and say, “Oh dear! Oh dear!”
There was no more reason for this to stop than for a merry-go-round to stop turning. At last, however, the door opened and Miss Noble was announced.

Dorothea warmly welcomed the little old lady, whose bonnet scarcely reached her shoulder. But while her hand was clasped, Miss Noble made many of her beaver-like sounds, as though she had something difficult to say.
“Please sit down,” Dorothea said, moving a chair forward. “Is there something I’m needed for? I’d be so glad to help.”

“I won’t stay,” Miss Noble answered, putting a hand into her little basket and nervously holding something inside it. “I’ve left a friend in the churchyard.” She relapsed into wordless sounds, unconsciously drawing out the object she was fingering. It was the tortoiseshell lozenge box. Dorothea felt her cheeks grow warm.
“Mr. Ladislaw,” the timid little woman continued. “He’s afraid he has offended you. He asked me to find out whether you would see him for a few minutes.”

Dorothea did not answer immediately. She was thinking that she could not receive him in this library, where her husband’s prohibition seemed still to dwell. She glanced towards the window. Could she meet him outside in the grounds? The sky was heavy, and the trees had begun trembling as though a storm were coming. Besides, she recoiled from going out to him.
“Please see him, Mrs. Casaubon,” Miss Noble pleaded. “Otherwise I must go back and say no, and that will hurt him.”
“Yes, I’ll see him,” Dorothea said. “Please ask him to come in.”

What else could she do? At that moment she longed for nothing except to see Will. The possibility had insistently thrust itself between her and every other object. Yet her excitement throbbed like alarm; she felt she was committing some daring act of defiance for his sake.

When the little lady had trotted off on her errand, Dorothea stood in the middle of the library, clasped hands hanging before her. She made no attempt to arrange herself in a pose of dignified indifference. Her own body was what she noticed least. She thought of what might be in Will’s mind and of the harsh feelings others held towards him. How could duty require her to be harsh? Resistance to unjust criticism had been mingled with her feelings for him from the beginning, and now, as her heart recovered from anguish, it was stronger than ever. “If I love him too much, it’s because he’s been treated so badly.” An inward voice was saying this to an imagined audience in the library when the door opened and Will stood before her.

She did not move. He approached with more uncertainty and shyness than she had ever seen in his face. His doubts made him fear that a look or word might condemn him to a new distance from her; Dorothea feared her _own_ emotion. She looked as if a spell held her motionless, unable to unclasp her hands, while a deep, solemn longing remained imprisoned in her eyes. Seeing no hand extended in the usual greeting, Will stopped a yard away and said awkwardly, “Thank you so much for agreeing to see me.”

“I wanted to see you,” Dorothea replied, unable to find any other words. It never occurred to her that they might sit down. Will could draw little comfort from this queenly manner of receiving him, but he continued with what he had resolved to say.

“I’m afraid you think it foolish, perhaps wrong, that I’ve returned so soon. My impatience has been punished. You know—everyone knows now—a painful story about my family. I knew it before I left. I always meant to tell you, if—if we ever met again.”
Dorothea stirred slightly and unclasped her hands, only to fold them over one another again.

“But now it’s common gossip,” Will continued. “I wanted you to know that something connected with it, something that happened before I left, helped bring me back. At least I thought it justified coming. I wanted to persuade Bulstrode to use some money for a public benefit, money he had considered giving me. Perhaps it counts in his favor that he privately offered compensation for an old wrong. He offered me a good income to make amends. But I suppose you’ve heard the unpleasant story?”

Will looked uncertainly at Dorothea, though his manner was regaining some of the defiant courage with which he always considered this fact of his life. “You understand how entirely painful it must be to me,” he added.
“Yes, yes, I understand,” Dorothea said quickly.

“I refused an income from that source. I was sure you couldn’t respect me if I accepted,” Will said. Why should he hesitate to say such things now? She knew he had declared his love for her. “I felt that—” Nevertheless, he stopped.
“You did exactly what I would have expected of you,” Dorothea said, her face brightening, her head lifting a little on its beautiful stem.

“I never believed the circumstances of my birth would prejudice you against me, although they certainly would other people,” Will said, tossing his head back in his old manner and looking into her eyes with a grave appeal.

“If it were a new hardship, it would give me another reason to stand by you,” Dorothea answered fervently. “Nothing could have changed my feelings except—” Her swelling heart made speech difficult. With a great effort she continued in a low, shaking voice, “except believing you were different, less good than I thought.”

“You’re bound to think me better than I am in everything except one thing,” Will said, yielding to his feelings now that hers were so evident. “I mean my faithfulness to you. When I thought you doubted that, nothing else mattered. I believed everything was over for me. There was nothing left to work towards, only things to bear.”
“I don’t doubt you anymore,” Dorothea said, offering her hand. An uncertain fear for him urged on her inexpressible tenderness.

He took the hand and pressed it to his lips with something like a sob. Yet with his hat and gloves still in his other hand, he might have posed for a Royalist’s portrait. Letting go was difficult. Dorothea withdrew her hand in distressing confusion and turned her gaze and steps away.
“Look how dark the clouds are, and how the trees are blowing,” she said, going towards the window with only a vague awareness of her own words and movements.

Will followed a little behind and leaned on the tall back of a leather chair. Now he ventured to lay his hat and gloves there, releasing himself from the intolerable prison of formality to which he had been condemned for the first time in Dorothea’s presence. It must be admitted that, leaning on that chair, he felt very happy. He was no longer greatly afraid of anything she might feel.

They stood silently, looking not at one another but at the evergreens, whose tossing branches exposed pale undersides of leaves against the darkening sky. Will had never welcomed an approaching storm so much: it freed him from the need to leave. Leaves and small branches flew about; thunder drew closer. The light grew increasingly somber until a lightning flash startled them into looking at each other and smiling. Dorothea began to express what she had been thinking.

“You were wrong to say there would have been nothing to work for. Even if we lost our own greatest happiness, other people’s good would remain, and that’s worth working for. Some people can be happy. When I was most miserable, I seemed to understand that more clearly than ever. I hardly know how I could have borne the pain if that feeling hadn’t given me strength.”
“You’ve never known the misery I felt,” Will said, “the misery of knowing you must despise me.”
“But I felt something worse. It was worse to think badly—” Dorothea began impetuously, then stopped.
Will flushed. He felt that behind everything she said was the vision of a fate that kept them apart. After a moment’s silence he spoke passionately—
“At least we can have the comfort of speaking honestly. Since I must leave, since we must always be separated, you can think of me as someone at the edge of the grave.”

As he spoke, a brilliant flash of lightning illuminated each of them for the other. Its light seemed the terror of hopeless love. Dorothea instantly sprang away from the window. Will followed and seized her hand in an involuntary movement. They stood holding hands like two children, watching the storm as thunder cracked and rolled tremendously overhead and rain began pouring down. Then they turned towards each other, his last words still alive in their faces, and neither let go.

“There’s no hope for me,” Will said. “Even if you loved me as much as I love you, even if I meant everything to you, I’ll probably always be very poor. Judged soberly, I can count on nothing but a life of slow struggle. We can never belong to each other. Perhaps it was wrong of me to ask you for a word. I meant to leave in silence, but I haven’t been able to carry out my intention.”
“Don’t regret it,” Dorothea said in her clear, tender voice. “I’d rather share all the pain of our parting.”
Her lips trembled, and his did too. No one ever knew whose lips moved first towards the other’s. They kissed, trembling, and then drew apart.
Rain lashed the windows as though an angry spirit possessed it, with the great rush of wind behind. It was one of those moments that make both busy people and idle ones pause in awe.

Dorothea sat on the nearest seat, a long, low ottoman in the center of the room. Folding her hands on her lap, she looked out at the dreary world. Will stood watching her for a moment, then sat beside her and laid his hand on hers. It turned upwards to be held. They stayed like that, without looking at each other, until the rain eased and fell quietly. Both were full of thoughts neither could begin to speak.
When the rain grew quiet, Dorothea turned to look at Will. With a passionate cry, as though some instrument of torture threatened him, he sprang up. “It’s impossible!”
He returned to the chair back and leaned against it, appearing to struggle with his anger while she watched him sadly.
“It’s as final as murder or any other horror that separates people,” he burst out again. “Worse, more unbearable—to have our lives crippled by petty accidents.”
“No, don’t say that. Your life doesn’t have to be crippled,” Dorothea said gently.

“Yes, it does,” Will answered angrily. “It’s cruel to talk like that, as though there were any comfort. Perhaps you can see beyond the misery; I can’t. Speaking like that in the face of the facts is unkind. It throws my love back at me as though it were nothing. We can never marry.”
“Someday—we might,” Dorothea said, her voice trembling.

“When?” Will asked bitterly. “What’s the use of relying on my success? Whether I’ll ever earn more than a decent living is pure chance, unless I sell myself as a mere pen and mouthpiece. I can see that clearly. I couldn’t offer myself to any woman, even one with no luxuries to give up.”

Silence followed. Dorothea’s heart held something she longed to say, but the words were too difficult. They possessed her entirely; for the moment there was no inner debate. It was terribly hard to be unable to speak them. Will stared angrily out of the window. If only he would look at her, if only he had not left her side, she thought it would be easier. At last he turned, still leaning on the chair, and reached automatically for his hat. With a kind of exasperation he said, “Goodbye.”

“Oh, I can’t bear it! My heart will break!” Dorothea sprang up. The force of her young passion swept away every obstacle that had kept her silent, great tears welling and falling at once. “I don’t care about poverty. I hate my wealth.”

In an instant Will was beside her, his arms around her. But she drew her head back and gently held his away so that she could go on. Her large, tear-filled eyes looked simply into his as she said, sobbing like a child, “We could live perfectly well on my own money. It’s too much—seven hundred a year. I need so little—no new clothes—and I’ll learn what everything costs.”

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXIV
paragraphs:
“Though it be songe of old and yonge,
That I sholde be to blame,
Theyrs be the charge, that spoke so large
In hurtynge of my name.”
—_The Not-Browne Mayde_.

The Lords had just rejected the Reform Bill. That explains why Mr. Cadwallader was walking down the sloping lawn near Freshitt Hall’s great conservatory, the “Times” held behind his back, discussing the country’s prospects with Sir James Chettam in the detached spirit of a trout fisherman. Mrs. Cadwallader, the Dowager Lady Chettam, and Celia alternated between sitting in garden chairs and walking to meet little Arthur as he was pulled about in his chariot. As befitted this infant Buddha, his sacred umbrella sheltered him beneath a handsome silk fringe.

The ladies discussed politics too, though less continuously. Mrs. Cadwallader held strong views on the proposed creation of peers. Her cousin had assured her that Truberry had changed sides entirely at his wife’s prompting. From the first mention of Reform, Mrs. Truberry had smelled peerages in the air; she would sell her soul to outrank her younger sister, who had married a baronet. Lady Chettam considered this conduct deeply improper and recalled that Mrs. Truberry’s mother had been a Miss Walsingham of Melspring. Celia admitted that being “Lady” was nicer than being “Mrs.” and said Dodo never cared about precedence provided she got her own way. Mrs. Cadwallader thought taking precedence gave little satisfaction when everyone around knew you had not a drop of good blood. Celia stopped to look at Arthur again. “Still, it would be very nice if he were a Viscount—and his lordship’s little tooth coming through! He could have been, if James had been an Earl.”
“My dear Celia,” the Dowager said, “James’s title is worth much more than any newly created earldom. I never wanted his father to be anything but Sir James.”
“Oh, I only meant Arthur’s little tooth,” Celia said contentedly. “But look, here comes my uncle.”

She hurried to meet him while Sir James and Mr. Cadwallader joined the ladies. Slipping her arm through her uncle’s, she received a pat on the hand and a rather mournful “Well, my dear!” As they drew near, everyone could see Mr. Brooke looked dejected, though politics fully accounted for that. He shook hands all round, saying only, “Well, you’re all here, you know.” The Rector said with a laugh—
“Don’t take the Bill’s rejection so badly, Brooke. All the country’s riffraff are on your side.”

“The Bill, eh? Ah!” Mr. Brooke replied with mild distraction. “Rejected, you know, eh? The Lords are going too far, though. They’ll have to stop. Sad news, you know. I mean here at home—sad news. But you mustn’t blame me, Chettam.”
“What’s happened?” Sir James asked. “Surely not another gamekeeper shot? That’s what I’d expect when a fellow like Trapping Bass gets off so lightly.”

“A gamekeeper? No. Let’s go inside; I can tell you there,” said Mr. Brooke, nodding to include the Cadwalladers in his confidence. As they entered, he continued, “As for poachers like Trapping Bass, Chettam, when you become a magistrate, you won’t find committing them so easy. Severity is all very well, but it’s much easier when somebody else does it for you. You’ve a soft spot yourself, you know. You’re no Draco or Jeffreys, that sort of thing.”

Mr. Brooke was visibly agitated and nervous. When he had painful news to deliver, his usual method was to introduce it among a collection of disconnected details, as though mixing a medicine with other ingredients might soften its taste. He continued talking to Sir James about the poachers until everyone was seated. Then Mrs. Cadwallader, impatient with all this rambling, said—
“I’m dying to hear this sad news. We’ve established that the gamekeeper hasn’t been shot. What is it, then?”

“Well, it’s a very distressing matter, you know,” Mr. Brooke said. “I’m glad you and the Rector are here. A family matter, but you’ll help us bear it, Cadwallader. I must break it to you, my dear.” He looked at Celia. “You haven’t any idea what it is. And Chettam, it will upset you dreadfully, but you see, you’ve been no more able to prevent it than I have. There’s something strange about things: they come round, you know.”
“It must concern Dodo,” said Celia, accustomed to considering her sister the dangerous component of the family machinery. She had settled on a low stool against her husband’s knee.
“For God’s sake, tell us what it is!” Sir James exclaimed.
“Well, Chettam, I couldn’t prevent Casaubon’s will. It was the kind of will that made everything worse.”
“Precisely,” Sir James said impatiently. “But _what_ has become worse?”

“Dorothea means to marry again, you know,” Mr. Brooke said, nodding towards Celia. She instantly looked up at her husband in alarm and laid her hand on his knee. Sir James was nearly white with anger, but said nothing.
“Heaven have mercy!” cried Mrs. Cadwallader. “Not _young_ Ladislaw?”
Mr. Brooke nodded. “Yes, Ladislaw.” Then he prudently fell silent.

“There, Humphrey!” Mrs. Cadwallader waved an arm towards her husband. “Next time you’ll admit I have some foresight. Or rather, you’ll contradict me and remain as blind as ever. _You_ thought the young gentleman had left the country.”
“He might have done and still returned,” the Rector said calmly.
“When did you find out?” Sir James asked. He disliked hearing anyone else speak, though speech was difficult for him too.

“Yesterday,” Mr. Brooke answered meekly. “I went to Lowick. Dorothea sent for me, you know. It happened quite suddenly. Neither of them imagined it two days ago, not the slightest idea. Things are singular. But Dorothea is absolutely determined. Opposition is useless. I argued strongly. I did my duty, Chettam. But she’s free to do as she chooses.”
“I ought to have challenged him and shot him a year ago,” Sir James said, not out of bloodthirstiness but from a need for something forceful to say.
“Really, James, that would have been most unpleasant,” Celia replied.
“Be reasonable, Chettam. Try to look at it calmly,” Mr. Cadwallader said, distressed to see his good-natured friend so consumed by anger.

“That’s not easy for a man with any dignity or sense of right when it happens in his own family,” Sir James answered, still pale with indignation. “It’s scandalous. Had Ladislaw possessed a spark of honor, he would have left the country immediately and never shown his face here again. But I’m not surprised. The day after Casaubon’s funeral I said what needed doing. Nobody listened.”

“You wanted the impossible, Chettam,” Mr. Brooke said. “You wanted him shipped away. I told you we couldn’t do whatever we liked with Ladislaw. He had his own ideas. A remarkable fellow—I always said he was remarkable.”

“Yes,” Sir James retorted, unable to contain himself, “it’s rather unfortunate you thought so highly of him. We owe his residence here to that opinion. We owe it the spectacle of a woman like Dorothea lowering herself by marrying him.” He paused between clauses, the words coming with difficulty. “A man singled out in her husband’s will, whom delicacy should have prevented her from ever seeing again. A man who draws her below her proper rank—into poverty—who is mean enough to accept the sacrifice—whose position has always been objectionable—whose origins are bad—and who, _I believe_, has little principle and a frivolous character. That is my opinion.” He finished emphatically, turned aside, and crossed his leg.

“I explained it all to her,” Mr. Brooke said apologetically. “The poverty, I mean, and giving up her position. I said, ‘My dear, you don’t understand living on seven hundred a year, without a carriage and that sort of thing, among people who don’t know who you are.’ I put it strongly. But you should talk to her yourself. The truth is, she dislikes Casaubon’s property. You’ll hear what she says.”
“No, excuse me, I won’t,” Sir James answered more coolly. “I can’t bear to see her again. It’s too painful. That a woman like Dorothea should do wrong hurts me too deeply.”

“Be fair, Chettam,” said the easygoing, full-lipped Rector, who disliked this unnecessary distress. “Mrs. Casaubon may be imprudent. She’s giving up a fortune for a man, and we men think so poorly of one another that we can hardly call a woman wise for doing that. But I don’t think you should condemn it as morally wrong in the strict sense.”
“Yes, I do,” Sir James replied. “I consider Dorothea wrong to marry Ladislaw.”

“My dear fellow, we’re rather inclined to call things wrong when they’re unpleasant for us,” the Rector said quietly. Like many men who take life easily, he could occasionally deliver a home truth to those who considered their bad temper virtuous. Sir James took out his handkerchief and began biting its corner.
“It is very dreadful of Dodo, though,” Celia said, hoping to justify her husband. “She said she would _never_ marry again, not anyone.”
“I heard her say so myself,” Lady Chettam declared majestically, as though offering royal testimony.

“Oh, usually there’s an unspoken exception,” Mrs. Cadwallader said. “I only wonder that any of you are surprised. You did nothing to stop it. If you’d brought Lord Triton here to court her with his philanthropy, he might have carried her off before the year ended. Nothing else could have made things safe. Mr. Casaubon prepared it all beautifully. He made himself disagreeable—or God chose to make him so—and then dared her to contradict him. Put that sort of high price tag on any rubbish and you make it tempting.”

“I don’t know what you mean by wrong, Cadwallader,” Sir James said, still stung, turning his chair towards the Rector. “He isn’t a man we can welcome into the family. At least, I speak for myself,” he continued, carefully avoiding Mr. Brooke’s eyes. “Others may enjoy his company too much to care whether it’s proper.”

“Well, Chettam,” Mr. Brooke answered amiably, cradling his leg, “I can’t turn my back on Dorothea. Up to a point I must be a father to her. I said, ‘My dear, I won’t refuse to give you away.’ I’d spoken firmly beforehand. But I can break the entail, you know. It would cost money and involve trouble, but I can do it.”

He nodded at Sir James, feeling he had both demonstrated his own resolve and soothed the justified part of the baronet’s anger. His defense was more ingenious than he knew: he had touched a motive Sir James was ashamed of. Much of Sir James’s feeling about the marriage came from understandable prejudice or even reasonable judgment, and much from a jealous aversion scarcely weaker towards Ladislaw than it had been towards Casaubon. He was convinced the marriage would ruin Dorothea. But through those feelings ran a vein he was too honorable and good to welcome even in private. The prospect of uniting Tipton and Freshitt, two estates delightfully enclosed within one boundary, undeniably flattered his hopes for his son and heir. When Mr. Brooke nodded towards that motive, Sir James suddenly grew embarrassed. His throat tightened; he even blushed. The first burst of anger had made him unusually eloquent, but Mr. Brooke’s attempt to placate him blocked his tongue more effectively than Mr. Cadwallader’s sharp observation.

Celia was glad to have a chance to speak after her uncle’s mention of the wedding ceremony. With no more apparent eagerness than if the subject were a dinner invitation, she asked, “Do you mean Dodo is getting married immediately, uncle?”
“In three weeks,” Mr. Brooke said helplessly. “I can do nothing to prevent it, Cadwallader,” he added, turning for support to the Rector, who replied—

“_I_ wouldn’t make a fuss. If she wants to be poor, that’s her business. Nobody would object if she married him for being rich. Plenty of clergy with livings have less than they will. Take Elinor,” this provoking husband continued. “She upset her friends by marrying me. I had barely a thousand a year; I was a lout; nobody saw anything in me; my shoes were cut wrong; all the men wondered how any woman could like me. Upon my word, until I hear worse of Ladislaw, I must defend him.”

“Humphrey, that’s sophistry, and you know it,” his wife said. “Everything is the same to you, from beginning to end. As if you hadn’t been a Cadwallader! Does anyone imagine I would have accepted such a monster under any other name?”
“And a clergyman as well,” Lady Chettam added approvingly. “Nobody can say Elinor married beneath her rank. It’s hard to say what Mr. Ladislaw is, isn’t it, James?”
Sir James answered with a small grunt, less respectfully than he generally addressed his mother. Celia looked up at him like a thoughtful kitten.

“You must admit his blood is a dreadful mixture!” Mrs. Cadwallader said. “The Casaubon cuttlefish fluid to start with, then a rebellious Polish fiddler—or was it a dancing master?—and then an old clo—”
“Nonsense, Elinor,” the Rector interrupted, getting up. “We should be going.”
