“Still, he’s a handsome young sprig,” Mrs. Cadwallader said, rising too and wishing to make amends. “Like the fine old Crichley portraits before the idiots appeared in the family.”
“I’ll come with you,” said Mr. Brooke, springing up eagerly. “You must all dine with me tomorrow, you know. Won’t you, Celia, my dear?”
“You will, James, won’t you?” Celia asked, taking his hand.
“Of course, if you wish,” Sir James said, tugging his waistcoat down, though he could not yet compose a pleasant expression. “Provided we aren’t to meet anyone else.”
“No, no, no,” Mr. Brooke replied, understanding. “Dorothea wouldn’t come unless you’d visited her first.”
Once she and Sir James were alone, Celia asked, “Would you mind if I took the carriage to Lowick, James?”
“What, now? Immediately?” he asked in some surprise.
“Yes. It’s very important,” Celia said.
“Remember, Celia, I can’t see her,” Sir James warned.
“Not even if she gave up the marriage?”
“What’s the use of saying that? Anyway, I’m going to the stables. I’ll tell Briggs to bring the carriage.”

Celia thought there was plenty of use, if not in saying it, at least in going to Lowick to influence Dorothea. Throughout their girlhood she had believed a well-placed word could affect her sister, opening a little window for the daylight of her own understanding among the strangely colored lamps through which Dodo habitually saw. Now, as a wife and mother, Celia naturally felt even better qualified to advise her childless sister. Who could understand Dodo as well as she did, or love her so tenderly?

Dorothea was occupied in her boudoir. Seeing her sister so soon after the disclosure of her intended marriage filled her with a warm pleasure. She had pictured her friends’ disgust, even exaggerated it, and had feared that Celia might be kept away from her.
“Oh, Kitty, I’m so glad to see you!” Dorothea laid her hands on Celia’s shoulders and smiled radiantly at her. “I almost thought you wouldn’t come.”
“I left Arthur behind because I was in a hurry,” Celia said. They sat facing each other on two little chairs, their knees touching.

“You know, Dodo, it’s very bad,” Celia said in her calm, throaty voice, looking as pretty and unruffled as possible. “You’ve disappointed us all terribly. And I can’t believe it really _will_ happen. You can’t possibly live like that. Then there are all your plans! You can’t have considered them. James would have taken any trouble for you, and you could have spent your whole life doing whatever you liked.”
“Quite the opposite, dear,” Dorothea replied. “I’ve never been able to do what I liked. I haven’t carried out a single plan.”

“That’s because you always wanted things that wouldn’t work. Other plans would have come. And how _can_ you marry Mr. Ladislaw, when none of us ever imagined you _could_? James is terribly shocked. Besides, it’s so unlike everything you’ve always been. You insisted on Mr. Casaubon because his soul was so great and he was so old and gloomy and learned. Now you mean to marry Mr. Ladislaw, who hasn’t an estate or anything. I suppose you simply have to make yourself uncomfortable somehow.”
Dorothea laughed.
“It is serious, Dodo,” Celia said more solemnly. “How will you manage? You’ll go away among strange people. I’ll never see you, and you won’t care about little Arthur. I thought you always would—”
Tears, rare for Celia, filled her eyes, and the corners of her mouth trembled.
“Dear Celia,” Dorothea said with tender seriousness, “if you never see me, it won’t be my fault.”

“Yes, it will,” Celia answered, her small features still touchingly distorted. “How can I visit you or have you here when James can’t bear it? It’s because he thinks it’s wrong. He thinks you’re behaving so badly, Dodo. But you always have been wrong; I just can’t help loving you. And nobody knows where you’ll live. Where can you go?”
“I’m moving to London,” Dorothea answered.
“How can you bear living in a street forever? And you’ll be so poor. I could give you half my things, but how can I if I never see you?”
“Bless you, Kitty,” Dorothea said warmly and gently. “Don’t worry. Perhaps James will forgive me eventually.”

“But it would be much better not to marry,” Celia said, drying her eyes and returning to her argument. “Then nothing would be uncomfortable, and you wouldn’t do something nobody thought you capable of. James always said you ought to be a queen. This is nothing like being a queen. You know how many mistakes you’ve made, Dodo; this is another. Nobody thinks Mr. Ladislaw is a suitable husband. And you _said_ you’d never marry again.”

“It’s quite true I could be wiser, Celia,” Dorothea replied, “and if I had been better, I might have done something better. But this is what I’m going to do. I’ve promised to marry Mr. Ladislaw, and I will marry him.”
Celia had long since learned to recognize that note in Dorothea’s voice. She fell silent briefly, then spoke as though all argument were finished. “Does he love you very much, Dodo?”
“I hope he does. I love him very much.”
“That’s nice,” Celia said comfortably. “Only I’d rather you had a husband like James, with a house nearby that I could drive to.”
Dorothea smiled. Celia grew thoughtful, then said, “I can’t imagine how it happened.” She thought hearing the story would be pleasant.
“I dare say you can’t,” Dorothea replied, pinching her sister’s chin. “If you knew how it happened, it wouldn’t seem so extraordinary.”
“Couldn’t you tell me?” Celia asked, settling her arms comfortably.
“No, dear. You’d have to feel what I felt, or you could never understand.”

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXV
paragraphs:
“Then went the jury out whose names were Mr. Blindman, Mr. No-good, Mr.
Malice, Mr. Love-lust, Mr. Live-loose, Mr. Heady, Mr. High-mind, Mr.
Enmity, Mr. Liar, Mr. Cruelty, Mr. Hate-light, Mr. Implacable, who
every one gave in his private verdict against him among themselves, and
afterwards unanimously concluded to bring him in guilty before the
judge. And first among themselves, Mr. Blindman, the foreman, said, I
see clearly that this man is a heretic. Then said Mr. No-good, Away
with such a fellow from the earth! Ay, said Mr. Malice, for I hate the
very look of him. Then said Mr. Love-lust, I could never endure him.
Nor I, said Mr. Live-loose; for he would be always condemning my way.
Hang him, hang him, said Mr. Heady. A sorry scrub, said Mr. High-mind.
My heart riseth against him, said Mr. Enmity. He is a rogue, said Mr.
Liar. Hanging is too good for him, said Mr. Cruelty. Let us despatch
him out of the way said Mr. Hate-light. Then said Mr. Implacable, Might
I have all the world given me, I could not be reconciled to him;
therefore let us forthwith bring him in guilty of death.”—_Pilgrim’s
Progress_.

When the immortal Bunyan pictures the persecuting passions delivering their guilty verdict, who feels pity for Faithful? To know oneself innocent before a condemning crowd, to be certain that only the good in us is being denounced, is a rare and blessed fate denied even to some of the greatest men. The truly pitiable man cannot call himself a martyr, even if he persuades himself that those stoning him are merely ugly passions in human form. He knows they stone him not for declaring what is right, but for failing to be the man he claimed to be.

This awareness was withering Bulstrode as he prepared to leave Middlemarch and end his wounded life in that melancholy refuge, the indifference of unfamiliar faces. His wife’s dutiful, merciful faithfulness had relieved one terror. Yet her presence remained a court before which he shrank from confessing and longed for someone to plead his case. His evasive arguments with himself over Raffles’s death had preserved his conception of the all-knowing Being to whom he prayed. But terror prevented him from exposing those arguments to judgment in a full confession to his wife. The acts he had washed and diluted in inward reasoning and motives, for which invisible forgiveness seemed comparatively easy to obtain—what would she call them? He could not bear the thought that, even silently, she might call them Murder. Her uncertainty sheltered him. Knowing she could not yet feel justified in pronouncing that worst condemnation gave him strength to face her. Someday, perhaps when he was dying, he would tell her everything. In that deepening shadow, as she held his hand in the gathering darkness, perhaps she could listen without shrinking from his touch. Perhaps. But concealment had been his lifelong habit, and the impulse to confess was powerless against the fear of deeper humiliation.

He treated his wife with anxious tenderness, not simply because he dreaded a harsh judgment from her, but because her suffering caused him profound distress. She had sent their daughters to a boarding school on the coast to conceal the crisis from them as much as possible. Their absence freed her from the intolerable need to explain her grief or watch their frightened bewilderment. She could now live openly with the sorrow that daily streaked her hair with white and left her eyelids heavy.

“Tell me anything you would like me to do, Harriet,” Bulstrode had said. “I mean about the arrangements for our property. I intend to keep the land I own around here and leave it to you as a secure provision. If you have any wishes in these matters, please don’t hide them.”
A few days later, after returning from a visit to her brother’s house, she began speaking to her husband about a subject she had been considering for some time.

“I _would_ like to help my brother’s family, Nicholas. I think we owe Rosamond and her husband some amends. Walter says Mr. Lydgate will have to leave town. His practice is worth almost nothing, and they have very little to set themselves up elsewhere. I’d gladly give up something of our own to make amends to my poor brother’s family.”

Mrs. Bulstrode did not want to approach the facts more closely than “make amends”; she knew her husband must understand. For a particular reason unknown to her, her suggestion made him wince. He hesitated before replying—

“We can’t carry out your wish in that way, my dear. Mr. Lydgate has effectively refused any further help from me. He has repaid the thousand pounds I lent him. Mrs. Casaubon advanced him the money for that purpose. This is his letter.”

The letter seemed to wound Mrs. Bulstrode deeply. The reference to Mrs. Casaubon’s loan reflected the public feeling that naturally everyone would avoid any connection with her husband. She remained silent for some time. Tears fell one after another, her chin shaking as she wiped them away. Sitting opposite, Bulstrode ached to see that grief-worn face, so bright and blooming only two months before. It had aged to accompany his own withered features in sadness. Driven to attempt some comfort, he said—

“There is another way I could help your brother’s family, Harriet, if you’re willing to take part. It would benefit you as well, I think: it would be a good arrangement for managing the land I intend you to have.”
Her expression became attentive.

“Garth once considered taking charge of Stone Court and putting your nephew Fred there. The stock would stay as it is, and instead of ordinary rent they would pay an agreed share of the profits. Combined with his work under Garth, that would give the young man a good start. Would that please you?”
“Yes, it would,” Mrs. Bulstrode answered with renewed energy. “Poor Walter is so dejected. Before leaving, I would try anything in my power to help him. We’ve always been brother and sister.”

“You must put the proposal to Garth yourself, Harriet,” Bulstrode said. He disliked saying what followed, but wanted the arrangement for reasons beyond comforting his wife. “Tell him the land is effectively yours and he need have no dealings with me. Everything can pass through Standish. I mention it because Garth resigned as my agent. I can give you a paper he drew up himself, setting out the terms. You can ask him to accept them again. I think he may agree when you propose it for your nephew’s sake.”

chapters.title: Book VIII: Sunset And Sunrise — Chapter LXXXVI
paragraphs:
“Le cœur se sature d’amour comme d’un sel divin qui le conserve; de là
l’incorruptible adhérence de ceux qui se sont aimés dès l’aube de la
vie, et la fraîcheur des vielles amours prolongées. Il existe un
embaumement d’amour. C’est de Daphnis et Chloé que sont faits Philémon
et Baucis. Cette vieillesse-là, ressemblance du soir avec
l’aurore.”—VICTOR HUGO: _L’homme qui rit_.
Hearing Caleb in the passage around teatime, Mrs. Garth opened the parlor door. “There you are, Caleb. Have you eaten dinner?” Mr. Garth’s meals often had to give way to “business.”
“Oh yes, a good dinner. Cold mutton and I forget what else. Where’s Mary?”
“I think she’s in the garden with Letty.”
“Has Fred arrived yet?”
“No. Surely you’re not going out again without tea, Caleb?” Mrs. Garth asked, seeing her distracted husband replace the hat he had just removed.
“No, no. I only want a minute with Mary.”

Mary stood in a grassy corner of the garden, where a swing hung high between two pear trees. She had tied a pink kerchief over her head, its little projecting edge shading her eyes from the low sun. She was giving Letty a splendid swing, and the child shrieked and laughed with delight.
At the sight of her father, Mary left the swing and came towards him, pushing back her pink kerchief and smiling from a distance with the spontaneous pleasure of affection.
“I was looking for you, Mary,” Mr. Garth said. “Let’s walk a little.”

She knew he had something particular to say. His eyebrows formed their touching angle, and his voice was tenderly serious, signs she had recognized since she was Letty’s age. She took his arm, and they turned along the row of nut trees.
“It will be a sadly long time before you can marry, Mary,” her father said, looking at the end of the stick in his other hand rather than at her.

“Not sadly, father. I intend to be cheerful,” Mary answered with a laugh. “I’ve been single and cheerful for more than twenty-four years. I don’t suppose it will be quite that long again.” After a pause she bent her face towards his and added more seriously, “If you’re satisfied with Fred?”
Caleb pursed his mouth and turned his head aside with an air of wisdom.
“Now, father, you praised him last Wednesday. You said he understood stock unusually well and had a good eye for things.”
“Did I indeed?” Caleb asked, rather slyly.

“Yes. I wrote it all down, with the date, _anno Domini_, everything,” Mary said. “You like accurate records. And his behavior towards you really is good, father. He respects you deeply. Nobody could have a better temper than Fred.”
“Ay, ay. You’re trying to coax me into thinking him an excellent match.”
“Really, father, no. I don’t love him because he’s an excellent match.”
“Why do you, then?”
“Oh dear, because I’ve always loved him. I’d never enjoy scolding anyone else nearly so much, and that’s certainly something to consider when choosing a husband.”

“Then your mind is quite made up, Mary?” Caleb returned to his earlier tone. “Nothing that’s happened lately has given you any different wish?” That vague phrase meant a great deal to him. “Because better late than never. A woman mustn’t force her heart. That won’t do a man any good.”

“My feelings are unchanged, father,” Mary said quietly. “I’ll be faithful to Fred as long as he’s faithful to me. I don’t think either of us could do without the other, or love someone else better, however much we admired them. It would change too much for us, like finding all the old places altered and everything given a different name. We’ll have a long wait, but Fred knows that.”

Caleb did not answer at once. He stopped and twisted his stick into the grassy path. Then, with feeling in his voice, he said, “Well, I have some news. How would you like Fred to live at Stone Court and manage the land?”
“How could that possibly happen, father?” Mary asked in astonishment.

“He’d manage it for his aunt Bulstrode. The poor woman has been begging and pleading with me. She wants to help the lad, and it could be an excellent chance. If he saves, he could gradually buy the stock. He has a gift for farming.”
“Oh, Fred would be so happy! It’s almost too good to believe.”

“Ah, but remember,” Caleb said, turning his head warningly, “I’d have to shoulder the responsibility and oversee everything. That will trouble your mother a little, even if she says nothing. Fred will need to be careful.”
“Perhaps it’s too much to ask, father,” Mary said, her delight checked. “We couldn’t be happy bringing you fresh trouble.”

“No, no, child. Work is my pleasure, so long as it doesn’t worry your mother. And if you and Fred marry”—his voice trembled almost imperceptibly—“he’ll be steady and economical. You have your mother’s cleverness and mine too, in a woman’s way, and you’ll keep him in order. He’ll be here before long. I wanted you to know first because I thought you might like to tell _him_ privately. Afterwards I can discuss it properly with him, and we can consider the business and the nature of things.”

“Oh, my dear, good father!” Mary cried, putting her arms around his neck. He peacefully bowed his head, pleased to receive the caress. “I wonder whether any other girl thinks her father the best man in the world!”
“Nonsense, child. You’ll think your husband better.”
“Impossible,” Mary replied, returning to her usual manner. “Husbands are an inferior class of men who need to be kept in order.”
As they approached the house with Letty, who had run to join them, Mary saw Fred at the orchard gate and went to meet him.
“What elegant clothes, you extravagant young man!” she said as he stopped and raised his hat with playful ceremony. “You aren’t learning to economize.”
“That’s unfair, Mary,” Fred protested. “Look at the edges of my cuffs! Thorough brushing is the only thing keeping me respectable. I’m saving three suits, one of them for the wedding.”
“How funny you’ll look, like a gentleman out of an old fashion plate!”
“Oh no. They’ll last two years.”
“Two years! Be sensible, Fred,” Mary said, turning to walk. “Don’t cultivate flattering expectations.”
“Why not? They’re better to live on than unflattering ones. If we can’t marry in two years, the truth will be unpleasant enough when it arrives.”
“I’ve heard of a young gentleman who once cultivated flattering expectations and came to harm through them.”

“Mary, if you have something discouraging to tell me, I’ll run away into the house to Mr. Garth. I’m depressed already. My father is so upset, home doesn’t feel like home. I can’t bear more bad news.”

“Would you call it bad news to hear that you could live at Stone Court, manage the farm, behave with remarkable prudence, and save every year until you owned all the stock and furniture? Then you could become a distinguished agricultural character, as Mr. Borthrop Trumbull puts it—rather stout, I’m afraid, with your Greek and Latin sadly weathered.”
“You’re only talking nonsense, aren’t you, Mary?” Fred asked, though he colored a little.
“My father has just told me it may happen, and he never talks nonsense,” she replied, looking up at him. As they walked he seized her hand so tightly it hurt, but she would not complain.
“Oh, I could become a tremendously good fellow then, Mary! And we could marry straightaway.”
“Not so fast, sir. How do you know I wouldn’t prefer to postpone it for years? That would give you time to misbehave, and if I found someone I liked better, I’d have an excuse to jilt you.”
“Please don’t joke, Mary,” Fred said intensely. “Tell me seriously that it’s all true and you’re happy about it, because you love me best.”
“It’s all true, Fred, and I’m happy about it because I love you best,” Mary repeated like an obedient pupil.
They lingered on the doorstep beneath the steep-roofed porch. Almost whispering, Fred said—
“When we first got engaged with the umbrella ring, Mary, you used to—”
Joy began laughing more openly in Mary’s eyes. But the disastrous Ben came racing to the door, Brownie yapping behind him. Bumping into them, he cried—
“Fred and Mary! Will you ever come inside, or can I eat your cake?”

chapters.title: Finale
paragraphs: Every boundary marks a beginning as well as an end. After keeping company with young lives for so long, who can leave them without wanting to know what happened in later years? A fragment of life, however representative, is no sample of a uniformly woven cloth. Promises may go unfulfilled, and a passionate beginning may lead to decline. Hidden abilities may finally find their opportunity; an old mistake may inspire a great recovery.

Marriage, the destination of so many stories, remains a great beginning. So it was for Adam and Eve, who honeymooned in Eden but had their first child among the wilderness’s thorns and thistles. It still begins the domestic epic: the gradual winning, or irretrievable loss, of that complete union which makes the passing years a culmination and old age a harvest of sweet, shared memories.
Some set out like the old Crusaders, gloriously equipped with hope and enthusiasm, only to break down on the road for lack of patience with each other and the world.

Everyone who has cared about Fred Vincy and Mary Garth will be glad to know that they avoided such failure and achieved lasting happiness together. Fred surprised his neighbors in several ways. In his part of the county he became quite distinguished as both a practical and theoretical farmer. His work on the “Cultivation of Green Crops and the Economy of Cattle-Feeding” brought warm congratulations at agricultural meetings. Middlemarch was less enthusiastic. Most people there credited his wife with the merits of the book, since nobody had expected Fred Vincy to write about turnips and mangel-wurzel.

Yet when Mary wrote a little book for her boys, “Stories of Great Men, taken from Plutarch,” and Gripp & Co. of Middlemarch printed and published it, everyone in town readily credited Fred. He had, they pointed out, attended the University, “where the ancients were studied,” and could have become a clergyman if he had wanted.
Thus Middlemarch demonstrated that it had never been mistaken. Nor was there any need to praise someone for writing a book, since someone else had invariably written it.

Fred also remained entirely steady in his conduct. Several years after marrying, he told Mary he owed half his happiness to Farebrother, who had checked him firmly at just the right moment. I cannot claim that optimism never misled him again. Harvests and profits from cattle sales generally fell short of his estimates. He was always apt to think he could profit by buying a horse that turned out badly, though, as Mary remarked, that was naturally the horse’s fault rather than Fred’s judgment. He still loved riding but seldom permitted himself a day’s hunting. When he did, he was remarkably willing to be mocked for timidity at fences: he seemed to see Mary and the boys sitting on the five-barred gate, or their curly heads appearing between hedge and ditch.

They had three boys. Mary was not dissatisfied to have only sons. When Fred wished for a girl like her, she laughingly replied, “That would be too much of a trial for your mother.” In her later years, with her household’s splendor diminished, Mrs. Vincy took great comfort in seeing that at least two of Fred’s boys were true Vincys and did not “feature the Garths.” Mary, however, secretly delighted in the youngest. He was very like what her father must have been as a boy in a round jacket, and showed astonishing accuracy when shooting marbles or throwing stones to knock down ripe pears.

Ben and Letty Garth became uncle and aunt before they were far into their teens. They often disputed whether nephews or nieces were preferable. Ben argued that girls were plainly less useful than boys; otherwise they would not always wear petticoats, which showed how little they were intended to do. Letty, whose arguments often came from books, angrily replied that God had made coats of skins for Adam and Eve alike. It also occurred to her that men in the East wore petticoats too. But this second argument weakened the majesty of the first and was one too many. “All the more fools they!” Ben answered contemptuously, then immediately appealed to his mother to say whether boys were not better than girls. Mrs. Garth pronounced them equally naughty, but declared boys unquestionably stronger, faster runners, and able to throw farther and more accurately. Ben was thoroughly satisfied with this oracle, disregarding the naughtiness. Letty resented it: her sense of superiority exceeded her muscular strength.

Fred never grew rich; even his optimism had not led him to expect that. But he gradually saved enough to own the stock and furniture at Stone Court, and the work Mr. Garth entrusted to him kept him comfortable through those “bad times” that are always with farmers. As a mother, Mary grew as substantial in figure as her own mother. Unlike Mrs. Garth, however, she gave the boys little formal instruction, alarming their grandmother, who feared they would never have a sound foundation in grammar and geography. Nevertheless, they proved quite advanced enough when they went to school, perhaps because nothing had pleased them more than being with their mother. Riding home on winter evenings, Fred would picture the bright fire in the paneled parlor and pity other men who could not have Mary as their wife, especially Mr. Farebrother. “He deserved you ten times more than I did,” Fred could now say generously. “Of course he did,” Mary answered, “which is why he could manage better without me. But you—I shudder to imagine what you would have become: a curate in debt for hired horses and cambric handkerchiefs!”

If someone inquired, they might discover that Fred and Mary still live at Stone Court; that climbing plants still spill their foaming blossoms over the fine stone wall into the field with its stately row of walnut trees; and that on sunny days the lovers first engaged with an umbrella ring can still be seen, white-haired and peaceful, at the open window where, in old Peter Featherstone’s time, Mary Garth was so often ordered to watch for Mr. Lydgate.

Lydgate’s hair never turned white. He died at only fifty, leaving substantial life insurance to provide for his wife and children. He had established an excellent practice, moving with the seasons between London and a Continental spa, and written a treatise on gout, a disease with considerable wealth on its side. Many paying patients trusted his skill, but he always considered himself a failure: he had not accomplished what he once intended. His acquaintances envied his charming wife, and nothing ever disturbed that opinion. Rosamond never again committed a compromising indiscretion. She merely remained mild in manner, unbending in judgment, ready to correct her husband and capable of defeating him through strategy. As the years passed, he resisted less and less, leading her to conclude that he had learned to appreciate her opinions. She, in turn, believed more firmly in his talents now that he earned a good income and, instead of the threatened cage in Bride Street, supplied one adorned with flowers and gilding, suitable for the bird of paradise she resembled. In short, Lydgate was what people call successful. But diphtheria killed him prematurely. Afterwards Rosamond married a wealthy elderly physician who treated her four children kindly. She and her daughters made a very pretty spectacle driving in their carriage. She often called her happiness “a reward,” without specifying for what. Probably she meant her patience with Tertius, whose temper never became perfect. Even at the end he occasionally let fall some bitter remark more memorable than his subsequent signs of regret. Once he called her his basil plant. Asked what he meant, he explained that basil had once flourished wonderfully on a murdered man’s brains. Rosamond met such remarks with a calm but forceful answer. Why had he chosen her, then? What a pity he had not married Mrs. Ladislaw, whom he was forever praising and setting above her. So the conversation ended to Rosamond’s advantage. Yet fairness requires us to add that she never spoke slightingly of Dorothea. She preserved an almost sacred memory of the generosity that had helped her at her life’s sharpest crisis.

Dorothea herself never dreamed of being praised above other women. She always felt she might have done something better if only she had been better and understood more. Yet she never regretted giving up rank and fortune to marry Will Ladislaw. Had she regretted it, he would have felt the deepest shame as well as sorrow. Their love bound them more strongly than any impulse that might have damaged it. Dorothea could not have lived without emotion. Now her life also contained useful, generous activity which she no longer had the uncertain labor of discovering and planning alone. Will became a passionate public man. He worked well in those days when reforms began with a youthful hope of immediate benefit, a hope much restrained in our own time. Eventually a constituency elected him to Parliament and paid his expenses. Since wrongs existed, Dorothea wanted nothing more than to see her husband fighting in their midst, with herself helping as his wife. Many who knew her thought it a pity that so substantial and exceptional a being should be absorbed into another person’s life, known within a limited circle only as a wife and mother. But nobody specified what else within her power she ought to have done. Even Sir James Chettam offered only the negative prescription that she should not have married Will Ladislaw.

His opinion, however, did not permanently divide the family. The way their unity returned was characteristic of everyone involved. Mr. Brooke could not resist the pleasure of writing to Will and Dorothea. One morning, after his pen had flowed particularly freely on the prospects for Municipal Reform, it ran on into an invitation to the Grange. Once written, the invitation could only be removed by sacrificing the entire valuable letter, an almost unthinkable loss. Throughout these months of correspondence, Mr. Brooke had repeatedly implied or assumed in conversation with Sir James that he still intended to break the entail. On the very day his pen issued that daring invitation, he went expressly to Freshitt to suggest that he felt more strongly than ever the need for this energetic precaution against any admixture of low blood in the Brookes’ heir.

But something stirring had happened at the Hall that morning. A letter had reached Celia, who wept silently while reading it. Sir James, unaccustomed to her tears, anxiously asked what was wrong. She broke into a wail unlike anything he had heard from her.

“Dorothea has a little boy, and you won’t let me visit her. I’m sure she wants to see me. She won’t know what to do with the baby; she’ll do the wrong things. And they thought she would die. It’s dreadful! Suppose it had been me and little Arthur, and Dodo had been prevented from coming! I wish you weren’t so unkind, James!”
“Good heavens, Celia!” Sir James exclaimed, deeply moved. “What do you want? I’ll do anything you wish. I’ll take you to London tomorrow if you like.” Celia did like.

Mr. Brooke arrived after this. Meeting the baronet in the grounds, he began chatting without knowing the news, which for some reason Sir James did not immediately mention. But when the entail came up as usual, he said, “My dear sir, I can’t tell you what to do, but I would leave that alone. I would keep things as they are.”
Mr. Brooke was so astonished that he did not immediately realize how relieved he was to find that no particular action was expected of him.

With Celia’s heart inclined this way, Sir James was bound to consent to reconciliation with Dorothea and her husband. When women love one another, men learn to suppress their mutual dislike. Sir James never liked Ladislaw, and Will always preferred Sir James’s company diluted with other people’s. They settled into reciprocal tolerance, fully at ease only when Dorothea and Celia were present.

It became understood that Mr. and Mrs. Ladislaw would visit the Grange at least twice a year. Gradually a small line of cousins appeared at Freshitt, delighted to play with the two cousins visiting Tipton, just as if those cousins’ ancestry had been less dubiously mixed.

Mr. Brooke lived to a good old age. His estate passed to Dorothea’s son, who could have represented Middlemarch in Parliament but declined, believing his opinions would be less easily stifled if he stayed outside.

Sir James always considered Dorothea’s second marriage a mistake. That remained the accepted story in Middlemarch, where younger people heard of a fine girl who married a sickly clergyman old enough to be her father, then, a little over a year after his death, surrendered her estate to marry his cousin: a man young enough to be his son, without property or good birth. Those who had never seen Dorothea generally concluded that she could not have been “a nice woman,” or she would never have married either man.

Certainly the decisive acts of her life were not perfectly beautiful. They were the mixed outcome of young, noble impulses struggling within an imperfect society, where great feelings often look like mistakes and great faith like delusion. No being has an inner life so powerful that outside circumstances do not profoundly shape it. A new Theresa is scarcely likely to reform convent life, any more than a new Antigone will spend her heroic devotion risking everything to bury a brother. The world in which their passionate actions took form is gone forever. Yet we insignificant people, through our daily words and deeds, are shaping the lives of many Dorotheas. Some may make a far sadder sacrifice than the Dorothea whose story we know.

Her sensitive spirit still produced fine effects, although few people saw them. Her abundant nature, like the river whose force Cyrus broke, poured itself into channels without famous names on earth. Yet her influence spread incalculably through the lives around her. The world’s growing goodness depends partly on acts that history never records. If life is less troubled for you and me than it might have been, we owe half of that to the many who lived faithfully out of sight and now rest in graves no one visits.
